title: The regulatory map
oneLiner: A Canadian bank answers to federal law, several regulators and a layered set of rules, each with different legal force.
keyPoints: **Federal bank:** A bank is federally regulated under the Bank Act, so federal law and OSFI set the core rules. Provinces still govern much of consumer protection and most other financial sectors.

**Many regulators:** The Minister of Finance, OSFI, FCAC, FINTRAC, CDIC and the Privacy Commissioner each hold a separate remit. OBSI handles external complaints. The Bank of Canada adds payments oversight. No single authority does it all.
**Legal force varies:** Acts and regulations bind. OSFI guidelines do not, but OSFI supervises against them and can direct the bank over an unsafe or unsound practice under [[s.645|Superintendent]].
**Voluntary commitments:** Codes and public commitments must be published, and breaching one can count as wrongdoing for whistleblowing purposes (s.627.66; s.979.1).

**Vendors:** [[Third-party arrangements|third-party arrangement]] fall under OSFI Guideline B-10. The bank stays accountable for personal information it sends to a processor (PIPEDA Sch. 1, cl. 4.1.3).

**Hong Kong contrast:** The HKMA is one authority for prudential supervision under the Banking Ordinance. Canada splits that work across several bodies, so one question can reach more than one regulator.

conceptMap.caption: A federally regulated bank sits at the centre. OSFI, FCAC, FINTRAC, CDIC and the Privacy Commissioner each cover a different slice of its obligations.

deepDive.heading: Federal power, provincial reach
deepDive.lede: Banking is a federal subject, but the bank also meets provincial law of general application.

visual.caption: Federal law governs the bank's charter and core business. Provincial law covers the adjacent areas.

items.label: Federal: the Bank Act
items.note: Charter, permitted business, consumer rules and OSFI powers

items.label: Provincial law
items.note: Securities, insurance, credit unions, and laws of general application

points: **Constitution Act, 1867, s.91(15):** Parliament has power over banking and the incorporation of banks, so provinces cannot charter a bank (reported; check).
**Bank Act s.13:** The Act is the charter of, and applies to, each bank.

**Bank Act s.409:** A bank may carry on only the business of banking and the business that appertains to it. That business includes financial services, financial agency, portfolio management and card issuing.
**Provincial areas:** Securities, insurance distribution, credit unions and most consumer protection beyond the Bank Act are provincial matters.
**Provincial overlay:** Laws of general application still reach the bank, such as Quebec privacy law and the contest rules in Quebec (reported; check).
deepDive.takeaway: Trace each obligation to its source: a federal statute, an OSFI expectation or a provincial law.

deepDive.heading: Who regulates what
deepDive.lede: Each regulator has a defined statutory remit, and the remits meet at the edges.
points: **Minister of Finance:** Grants letters patent to a bank and approves significant ownership under Bank Act s.373.
**OSFI:** Supervises for sound financial condition and compliance with the governing statute, and for adequate policies against threats to integrity and security (O-2.7 s.4(2)(a), (a.1)).
**FCAC:** Supervises compliance with the consumer provisions, including Bank Act Part XII.2. Penalties for violations can reach $10 million (FCAC Act s.19(2)).
**FINTRAC:** Administers the PCMLTFA for banks as reporting entities (PCMLTFA s.5(a)).
**CDIC:** Insures deposits and acts as the resolution authority for its member institutions (CDIC Act s.7(a), (d)).

**Privacy and payments:** The Privacy Commissioner oversees PIPEDA for commercial personal information. The Bank of Canada oversees payment activity and registers non-bank payment providers under the RPAA (banks' own retail payments are excluded, s.9(a)). It is also to administer the consumer-driven banking framework (Part 2 of Bill C-8; check commencement). The Competition Bureau and CRTC sit outside this stage. Payments Canada membership is mandatory for all banks.

deepDive.heading: Layers of legal force
deepDive.lede: The same obligation can carry very different weight depending on where it sits.

visual.caption: Binding rules sit at the top. Guidance and voluntary commitments carry weight in supervision, not as law.

items.label: Acts
items.note: Binding; the Superintendent can direct the bank under s.645

items.label: Regulations
items.note: Binding, e.g. the consumer Regulations

items.label: OSFI guidelines
items.note: Expectations that OSFI supervises against, not law

items.label: Advisories and letters
items.note: Supervisory expectations backed by supervisory consequences

items.label: FCAC and FINTRAC guidance
items.note: Persuasive interpretation of the statutes

items.label: Voluntary codes
items.note: Public commitments; disclosed under s.627.66. A breach can be wrongdoing under s.979.1.

points: **Acts and regulations:** These bind. Breach can lead to directions, penalties or prosecution, depending on the statute.
**OSFI guidelines:** OSFI expects the bank to follow them, rates the bank against them and can act under [[s.645|Superintendent]] for an unsafe or unsound practice.
**Supervisory information:** Ratings and intervention stages are confidential, and must not go to vendors.
**Codes and commitments:** Voluntary codes and public commitments must be published (s.627.66). Breaching one can count as wrongdoing (s.979.1).
**Agency guidance:** FCAC and FINTRAC guidance shows how each reads its statute. It is persuasive, not binding.
deepDive.takeaway: Ask which layer a requirement sits in before deciding how strictly to treat it.

deepDive.heading: Bank Act anatomy
deepDive.lede: The Bank Act is organized in Parts. A few carry most of the supervisory and consumer weight.

visual.caption: Four Parts matter most to this volume. Each maps to a different team and regulator.

items.label: Part XII.2
items.note: Dealings with customers and the public

items.label: Part XIII
items.note: Superintendent's examination and direction powers

items.label: Part XI
items.note: Related-party transactions and service contracts

items.label: Part XVI.1
items.note: Whistleblowing and wrongdoing

points: **Part XIII:** Gives the Superintendent examination (s.643), prudential agreement (s.644.1) and direction (s.645) powers.
**Part XII.2:** Sets the consumer provisions. This is the Financial Consumer Protection Framework, in force since 30 June 2022.
**Part XI:** Restricts related-party transactions. If management functions pass to non-employees under a service contract, the Superintendent may order changes (s.495(2)).
**Part XVI.1:** Whistleblowing rules, including breach of a published commitment as wrongdoing (s.979.1).
**Mapping:** Tag each obligation with its Part so compliance, legal and technology teams work from the same source.
deepDive.takeaway: Read the Part first, then the regulations and guidelines under it.

deepDive.heading: Hong Kong comparison
deepDive.lede: The HKMA model is more concentrated than Canada's split model.
points: **One authority in Hong Kong:** The HKMA supervises authorized institutions under the Banking Ordinance, and its SPM modules set the expectations.
**Canada's split:** OSFI handles prudential supervision, FCAC handles conduct, FINTRAC handles AML, CDIC handles deposit insurance and resolution, and the Privacy Commissioner handles privacy.
**Guidance style:** SPM modules and OSFI guidelines both set expectations. OSFI's are not law, but OSFI can still direct the bank.
**Third-party contrast:** Unlike SA-2, OSFI Guideline B-10 has no advance-discussion gate. It applies to every third-party arrangement, scaled to risk and criticality.
**Practical effect:** Expect more than one regulator to ask about the same vendor, so align the answers before any of them asks.
deepDive.takeaway: Plan for several regulators, one set of facts.

provisions.title: Application of Act
provisions.summary: The Act is the charter of, and applies to, each bank. It is the starting point for what a bank may do and how it is supervised.
provisions.counselNote: Start with the Bank Act when a question concerns the bank's powers or duties. Most federal obligations trace back to it.

provisions.title: Main business
provisions.summary: Limits a bank to the business of banking and the business that appertains to it. Subsection (2) gives examples, including financial services, financial agency and card issuing.
provisions.counselNote: Any new product or partnership must fit the business of banking. A digital bank's services, such as payments and investment products, should be checked against this limit.

provisions.title: Dealings with Customers and the Public
provisions.summary: The consumer provisions, known as the Financial Consumer Protection Framework and in force since 30 June 2022. They cover training, misleading information, appropriate products, advertising, complaints and agents.
provisions.counselNote: The bank must not use agents or intermediaries to sell its products unless they meet these duties as if they were an institution, and customers can use the bank's complaint procedures (s.627.15). Vendors and partners selling products are covered.

provisions.title: Regulation of Banks, Superintendent
provisions.summary: Gives the Superintendent examination, records-access, prudential agreement and direction powers over banks. Section 643 covers the annual examination and s.645 covers directions.
provisions.counselNote: These are the powers OSFI uses in practice. The bank must cooperate with examinations, and the Superintendent's access reaches records held by vendors for the bank (s.643(2)(a)).

provisions.title: Superintendent's directions to bank
provisions.summary: The Superintendent may direct a bank to stop an unsafe or unsound practice and to remedy it (s.645(1)). The same power applies where the bank lacks adequate policies against threats to its integrity or security (s.645(1.1)).
provisions.counselNote: This is OSFI's main compulsory tool. The test is an unsafe or unsound practice (s.645(1)) or inadequate integrity and security policies (s.645(1.1)). OSFI guidelines are not the statutory test, though OSFI may cite them in supervision (confirm current OSFI practice before relying on it).

provisions.instrument: Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions Act (O-2.7)
provisions.title: Office established; objects
provisions.summary: Establishes OSFI and sets its objects for financial institutions. OSFI supervises for sound financial condition and compliance, and for adequate protection against threats to integrity and security, including foreign interference.
provisions.counselNote: The integrity and security objective explains why OSFI asks about vendor background checks and foreign ownership, not only about financial risk.

provisions.instrument: Financial Consumer Agency of Canada Act (F-11.1)
provisions.title: Establishment and objects
provisions.summary: Establishes FCAC and sets its objects. FCAC supervises financial institutions and the external complaints body for compliance with the consumer provisions that apply to them.
provisions.counselNote: FCAC examines conduct, including how products are sold and how complaints are handled. Its findings can cover vendors and partners who deal with customers for the bank.

provisions.instrument: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (P-24.501)
provisions.title: Application of Part
provisions.summary: Makes Part 1 apply to banks, and to authorized foreign banks in respect of their business in Canada. These are reporting entities under the Act.
provisions.counselNote: Once a bank is a reporting entity, its identity verification, record-keeping and reporting duties apply, including where it relies on an agent (PCMLTFR s.106).

provisions.title: Objects
provisions.summary: Sets CDIC's objects. These include insuring deposits against loss and acting as the resolution authority for its members.
provisions.counselNote: CDIC's role as resolution authority is why vendor contracts must survive a bank's failure. See the resolution stage.

provisions.instrument: Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (P-8.6)
provisions.title: Application
provisions.summary: Applies to every organization in respect of personal information it collects, uses or discloses in the course of commercial activities.
provisions.counselNote: A bank's personal information handling is covered, including data passed to vendors for processing. The bank remains responsible for data sent to a vendor for processing and must use contracts or other means to give it comparable protection (Sch. 1, cl. 4.1.3).

provisions.instrument: OSFI Guideline B-10, Third-Party Risk Management Guideline
provisions.title: Third-Party Risk Management Guideline
provisions.summary: OSFI's expectations for any third-party arrangement, by contract or otherwise. It applies in effect from 1 May 2024, scaled to the risk and criticality of each arrangement, and it replaced the 2009 outsourcing guideline.
provisions.counselNote: B-10 is the main OSFI guideline for vendors and group companies. It is an expectation, not law, and OSFI does not need advance notice of arrangements.

provisions.title: Supervisory Framework
provisions.summary: Describes how OSFI assesses each institution. It assigns an Overall Risk Rating on a scale of 1 to 8 and a Tier Rating, and sets the intensity of supervision from them.
provisions.counselNote: Ratings are confidential supervisory information. Ask OSFI for its view before sharing a rating, and keep ratings from vendors.

checklist: **Map the regulators:** List each regulator, its statute or guideline, and the legal force of each. Start with the bank's own product lines.
**Tag obligations by force:** Mark acts, regulations, OSFI expectations and voluntary commitments separately, so the team knows what is binding.
**Test each business line against s.409:** Confirm each service, including partner-delivered products, falls within the business of banking.
**Rate vendors by risk and criticality:** Use the bank's own method to identify high-risk or critical arrangements under B-10. Stage 5 covers the contract terms.
**Track Part XII.2 duties for intermediaries:** Confirm that agents and partners selling products meet the consumer provisions, and that customers can use the bank's complaint procedures (s.627.15).
**Add the provincial overlay:** For each product, check Quebec privacy rules and provincial consumer law (reported; check).
**Set one supervisor contact protocol:** Name a point of contact for OSFI, FCAC, FINTRAC and CDIC, so requests reach the right people.
**Calendar the in-force dates:** E-21 full adherence was due 1 September 2026, and testing of all critical operations is due 1 September 2027.
itAngle: **Source-of-truth matrix:** Keep one matrix of obligations, regulators and systems. Technology teams then build controls against the right source.

**Records location:** Bank Act s.239(1) requires the records described in s.238 to be kept at the head office or another place in Canada, and s.244 extends the safeguard duty to the bank's agents. Tag where each vendor stores data.
**Incident clocks differ:** OSFI's advisory expects a report within 24 hours of a reportable incident, and PIPEDA requires breach reports as soon as feasible. The map should show every clock.
**Model inventory:** Guideline E-23 covers vendor and third-party models from 1 May 2027, so the model inventory must include them.
virtualBankNotes: **No branches:** The app and its vendors deliver onboarding, records and complaints. Vendor controls therefore carry much of the bank's compliance weight.
**No separate licence:** Canada has no separate licence for a digital bank. It is a bank under the Bank Act and meets the same OSFI and FCAC rules as any other bank (s.409).
**Partners carry the front end:** Where a fintech offers banking products through a partner bank, the partner bank keeps the Bank Act and OSFI duties, and the arrangement must meet B-10.

**App flows are the evidence:** Supervisors may test app screens, disclosures and onboarding flows as well as written policy (check the current supervisory approach), because the app is the bank's public face.
pitfalls: **Treating guidelines as optional:** OSFI expectations are not law, but OSFI can still direct the bank under s.645(1).
**Single-regulator thinking:** Assuming OSFI alone covers a product. Consumer, AML and privacy duties sit with other bodies.
**Missing the Quebec layer:** Applying only federal privacy rules to Quebec customers (reported; check).
**Sharing supervisory ratings:** Giving vendors ratings or intervention stages, which are prescribed supervisory information.

glossary.definition: The head of OSFI, who exercises the Bank Act's supervisory powers over banks, including examinations (s.643) and directions (s.645).
The Minister of Finance's instrument creating a bank under Part III of the Bank Act. The bank still needs an order from the Superintendent before it can start business.
A foreign bank authorized under the Bank Act to carry on business in Canada through an agency or other office in Canada.
OSFI's written expectations on a topic, such as B-10. Not law, but OSFI supervises against them and can act on the bank's unsafe or unsound practices.
Ratings, intervention stages, orders, prudential agreements and directions. A bank may disclose them only to listed recipients under the Supervisory Information (Banks) Regulations.
The consumer provisions in Bank Act Part XII.2, in force since 30 June 2022. FCAC supervises compliance with them.
The body every bank must belong to for complaints it cannot resolve. For banks this is OBSI.
OSFI's rating of an institution's overall risk on a scale of 1 to 8. It drives the stage of supervisory intervention.
Any business or strategic arrangement with an outside party, by contract or otherwise, including outsourcing, cloud services and services from group companies (B-10).

title: Banks, the business of banking & the perimeter
oneLiner: Canada has one bank charter under the Bank Act; the word “bank” and the deposit-taking rules are where app-first products meet the perimeter.
keyPoints: **Single charter:** The Bank Act (S.C. 1991, c. 46) is the charter for banks. Schedules I, II and III sort banks by ownership and status, not by product or digital channel.
**Business powers:** Section 409 confines a bank to the business of banking and what goes with it. Sections 410 and 411 add ancillary and networking powers, and s.416 limits insurance.
**Deposits:** A bank may take deposits in Canada only through a [[member institution|Member institution]] route or a narrow authorization (s.413). Non-member banks face a small-deposit limit.
**Restricted word:** Only a bank may use “bank”, “banker” or “banking” to describe its business, products or services in Canada, subject to exceptions (s.983).

**Partners:** Most Canadian “neobanks” are not banks. They work through a bank, a credit union or another regulated financial institution (for example a trust company), or register as payment service providers under the RPAA. Check each partner's status.
**Counsel's role:** Map each app feature, brand and partner to a power or restriction before launch, and confirm the status of the 2026 Acts.
