deepDive.heading: Three bank types under one Act
deepDive.lede: Ownership and status decide which schedule a bank sits in, and the schedule drives how the Act treats it.

visual.caption: Schedules sort banks by ownership and status, as set out in Bank Act ss.14 and 14.1.

items.label: Schedule I bank
items.note: Not a subsidiary of a foreign bank

items.label: Schedule II bank
items.note: Subsidiary of a foreign bank

items.label: Authorized foreign bank
items.note: Foreign bank operating through a branch

points: **Schedule I:** Lists each bank incorporated under the Act that is not a subsidiary of a foreign bank, with its head office province (s.14(1)(a)).

**Schedule II:** Lists each [[Schedule II bank]] that is a subsidiary of a foreign bank (s.14(1)(b)). Schedules change when a bank is incorporated, renamed, moved or changes foreign ownership (s.14(2)).

**Schedule III:** Lists each [[Authorized foreign bank]] and whether it is under the [[Section 524(2) restrictions]] (s.14.1). A foreign bank needs a Minister's order before it can operate here (s.524(1)).
**Not a bank:** A Schedule III branch is not a “bank” under s.2, but the consumer rules reach it through the defined term “institution” (s.627.01(1)). Read each rule for the term it uses.
**Other charters:** Trust and loan companies and federal credit unions sit under other Acts. This stage does not cover them.
deepDive.takeaway: Confirm the schedule and the defined term before applying any Bank Act rule to a counterparty.

deepDive.heading: What a bank may do
deepDive.lede: The business powers are a list, not a general licence, and each activity needs a home in the Act.

visual.caption: Core business first, then ancillary and networking powers, bounded by the restrictions.

items.label: Business of banking
items.note: Financial services, financial agency, cards

items.label: Ancillary activities
items.note: Data, verification, real property, information services

items.label: Networking
items.note: Agency and referral, subject to s.416

items.label: Restrictions
items.note: No general trade; no insurance agency

points: **Main business:** A bank may carry on only the [[Business of banking|business of banking]] and business generally appertaining to it (s.409(1)). The business includes any financial service, acting as financial agent, investment counselling and portfolio management, and issuing payment, credit or charge cards (s.409(2)).

**Ancillary powers:** Section 410 lets a bank hold real property, provide prescribed data processing, and provide identification, authentication or verification services (s.410(1)(h)). Some information activities in Canada need the Minister's prior written approval (s.410(1)(c)).
**No general trade:** Except as the Act authorizes, a bank shall not deal in goods or merchandise, or engage in any other trade or business (s.410(2)).

**Investments:** Section 468 allows a bank to take control of, or a substantial investment in, listed entities. Entities limited to listed activities, such as group services or promotion of group products, also qualify (s.468(2)). Part XI still applies.
deepDive.takeaway: Map each partner service to a paragraph of s.409, 410, 411 or 468 before signing.

deepDive.heading: Deposits and the word bank
deepDive.lede: Two perimeter rules catch most fintech launches: who may take deposits, and who may use the word bank.
points: **Deposit routes:** A bank may accept deposits in Canada only if it is a [[Member institution|member institution]] under the CDIC Act, is authorized to take deposits without membership, or its order to commence business allows the limited deposits in s.413(3) (s.413(1)).

**Small deposits:** A non-member bank must ensure that, each day from 30 days after its authorization, deposits under $150,000 payable in Canada (averaged over the preceding 30 days) are at most 1% of all deposits payable in Canada (s.413(3)). Its agents may not take those deposits except as the regulations allow (s.413.2(1)).

**Use of the word:** It is an offence for a person other than a bank to use “bank”, “banker” or “banking” to describe its business, products or services in Canada, unless authorized (s.983(2.1)). Causing or authorizing another person to do so is also an offence (s.983(2.11)).
**Connection statements:** No one may say its business is connected or affiliated with a bank or foreign bank without authority (s.983(2.3)).
deepDive.takeaway: Treat app names, domains, card designs and partner marketing as regulated text, and have the bank clear them.

deepDive.heading: Partners, agents and payment providers
deepDive.lede: Most fintechs sit outside the bank perimeter and reach customers through a bank, a credit union or a registered payment provider.

visual.caption: The fintech route depends on who holds the product and who holds the money.

items.label: Fintech brand
items.note: Customer-facing app; not a bank

items.label: Bank as product provider
items.note: Holds the deposit or lending product

items.label: Intermediary duties
items.note: Consumer rules extend to the intermediary

points: **Payment providers:** The RPAA does not apply to a bank for its own retail payment activities (s.9(a)). A fintech payment partner that performs those activities is in scope and needs its own registration and duties (see stage 6).

**Intermediaries:** The bank must not arrange with representatives, agents or intermediaries to sell or further the sale of its products unless (a) they comply with the consumer provisions as if they were an institution, (b) customers can use the bank's complaint procedures, (c) their employees can use the whistleblowing channels, and (d) they observe s.979.4 as if they were a bank (s.627.15). See stage 8 for partner structures.

**Consumer-driven banking:** A 2026 Act (S.C. 2026, c. 3) replaces the 2024 Act. The Bank of Canada administers it and accredits third-party service providers. Most of its provisions take effect on a day fixed by order of the Governor in Council; confirm the commencement status before relying on it.
**Status claims:** A partner's “bank-like” description is not evidence of its status. Check the Schedule, the partner's registration and the bank's written confirmation.
deepDive.takeaway: Decide early whether the partner is an agent, a referral source or a payment provider, because each carries different duties.

deepDive.heading: Digital banks in Canada and the Hong Kong contrast
deepDive.lede: Canada has no virtual bank licence, so the questions are which schedule the bank sits in and which powers it holds.
points: **No separate licence:** An app-first bank is an ordinary Schedule I or II bank. EQ Bank is the digital brand of a Schedule I bank (reported; check). Tangerine and Simplii are reported to be divisions of large banks, not separate banks (reported; check).

**HK:** The Banking Ordinance sorts authorized institutions into three tiers: licensed banks, restricted licence banks and deposit-taking companies. HKMA has a separate virtual bank authorization guideline. Canada has one charter and no tiers.
**Neobanks:** Most Canadian neobanks, such as KOHO or Wealthsimple, are not banks. They partner with a bank or credit union, or register as payment providers (reported; check).

**Foreign bank branches:** A branch route under s.524 is subject to the deposit bar only if the order carries s.524(2) restrictions. Where it does, s.540(1) bars taking deposits, subject to s.540(4), and s.627.74 requires a disclosure that it does not accept deposits in Canada.
deepDive.takeaway: Ask first whether the product is a bank product at all, then which schedule the bank sits in.

provisions.title: Definitions
provisions.summary: Defines a bank as a bank listed in Schedule I or II, and an authorized foreign bank as a foreign bank subject to an order under s.524(1). Terms used across the Act, such as bank holding company, are defined here too.
provisions.counselNote: Start every perimeter analysis here. A Schedule III branch is not a bank under this definition, so check which defined term each rule uses.

provisions.title: Schedule I and Schedule II banks
provisions.summary: Requires Schedule I to list each bank that is not a subsidiary of a foreign bank, and Schedule II to list each bank that is one, with the head office province. The schedules are amended when a bank is incorporated, renamed, moved, or changes foreign ownership.
provisions.counselNote: Confirm the schedule in the bank's charter papers and update it on any change to foreign ownership. The schedule affects how the bank is treated under the Act.

provisions.title: Schedule III authorized foreign banks
provisions.summary: Requires Schedule III to list each authorized foreign bank, its principal office province, and whether it is subject to the restrictions in s.524(2). Amendments follow changes to the order.
provisions.counselNote: A foreign bank that wants to operate in Canada through a branch needs an order first, and the order may restrict it. Ask which Schedule III entry a counterparty holds.

provisions.title: Main business
provisions.summary: Confines a bank to the business of banking and business generally appertaining to it. The business includes any financial service, acting as financial agent, investment counselling and portfolio management, and issuing payment, credit or charge cards.
provisions.counselNote: Test every new product line against this section first. An activity outside it needs a power elsewhere in the Act.

provisions.title: Additional activities
provisions.summary: Lists activities a bank may engage in beyond s.409, including holding real property, prescribed data processing, and identification, authentication or verification services. Some information activities in Canada need the Minister's prior written approval, and s.410(2) bars general trade unless the Act allows it.
provisions.counselNote: Identity and verification services offered to partners often rely on s.410(1)(h). Decide whether the service is the bank's activity or the partner's own before contracting.

provisions.title: Networking
provisions.summary: Subject to s.416, lets a bank act as agent for any person in a service provided by a financial institution, a permitted entity or a prescribed entity, enter into an arrangement for it, and refer customers to that entity. Regulations may require disclosure of the principal and of any commission.
provisions.counselNote: Referral and agency arrangements need a written view on disclosure of the principal and any commission. Check the disclosure regulations before paying or receiving a referral fee.

provisions.title: Restriction on deposit taking
provisions.summary: A bank may accept deposits in Canada only if it is a CDIC member institution, is authorized under the CDIC Act to take deposits without membership, or its order to commence business allows the limited deposits in s.413(3). Those limited banks must keep, each day from 30 days after authorization, deposits under $150,000 payable in Canada (averaged over the preceding 30 days) at or below 1% of all deposits payable in Canada.
provisions.counselNote: A digital bank taking Canadian deposits needs one of these routes from the start. The small-deposit ratio is a daily control, so build it into the deposit system.

provisions.title: Restriction on insurance business
provisions.summary: A bank shall not act in Canada as agent for anyone placing insurance, and shall not lease or provide space in a branch to a person engaged in placing insurance. The regulations add detail and permit a bank to administer authorized types of insurance (SOR-92-330 s.4(1)).
provisions.counselNote: An embedded insurance offer in an app needs a check against s.416(2) and the regulations before launch, and the partner's role must be defined in the contract.

provisions.title: Permitted investments
provisions.summary: Lets a bank acquire control of, or a substantial investment in, listed entities, and in entities whose business is limited to listed activities. Those activities include services to the bank or its group, and promotion or distribution of group products. Part XI still applies, and s.468(3) limits deposit-taking or mixed entities.
provisions.counselNote: A fintech stake or a service company set up by the bank must fit a listed business and stay inside its limits. Check any related-party element under Part XI.

provisions.title: Order permitting carrying on of business in Canada, etc.
provisions.summary: The Minister may order that a foreign bank may establish a branch in Canada, after consulting the Superintendent, and only if the applicant is a bank in its home jurisdiction whose principal activity is financial services or services a Canadian bank could provide. The order may carry restrictions under s.540(1) and requirements under s.627.74. For a non-WTO member, the Minister must also be satisfied of reciprocal treatment for Canadian banks in the bank's home jurisdiction (s.524(3)).
provisions.counselNote: A foreign bank branch is an entry route distinct from a Schedule II subsidiary. Check the order and its conditions before a foreign bank partner offers products here.

provisions.title: Use of name
provisions.summary: Makes it an offence for an entity other than a bank to adopt a name, domain or mark that includes “bank”, “banker” or “banking” for a business in Canada without authority. The same applies to using those words to describe its business or products, to causing another to do so, and to statements that a business is connected with a bank or foreign bank.
provisions.counselNote: Read “bank” in app names, domains, card designs and partner marketing as a regulated term. The permitted-use exceptions in s.983(4) are narrow, so check the regulations before relying on one.

provisions.title: Payment service providers
provisions.summary: Excludes from the Act a payment service provider that performs retail payment activities if it is a bank, an authorized foreign bank, or one of several other listed institutions. Any other payment service provider is in scope for the Act's registration and duties.
provisions.counselNote: A bank's own payment products sit outside the RPAA. A fintech payment partner usually does not, so it needs its own registration and duties. See stage 6 for incident duties.

checklist: **Confirm the schedule:** Record whether the bank is Schedule I, II or III, and whether its parent is foreign.
**Map each product:** Tie every product, service and partner role to s.409, 410, 411 or 468, or to a restriction.
**Clear regulated words:** Check app names, domains, card designs and partner copy against s.983.
**Confirm the deposit route:** Record CDIC membership, the s.413 authorization or the s.413(3) limits.
**Check insurance offers:** Test any embedded insurance against s.416(2) and the insurance regulations.
**Document payment partners:** Record each partner's RPAA status under s.9 and its registration.
**Track the 2026 Acts:** Note the commencement status of the consumer-driven banking Act.
**Keep the charter file current:** Record the schedule, letters patent and any change of ownership in the regulatory map (see stage 3).
itAngle: **Name and domain register:** Keep a register of names, domains and app-store listings containing “bank”, “banker” or “banking”, with an owner and a clearance date.
**Product tagging:** Tag each product and feature with the Bank Act power or restriction it relies on, so a change triggers legal review.
**Copy controls:** Put regulated wording, such as deposit and insurance statements, behind approval workflows and feature flags, so it can be changed quickly.
**Partner systems:** Where a partner's interface moves customer money or data, the bank's controls and records (see stage 7) must reach that interface.
virtualBankNotes: **No licence step:** A digital bank still needs a Bank Act charter, a schedule and OSFI supervision. The app is not a separate licence.
**Every screen counts:** App store listings, emails and card designs are uses of the name, so s.983 applies to them.
**Deposit route first:** A digital bank that takes Canadian deposits needs a s.413 route from day one. See stage 9 for deposit insurance wording.

**Partner-led brands:** Where a partner sells the bank's product under its own brand, the partner is an intermediary under s.627.15. See stage 8. OSFI expects the bank to treat the arrangement as a third-party arrangement under Guideline B-10 (Third-Party Risk Management), scaled to its risk and criticality. Whether the partner is an intermediary under s.627.15 depends on the contract and its role, so confirm that first.
pitfalls: **Assuming neobank means bank:** Most are not banks. Check the schedule and the partner's own registration, not its marketing.
**Using bank in copy:** A non-bank that uses the word for its products commits an offence unless authorized (s.983(2.1)).
**Treating a branch as a bank:** A Schedule III branch is not a bank under s.2. The s.524 order and s.540 limits govern it.
**Relying on 2026 Acts as in force:** Several 2026 Acts take effect by order. Confirm the commencement status of each before relying on it.

glossary.definition: A bank incorporated under the Bank Act that is not a subsidiary of a foreign bank. Its name is listed in Schedule I (Bank Act s.14(1)(a)).
A bank incorporated under the Bank Act that is a subsidiary of a foreign bank. Its name is listed in Schedule II (Bank Act s.14(1)(b)).
A foreign bank that has a Minister's order under s.524(1) to carry on business in Canada through a branch. It is listed in Schedule III (s.14.1).
An institution that is a member of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation under the CDIC Act. A bank taking deposits in Canada must be one, or have another route (Bank Act s.413(1)).
The main business a bank may carry on under Bank Act s.409. Section 409(2) says it includes financial services, financial agency, investment counselling, portfolio management and card issuing.
A bank acting as agent for, or referring customers to, another financial institution or permitted entity, under Bank Act s.411. It is subject to the insurance limits in s.416.
The words “bank”, “banker” or “banking”. Only a bank may use them to describe its business in Canada, unless another Act authorizes it (Bank Act s.983(2.1)).
A person or entity that performs retail payment activities in Canada and is in scope of the Retail Payment Activities Act. Banks and some other institutions are excluded (RPAA s.9).
Restrictions a Minister's order can place on an authorized foreign bank, such as the s.540 limits on taking deposits. Check the order for the restrictions that apply.

title: Becoming a bank: letters patent and the order
oneLiner: A new bank needs letters patent from the Minister and an order from the Superintendent before it can start business.
keyPoints: **Two approvals:** The Minister issues [[letters patent]] under Bank Act s.22(1), which incorporate the bank. The Superintendent then makes an [[OCCB|order to commence and carry on business]]. Neither step lets the bank start business alone.
**No business before the order:** A bank may not carry on any business until the Superintendent makes the order (s.48(1)). Before then, its paid-in capital can only sit in limited places (s.51).
**OSFI's route:** OSFI's guide sets three phases: pre-application, letters patent and the order. Eligible innovators may use the [[streamlined approvals framework]], which has its own timetable.

**Capital and timing:** Before the order, the bank needs paid-in capital of at least $5 million, or more if the Minister specifies (s.52(1)(b)). The order must come within one year of incorporation (s.52(2)).

**Deposits:** A bank may take deposits in Canada only as a CDIC [[member institution]], or under a narrow authorization (s.413(1)). CDIC insures each deposit with a member, except the part of any one deposit above $100,000 (C-3 s.12).
**Counsel's role:** Build the business plan, ownership and third-party arrangements early. OSFI reviews them before the order, and the bank cannot open without it.

**Board and people:** The Bank Act requires at least seven directors, a majority of them resident in Canada (s.159), and no more than two thirds of them affiliated with the bank (s.163). OSFI expects a documented fit-and-proper assessment of directors and senior management before appointment (E-17).

conceptMap.caption: Letters patent give the bank its legal existence. The Superintendent's order is the separate gate that lets it start business.

items.label: Notice of intention
items.note: Four consecutive weeks, Gazette and local paper

items.label: Application filed
items.note: Filed with the Superintendent

items.label: Letters patent
items.note: Issued by the Minister of Finance

items.label: Pre-commencement review
items.note: OSFI on-site review before the order

items.label: Order to commence business
items.note: Made by the Superintendent; business starts after it

deepDive.heading: Letters patent, then the order
deepDive.lede: Canada splits the charter into two decisions by two different officials.

visual.caption: Two gates, one bank. Business starts only after the second.

items.label: Letters patent
items.note: Incorporate the bank (s.22(1))

items.label: Pre-commencement review
items.note: OSFI checks readiness; the guide says it may take months

items.label: Order to commence business
items.note: Required before any business (s.48(1))

points: **Two officials:** The Minister issues letters patent under s.22(1). The Superintendent makes the order under s.48(1), on the bank's application under s.49(1).

**Conditions:** The order may carry conditions or limitations on the bank's business (s.53(1)). The Superintendent may later vary them, after giving the bank a chance to make representations (s.54(1)).
**Public notice:** The bank must publish notice of the order in a local newspaper, and the Superintendent publishes it in the Canada Gazette (s.56).

**Unlike Hong Kong:** The HKMA's authorization under s.16 of the Banking Ordinance is one licensing decision, assessed against the Seventh Schedule criteria. Canada uses two decisions, so the timetable needs two sets of milestones.

**Ownership approval:** Acquiring a significant interest in a bank needs the Minister's approval (s.373(1)). A major shareholder, meaning a holder of more than 20% of a class of voting shares (s.2.2), faces further limits (s.372, and s.374 for a bank with equity of $12 billion or more). The ownership approval can run alongside the two charter decisions.
deepDive.takeaway: Plan the timetable around two approvals, and check that any order conditions are achievable at launch.

deepDive.heading: Applying for letters patent
deepDive.lede: The Minister decides after weighing the factors in s.27, and the application is filed with the Superintendent.
points: **Notice first:** Before filing, the applicants publish a notice of intention once a week for four consecutive weeks, in the Canada Gazette and in a newspaper near the head office (s.25(2)).
**Filing:** The application names the first directors, comes with any other information the Superintendent requires, and is filed with the Superintendent (s.25(1)).

**What the Minister weighs:** Financial resources, soundness of the plans, business record, character and integrity, competence of those who will run the bank, integration with the applicants' businesses, and the Superintendent's view of how the corporate structure affects supervision (s.27).

**Restricted applicants:** Letters patent may not issue on an application by a government or its agency, or by a foreign-government-controlled entity other than a foreign bank (s.23). A subsidiary of a non-WTO foreign bank needs reciprocal treatment in its home jurisdiction (s.24).
deepDive.takeaway: Treat the s.27 factors as the Minister's checklist, and evidence each one in the application file.

deepDive.heading: OSFI's phases and the streamlined route
deepDive.lede: OSFI's readiness steps set the real pace of the application.

visual.caption: Streamlined route timings are indicative and reported; check the current framework page.

items.label: Readiness letter
items.note: After the initial meeting with OSFI

items.label: Formal application
items.note: OSFI's review of a complete application

items.label: Operational readiness
items.note: Within 3 months of letters patent, or aligned with launch

points: **Phase 1:** A meeting with OSFI, written submissions on the business, ownership, capital and management, and a minimum five-year business plan (guide).
**Phase 2:** The formal application for letters patent and for the order, with fees, and OSFI's recommendation to the Minister.
**Phase 3:** After letters patent, OSFI carries out a pre-commencement on-site review. The guide says a new bank may need several months to prepare for it.
**Streamlined route:** OSFI may limit the number of applications it processes. Where gaps remain, it may issue an order with conditions or restrictions (reported; check).
**Timelines:** OSFI calls its timelines indicative. They depend on the quality of the submission, security checks and the applicant's responsiveness (reported; check).
deepDive.takeaway: Ask OSFI at the first meeting which route applies, because the streamlined route changes the timetable and the readiness deadlines.

deepDive.heading: The business plan and third-party arrangements
deepDive.lede: The business plan is where a digital bank's vendor stack first becomes a regulatory matter.
points: **Five-year plan:** The guide asks for a minimum five-year business plan, with liquidity and capital projections, pro forma statements and sensitivity analysis.

**Third parties:** The plan must describe the proposed high-risk or critical third-party arrangements, how they will be managed, and copies of the contracts. It must also describe integration with third-party systems (the guide predates OSFI Guideline B-10, Third-Party Risk Management, and uses older terms).
**IT and risk policies:** The bank also needs an IT policy, a governance structure, an end-user computing policy and operational risk policies covering outsourcing, continuity, records and security.
**Records access:** The business continuity plan must let the bank reach the records it needs to run operations, meet its obligations and answer OSFI.
**Current standard:** OSFI expects arrangements made on or after 1 May 2024 to meet B-10. See stage 5 for the vendor contract toolkit.

**Integrity and security:** OSFI assesses applicants for national security or international-relations concerns, and the plan should show integrity and security policies for the bank and its third parties (Integrity and Security Guideline, 31 January 2024; reported; check the current framework text).
deepDive.takeaway: Draft the vendor section of the plan from the actual contracts, so the description and the contracts match.

deepDive.heading: Capital, payments and the first year
deepDive.lede: Capital and timing rules bind the period between incorporation and the order.
points: **Capital:** Paid-in capital of at least $5 million is needed before the order, or a higher amount the Minister specifies (s.52(1)(b)). The guide expects capital to stay above target ratios for the longer of three years or the point of profitability in the base case.
**Shareholders' meeting:** Once $5 million has been received, the directors must call a shareholders' meeting without delay, and it must be held before the order (ss.46(1), 52(1)(a)).

**Pre-order money:** Until the order, incorporation and organization payments are limited to listed sums, such as the remuneration of up to two officers and clerical, legal and accounting costs (s.50).
**Application statement:** The application for the order must state the amounts paid or to be paid for incorporation and organization (s.49(2)).
**Payments Canada:** All chartered banks are mandatory members of Payments Canada, and the guide expects registration once the bank is incorporated.
deepDive.takeaway: Budget pre-order spend against s.50, and keep the capital in the permitted places until the order is made.

deepDive.heading: CDIC membership and deposit-taking
deepDive.lede: A bank that takes deposits in Canada needs CDIC membership, or a narrow authorization that most new banks will not use.

visual.caption: The usual route is full membership. The non-member routes carry a 1% test on small deposits.

items.label: Member bank
items.note: Full CDIC membership; deposits insured under C-3 s.12

items.label: Non-member authorization
items.note: Authorization under C-3 s.26.03; small deposits below 1%

items.label: Order-based deposits
items.note: Deposits only as the order allows, read with s.413(3)

points: **Membership:** The bank may accept deposits in Canada only as a member institution, or under one of the authorizations in s.413(1).

**Insurance limit:** CDIC insures each deposit with a member, but not the part of any one deposit above $100,000 (C-3 s.12(c)). CDIC's category rules then decide what each depositor is covered for (reported; check).
**Small deposits:** A non-member bank must keep deposits under $150,000 at no more than 1% of its deposits (s.413(3)), and may not act as agent for taking them (s.413.2).
**Foreign branches:** An authorized foreign bank that is not subject to the s.524(2) restrictions may not act as agent for taking deposits under $150,000 payable in Canada (s.546).

**Foreign banks:** A foreign bank may enter as a Schedule II subsidiary, or operate in Canada through a branch as an authorized foreign bank under Part XII.1, with an order under s.524(1) listed in Schedule III (s.14.1). A branch that is not subject to the s.524(2) restrictions may not act as agent for taking deposits under $150,000 (s.546(1)). A subsidiary's deposit route runs through s.413.
deepDive.takeaway: For a new digital bank, plan on CDIC membership from the order, and treat any non-member route as a specialist exception.

provisions.title: Incorporation of bank
provisions.summary: On an application made under the Act, the Minister may issue letters patent incorporating a bank. The Minister acts under this Part, so the application is decided by the Minister, not by OSFI.
provisions.counselNote: Letters patent create the bank but do not let it carry on business. Build the launch timetable around the order (s.48(1)), not the letters patent date.

provisions.title: Application for incorporation
provisions.summary: The application, naming the first directors and carrying any other information the Superintendent requires, is filed with the Superintendent. Before filing, one applicant must publish a notice of intention once a week for four consecutive weeks in the Canada Gazette and a local newspaper.
provisions.counselNote: The notice is public, so coordinate its timing with the OSFI pre-application meeting and the bank's communications plan.

provisions.title: Matters for consideration
provisions.summary: Before issuing letters patent, the Minister considers the applicants' financial resources, the soundness of the plans, their business record, character and integrity, the competence of those who will run the bank, the effect of integration, the Superintendent's view of how the corporate structure affects supervision, and the best interests of the financial system in Canada (s.27(i)).
provisions.counselNote: Evidence each factor in the file. Group companies and outsourced platforms show up under the integration and supervision factors, so document them early.

provisions.title: Order to commence and carry on business
provisions.summary: A bank may not carry on any business until the Superintendent has, by order, approved the commencement and carrying on of its business. The Superintendent makes the order on the bank's application under s.49(1).
provisions.counselNote: This is the gate for launch. Tie go-live dates, vendor cut-overs and marketing to the order date, not to incorporation.

provisions.title: No payments before order
provisions.summary: Until the order is made, incorporation and organization expenses may not be paid out of share proceeds, except reasonable sums for up to two officers, share issue costs, and clerical, legal, accounting, office and similar costs at one location.
provisions.counselNote: Payments from share proceeds on incorporation or organization expenses are limited to these categories. Check pre-order payments with the bank's finance team before any contract is signed.

provisions.title: Conditions for order
provisions.summary: The Superintendent may not make the order until the shareholders' meeting has been held, paid-in capital is at least $5 million or the higher amount the Minister specifies, the incorporation expenses are reasonable, and other requirements are met. The order must come within one year after the bank comes into existence.
provisions.counselNote: The one-year limit makes the readiness plan a legal deadline, not just a project date. Track it from the date of the letters patent.

provisions.title: Conditions of order
provisions.summary: The order may contain conditions or limitations on the bank's business that the Superintendent considers expedient and necessary. The Superintendent may later vary them by further order, after giving the bank an opportunity to make representations.
provisions.counselNote: Conditions can limit products, markets or growth at launch. Read them when the order is made, and build the launch scope to comply with them.

provisions.title: Restriction on deposit taking
provisions.summary: A bank may accept deposits in Canada only if it is a CDIC member institution, or if it is authorized to take deposits without membership, or if its order permits deposits solely in accordance with s.413(3). Deposits under $150,000 held by a non-member bank must stay at or below 1% of its deposits.
provisions.counselNote: A bank that takes deposits on the usual route is a CDIC member from the order. Any non-member route is an exception that needs its own analysis, including the 1% test.

provisions.instrument: Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act (R.S.C. 1985, c. C-3)
provisions.title: Duty to insure
provisions.summary: CDIC must insure each deposit with a member institution, except deposits not payable in Canada, deposits on which the Crown would be a preferred claimant, and the part of any one deposit above $100,000.
provisions.counselNote: The $100,000 limit is set per deposit by the statute. CDIC's category rules then shape what a customer is covered for, so product and disclosure teams should check deposit marketing against them (see stage 11).

provisions.title: Deposits less than $150,000
provisions.summary: An authorized foreign bank that is not subject to the restrictions and requirements in s.524(2) may not act as agent for anyone in taking a deposit under $150,000 payable in Canada. Regulations may set exceptions.
provisions.counselNote: This applies to a foreign bank branch, not to a Canadian-incorporated bank. A foreign branch route carries the sub-$150,000 agency limit in s.546 unless it is subject to the s.524(2) restrictions. A non-member Canadian bank faces the same kind of limit under s.413.2.

provisions.instrument: OSFI, Guide for Incorporating Banks and Federally Regulated Trust and Loan Companies
provisions.title: Phases, business plan and pre-commencement review
provisions.summary: Sets out OSFI's expectations for the three phases of an application: the pre-application meeting, letters patent and the order. It covers the business plan, capital, third-party arrangements, IT governance, CDIC and Payments Canada membership, and the pre-commencement on-site review. The guide was last revised in June 2015 and uses older terms.
provisions.counselNote: OSFI expects these contents, but the guide is not law. Check the streamlined framework first, and confirm the dated capital and third-party references with OSFI.

provisions.instrument: OSFI, Streamlined Approvals Framework for Targeted New Entrants (2026)
provisions.ref: Readiness, formal application and operational readiness
provisions.title: Streamlined route for innovative new entrants
provisions.summary: For entities with innovative banking models, OSFI sets an initial readiness letter within four weeks of a meeting, a review of a complete application within 12 months, and operational readiness within 3 months of letters patent. OSFI may limit the number of applications and may issue an order with conditions or restrictions. OSFI also assesses an orderly wind-down (exit) plan in Phase 2 (reported; check).
provisions.counselNote: Timelines are indicative, and eligibility is OSFI's decision. Ask early whether the bank qualifies, and check the framework page at each phase (reported; check).

checklist: **Map the two approvals:** Set separate milestones for letters patent (s.22) and the order (s.48), and track the one-year limit in s.52(2).
**Confirm the route early:** Ask OSFI at the first meeting whether the streamlined framework applies, and diarise its readiness letter and deadlines.
**Evidence each s.27 factor:** Prepare a file for the Minister covering financial resources, the business plan, character and integrity, competence and corporate structure.
**Fix the capital position:** Confirm paid-in capital of at least $5 million, the shareholders' meeting under s.46, and the placement rules in s.51.
**Control pre-order spend:** Approve every pre-order payment against s.50, and keep a record of incorporation costs for the statement required by s.49(2).
**Draft the plan with the vendors:** Describe every high-risk or critical third-party arrangement, attach the contracts, and show the cloud and core-system dependencies.
**Plan for conditions:** Expect conditions or limits in the order, and prepare how the launch scope will meet them and how a variation would be requested.
**Prepare CDIC and payments readiness:** Plan CDIC membership from the order, the deposit disclosures and Payments Canada registration before go-live.
itAngle: **Governance documents:** OSFI expects an IT policy, a governance structure and an end-user computing policy in the application. Keep them under document control, with named owners and review dates.
**Architecture as evidence:** The plan must describe integration with third-party systems, so architecture diagrams and interface inventories are regulatory documents, not only engineering material.

**Readiness at the order:** The pre-commencement review looks at whether the systems and third parties work as described (reported; check). Test environments, change control and incident runbooks need to be ready early.
**Records access:** The continuity plan must support access to records for the bank and for OSFI, so design data location and retrieval with that test in mind.
virtualBankNotes: **No branches:** Canada has no separate virtual bank licence. A digital bank goes through the same letters patent and order as any other bank, and the application describes its operating model.

**Stack in the application:** The operating model, cloud provider and core platform form part of the application. The applicant commits to give OSFI adequate advance notice of material changes to the business plan (guide).

**Signage without premises:** CDIC's digital symbol rules apply to the app and website. A staffed call centre that opens accounts is a place of business under CDIC's bulletin, so it needs the entrance and membership signs (reported; check the CDIC bulletin).
**Not every app is a bank:** Many apps marketed as banks are not banks. A licensed bank goes through this charter route, while non-bank apps partner with one (see stage 8).
pitfalls: **Launching early:** Running public launch activity or taking customers before the order. No business may be carried on until the order is made (s.48(1)).
**Treating guidance as law:** Relying on the guide's dated capital and third-party wording without checking the current framework and B-10.
**Pre-order spend:** Committing vendor, advisory or staff costs out of share proceeds beyond the categories in s.50.

**Letting the file drift:** The order cannot be made more than one year after the bank comes into existence (s.52(2)). No agreement with OSFI extends that limit, so track it from the date of the letters patent.

glossary.definition: The Minister's instrument incorporating a bank under Bank Act s.22(1). It creates the bank but does not let it carry on business.

glossary.term: order to commence and carry on business
glossary.definition: The Superintendent's order under Bank Act s.48(1) approving the start of business, known as the OCCB. It may carry conditions or limitations (s.53).
The Superintendent of Financial Institutions, who heads OSFI, receives the incorporation application and makes the order to commence business.
Capital actually paid in for shares. Before the order it must be at least $5 million, or the higher amount the Minister specifies (s.52(1)(b)).
The on-site review OSFI carries out after letters patent and before the order. The guide says a new bank may need several months to prepare.
A corporation with deposit insurance under the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act (C-3 s.2). A bank taking deposits in Canada generally must be one.
A foreign bank authorized under Bank Act Part XII.1 to carry on business in Canada through a branch. Such banks are listed in Schedule III.
OSFI's route for eligible innovative new entrants, with readiness, formal application and operational readiness phases and indicative timelines.

title: Owners, directors & governance
oneLiner: Who may own a Canadian bank, who must sit on its board, and what the board must oversee, including its vendors.
keyPoints: **Ownership:** A holder of more than 10% of a class of shares has a [[significant interest|significant interest]]. Acquiring or increasing one needs the Minister's approval under s.373.

**Major shareholders:** A holder of more than 20% of voting shares is a major shareholder. No person may be a major shareholder of a bank with equity of $12 billion or more, subject to exceptions in s.374(2) to (6), so the ownership plan must be set before the bank grows.
**Directors:** The bank needs at least seven directors, a Canadian-resident majority, and no more than two thirds affiliated with the bank (ss.159, 163).
**Board duty:** The directors manage or supervise the bank's business and must set up audit and conduct review committees and conflict procedures (s.157).

**Related-party contracts:** Services bought for the ordinary course of business need a written contract (s.495(1)(a)); transactions with insiders and group companies must be on market terms (s.501(1)), and the conduct review committee oversees the procedures (s.195(3)).

**Third parties:** OSFI expects the bank to remain accountable for every third-party arrangement (B-10, Principle 1), and the board's oversight of that risk follows from the Corporate Governance Guideline (2018).

conceptMap.caption: Shareholders and OSFI act on the board from outside. The board sets the committees, the risk appetite and the oversight of vendors and group contracts.

items.label: Senior management
items.note: Runs the day-to-day business

deepDive.heading: Who may own the bank
deepDive.lede: Ownership is controlled by thresholds, a ministerial approval and a size-based cap.

items.label: Significant interest
items.note: More than 10% of a class of shares, counting controlled entities

items.label: Minister's approval
items.note: Needed before acquiring or increasing a significant interest

items.label: Major shareholder
items.note: More than 20% of voting shares, or 30% of a non-voting class

items.label: Equity of $12 billion
items.note: No major shareholder allowed, subject to exceptions; divest within three years

points: **Significant interest:** Shares held through controlled entities count towards the 10% test, so a group structure cannot hide a stake (s.8).

**Approval:** No person may acquire shares that would create or increase a significant interest in a bank without the Minister's approval, and an amalgamation, merger or reorganization that produces one is treated as an acquisition (s.373(1), (2)).

**Size cap:** Once a bank's equity reaches $12 billion, a major shareholder must do what is needed to cease to be one within three years (s.375). Exceptions apply to widely held banks and bank holding companies, to some insurance holding companies and eligible financial institutions (s.374(2)-(6)), and the Minister may extend the three-year period (s.375(3)).
**Widely held:** A body corporate with no major shareholder is widely held (s.2.3). Ownership design should aim for that status where the bank plans to grow.
deepDive.takeaway: Map beneficial ownership, including controlled entities, before any investor or vendor takes equity.

deepDive.heading: Who runs the bank
deepDive.lede: The Act fixes the board's size, residence and independence, and who may not sit on it.
points: **Duty to manage:** The directors manage or supervise the business and affairs of the bank, and must set up audit and conduct review committees and conflict-of-interest procedures (s.157).
**Size and residence:** At least seven directors. A majority must be resident Canadians, or one half for a subsidiary of a foreign bank (s.159).

**Affiliation:** No more than two thirds of the directors may be affiliated with the bank at each annual meeting (s.163). The limit does not apply where a federally incorporated Canadian financial institution owns all the voting shares (other than directors' qualifying shares) (s.163(2)).

**Disqualified persons:** Under-18s, people of unsound mind (as found by a court), bankrupts, non-natural persons, federal and provincial ministers, and agents or employees of a foreign government cannot be directors (s.160).

**Unlike Hong Kong:** Under BO ss.70 and 71 the HKMA consents to controllers and approves chief executives and directors. In Canada the Minister approves shareholdings, and OSFI has no general approval of each director (reported; check). The bank runs the E-17 assessment itself.
deepDive.takeaway: Plan board composition against residence, affiliation and disqualification rules before each annual meeting.

deepDive.heading: Related-party dealings with group and vendors
deepDive.lede: Part XI treats insiders and their companies as [[related parties|related party]], which shapes how group services are contracted.

visual.caption: Part XI permits services from a related party by written contract (s.495(1)(a)), on market terms (s.501), under procedures the conduct review committee oversees (s.195(3)).

items.label: Related party
items.note: Includes significant-interest holders, directors, senior officers and their controlled entities

points: **Permitted route:** A related-party transaction is allowed where the Act permits it, such as a written contract for services used in the ordinary course of business (ss.489, 495(1)(a)).
**Market terms:** Every related-party transaction must be at least as favourable to the bank as market terms (s.501(1)).

**Management by outsiders:** If such contracts leave all or substantially all management functions with non-employees, the Superintendent may, if it considers that result inappropriate, order the bank to take steps so that integral management functions are exercised by employees (s.495(2)).

**Committee review:** The conduct review committee must require procedures for Part XI compliance, review their effectiveness, and identify related-party dealings that could affect the bank's stability or solvency (s.195(3)). The directors report on it to the Superintendent within 90 days after each financial year (s.195(6)).
deepDive.takeaway: Treat every intragroup vendor contract as a related-party contract, and document its market terms.

deepDive.heading: The board's role over third parties
deepDive.lede: OSFI expects senior management to own third-party risk, with the board overseeing it, and the framework to support that ownership.
points: **Principle 1:** Under OSFI Guideline B-10, Third-Party Risk Management, the bank is ultimately accountable for managing risk from all types of third-party arrangements, and it keeps accountability for outsourced services.

**Principle 2:** The bank should have a third-party risk framework with clear accountabilities, including oversight functions, a risk appetite, an inventory and reporting to senior management and the board.
**Corporate Governance Guideline (2018):** OSFI says the board is responsible for the business plan, strategy, risk appetite and culture, and oversees senior management and internal controls.

**Oversight functions:** Heads of risk, compliance and audit should have unfettered access to the board or the relevant committee. OSFI views separating the chair from the chief executive as critical.
**Currency:** The 2018 guideline is the version cited here; confirm on OSFI's site that it is still current before relying on it.
deepDive.takeaway: Put third-party risk on the board's standing agenda, tied to an approved risk appetite.

deepDive.heading: Background checks and integrity
deepDive.lede: Vetting covers directors, senior managers, employees and contractors, including vendor staff.

items.label: E-17, Background checks
items.note: Directors and senior management: assessed before appointment and reassessed at intervals of no more than five years

items.label: Integrity P6, Background checks
items.note: Responsible persons, employees and contractors: risk-based checks, renewed regularly

points: **Assessment policy:** Under E-17, every bank needs a written policy on the suitability and integrity of responsible persons, approved by senior management.
**Criminal records:** E-17 expects criminal records to be independently verified at least every seven years.
**Contractors:** The Integrity and Security Guideline covers non-employees supplied through another entity, such as an agency, so vendor staff with access are in scope.
**Higher-risk roles:** Minimum checks are identity and background verification. Higher-risk positions also need criminal record and credit checks.
**Accountability:** The bank keeps accountability for security, and OSFI says it cannot be contracted out. E-17 lets some assessment work be outsourced, but the bank makes the final decision.

**Statutory basis:** The OSFI Act directs supervision of institutions' policies to protect against threats to their integrity or security (s.4(2)(a.1)), and Bank Act s.645(1.1) lets the Superintendent direct a bank that lacks adequate policies to take remedial measures.
deepDive.takeaway: Extend the director and senior manager vetting process to contractors who hold system access.

provisions.title: Significant interest
provisions.summary: A person has a significant interest in a class of shares if the person, and entities the person controls, hold more than 10 per cent of that class. Membership shares of a federal credit union are treated the same way.
provisions.counselNote: Count controlled entities and the whole group when testing this threshold. Any change in holdings that crosses it or increases it needs the approval under s.373.

provisions.title: Acquisition of significant interest
provisions.summary: No person may acquire shares that would create, or increase, a significant interest in a bank without the Minister's approval. Amalgamations and reorganizations that create a significant interest are treated as acquisitions.
provisions.counselNote: Put the Minister's approval on the critical path of any equity deal, including vendor and partner stakes. Timing is set by the approval process, not by closing.

provisions.title: Limitations on share holdings
provisions.summary: No person may be a major shareholder of a bank with equity of $12 billion or more. Exceptions apply to certain widely held bank holding companies and banks that already controlled the bank when its equity reached that level. A major shareholder is defined in s.2.2.
provisions.counselNote: Model the equity trajectory of the bank as well as the ownership. Growth can force a major shareholder to divest, so raise this with the board before the bank reaches the threshold.

provisions.title: Duty to manage
provisions.summary: The directors manage or supervise the management of the bank's business and affairs. They must also set up an audit committee, a conduct review committee, procedures to resolve conflicts of interest and a committee to monitor them.
provisions.counselNote: Counsel's reading: s.157 keeps the board responsible for managing or supervising management, so outsourced management still needs directors able to supervise it, which is the link to B-10.

provisions.title: Minimum number of directors
provisions.summary: A bank must have at least seven directors. A majority of them must be resident Canadians, or at least one half for a subsidiary of a foreign bank, measured at each election or appointment.
provisions.counselNote: Track residency at each appointment, not only at the annual meeting. A foreign-owned digital bank may qualify for the one-half rule, which is a planning point to confirm with the corporate secretary.

provisions.title: Conduct review committee
provisions.summary: The committee has at least three directors, most of them unaffiliated with the bank. It requires and reviews procedures for complying with Part XI, and identifies related-party dealings that could affect the bank's stability or solvency. Directors report on its work to the Superintendent within 90 days after each financial year.
provisions.counselNote: This committee is the statutory check on intragroup vendor contracts. Give it a standing agenda item for related-party services, with evidence of market terms.

provisions.title: Services
provisions.summary: A bank may contract with a related party for services used in its ordinary course of business, under a written contract. If such contracts leave all or substantially all management functions with non-employees, the Superintendent may order the bank to use employees for functions integral to its business.
provisions.counselNote: Keep core management functions in employee hands, or document why not. A digital bank that runs most operations through affiliates is the case the order power is aimed at.

provisions.title: Market terms and conditions
provisions.summary: A transaction with a related party must be on terms at least as favourable to the bank as market terms. Market terms are defined by reference to the bank's public terms or to what an arm's-length party would agree.
provisions.counselNote: Keep a contemporaneous pricing file for each affiliate contract. Without it, the bank cannot show that the terms met the test.

provisions.instrument: Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions Act
provisions.title: Integrity and security supervision
provisions.summary: The Superintendent supervises financial institutions to determine whether they have adequate policies and procedures to protect against threats to their integrity or security, including foreign interference. Under Bank Act s.645(1.1), the Superintendent may direct a bank without adequate policies to take the measures needed to remedy the situation.
provisions.counselNote: Keep the integrity and security policy current and evidence the vendor background checks, since the Superintendent can direct remediation under s.645(1.1).

provisions.instrument: OSFI Guideline B-10, Third-Party Risk Management
provisions.title: Accountability and the third-party risk framework
provisions.summary: The bank is ultimately accountable for managing risk from all third-party arrangements, and keeps accountability for outsourced services. The bank should have a framework with clear accountabilities, oversight functions, risk appetite and reporting. OSFI guidance is not law.
provisions.counselNote: Use this as the basis for the board's own third-party paper: who is accountable, what the risk appetite is, and what the board receives each quarter.

provisions.title: Governance and background checks
provisions.summary: Important decisions on strategy, risk appetite and oversight of senior management should be subject to effective governance. Responsible persons, employees and contractors should be subject to risk-based background checks, renewed regularly.
provisions.counselNote: Contractors are named, so vendor staff with access need risk-based checks like employees. Ask for the check results to be reported to the board.

provisions.title: Board responsibilities and risk appetite
provisions.summary: The board is responsible for the bank's business plan, strategy, risk appetite and culture, and oversees senior management and internal controls. Oversight function heads should have unfettered access to the board or relevant committee. OSFI expects to be promptly notified of substantive issues.
provisions.counselNote: Use the guideline's language in board minutes on vendor oversight. Confirm on OSFI's site that the 2018 text is still current.

provisions.instrument: OSFI Guideline E-17, Background Checks on Directors and Senior Management of FREs
provisions.ref: Assessment Policy, timing and criminal records
provisions.title: Background checks for responsible persons
provisions.summary: Applies to directors and senior management. Each bank needs a written assessment policy approved by senior management. Assessments are made before appointment and updated at intervals of no more than five years. Criminal records are to be verified at least every seven years. Some assessment work may be outsourced, but the bank makes the final determination.
provisions.counselNote: Build E-17 checks into the director onboarding file. E-17 still cross-refers to the earlier B-10 outsourcing text, so take current outsourcing terms from the 2023 B-10.

checklist: **Map ownership:** Track beneficial holdings, including controlled entities, against the 10% and 20% thresholds and the $12 billion equity point.
**Build s.373 into equity deals:** Make the Minister's approval a condition of any investor or vendor stake that creates or increases a significant interest.
**Test board composition:** Check residency under s.159, the two-thirds affiliation limit in s.163 and the disqualifications in s.160 before each appointment.
**Confirm committees:** Verify the audit and conduct review committees exist, with the membership required by s.195(2).
**Keep a related-party register:** List group companies, significant holders, directors and senior officers, and their controlled entities (s.486).
**Set a contract standard:** Put every intragroup service in a written contract priced at market terms, with a pricing file (ss.495(1)(a), 501).
**Schedule board reporting:** Give the board a regular report on critical third-party arrangements, incidents and exit plans, consistent with B-10 Principle 2.
**Run background checks:** Apply E-17 to directors and senior management, and the Integrity and Security Guideline to contractors with system access.
itAngle: **Beneficial ownership data:** The holdings register must roll up controlled entities and voting classes to apply the s.8 and s.2.2 tests. Errors here are governance errors.

**Background-check records:** Background checks involve criminal-record and, for higher-risk roles, credit information (Integrity Guideline P6; E-17). Limit access and align retention with the privacy controls in stage 7.
**Board dashboards:** Vendor concentration, critical arrangement status and incident data need a board-ready view that draws on the third-party register.
**Intragroup services:** Shared platforms bought from affiliates are related-party contracts. Map each service to s.495 and keep the evidence of market terms with the service catalogue.
virtualBankNotes: **Vendor-run operations:** A bank with a small staff may have most management performed by vendors or affiliates. That engages s.495(2) and OSFI's view that accountability cannot be contracted out.

**Technology expertise on the board:** OSFI expects senior management to be accountable for technology and cyber risk, and to resource it (B-13, Principle 1; 1.1.1), so the board should test that accountability, and a digital bank's risk sits mainly in its technology and vendors.
**Investor pool:** Fintech and platform investors often take stakes near the 10% or 20% lines. Each threshold changes the approval, reporting or major shareholder position under ss.8, 373 and 2.2.

**Group oversight:** Where a parent or foreign bank owns the bank, the subsidiary board should be satisfied that group policies adopted from a parent suit its own strategy and risk appetite (Corporate Governance Guideline, 2018).
pitfalls: **Stake creep:** Crossing 10% or 20% through controlled entities or related holdings without seeking the Minister's approval (ss.8, 373, 2.2).
**Affiliate contracts off market:** Pricing related-party services below market, or leaving management functions with non-employees, invites s.501 and s.495(2) problems.
**Rubber-stamp board:** Approving vendor arrangements without risk appetite, reporting or exit planning falls short of B-10 Principle 1.
**Unchecked contractors:** Letting vendor staff with system access skip background checks because they are not employees.

glossary.definition: A holding of more than 10% of a class of shares of a bank, counting shares held through entities the holder controls (Bank Act s.8).
A person holding more than 20% of a class of voting shares, or more than 30% of a class of non-voting shares, of a body corporate, counting controlled entities (Bank Act s.2.2).
A body corporate with no major shareholder. Banks that are widely held are treated differently under several Part VII rules (Bank Act s.2.3).
A person defined in s.486, including a significant-interest holder, a director or senior officer, and their controlled entities. Part XI restricts transactions with them.
A director affiliated with the bank. No more than two thirds of a bank's directors may be affiliated at any time (Bank Act s.163).
A committee of at least three directors, mostly unaffiliated, that oversees the bank's Part XI compliance (Bank Act s.195).
The terms at which a bank would deal with an arm's-length party, or the bank's public terms for the same service, used as the test for related-party transactions (Bank Act s.501).
Directors and senior management who must be assessed for integrity and suitability under OSFI Guideline E-17 and the Integrity and Security Guideline.
The risk, compliance, internal audit and similar functions that report on the bank's risks and must have access to the board or its committees.

title: Third-party risk under B-10
oneLiner: Under OSFI Guideline B-10 the bank keeps accountability for every third-party arrangement and scales its controls to risk and criticality.
keyPoints: **Scope:** OSFI Guideline B-10, Third-Party Risk Management, covers every third-party arrangement, by contract or otherwise, except arrangements with customers and employment contracts. Group, cloud and consultant arrangements are all in scope.

**Accountability stays with the bank:** The bank remains accountable for outsourced activities, for data shared with providers and for the third-party risk it takes on. Responsibility for security cannot be transferred by contract.

**Timing:** B-10 took effect on 1 May 2024 and replaced the 2009 outsourcing guideline. Arrangements made on or after that date should meet it, and older ones were to be updated at the earliest opportunity.
**No approval gate:** OSFI does not approve arrangements or require advance notice. It does expect prompt notice of substantive issues that affect the bank's critical operations.

**Risk and [[criticality]] drive the work:** The bank sets its own method for rating risk and criticality, then scales assessment, due diligence, contract terms, monitoring and exit planning to the result.

**Statute underneath:** Bank Act s.643(2)(a) gives OSFI access to records held by or on behalf of the bank, and s.645 lets OSFI direct a bank to fix an unsafe practice or weak integrity controls. The records rules in ss.238–245 shape where vendors may hold data.

conceptMap.caption: The bank keeps accountability for every arrangement; OSFI expects its controls to scale with risk and criticality.

deepDive.heading: Scope: what counts as a third-party arrangement
deepDive.lede: The definition is wide and the exclusions are narrow.
points: **Definition:** Any business or strategic arrangement with an entity or individual, by contract or otherwise, is a [[third-party arrangement]]. Outsourcing is only one kind.

**Illustrative inclusions:** Outsourced activities, independent consultants, mortgage, insurance and deposit brokers, utilities, financial market infrastructures, and cloud and other technology providers.

**Group services:** Services from a parent, affiliate or subsidiary, or through a joint venture or partnership, are expressly included. The text sets no separate regime for group providers, so check how OSFI would read a group arrangement.
**Exclusions:** Arrangements with customers, such as depositors and borrowers, and employment contracts. A partner that sells the bank's products is a third-party arrangement; see stage 8.
**No written contract, still in scope:** Lacking a contract does not remove the arrangement or its risk. B-10 section 3.2 deals with these cases.
deepDive.takeaway: Build the inventory from the definition, not from the contracts the bank happens to hold.

deepDive.heading: The framework and the inventory come first
deepDive.lede: OSFI expects a framework and an inventory before it looks at individual contracts.
points: **Framework:** The bank needs an enterprise-wide third-party risk management framework (TPRMF) that matches its risk appetite, covers the lifecycle from sourcing to exit, and is reviewed regularly (1.2.1).

**Elements (1.2.2):** Accountability, including oversight functions; risk appetite and limits; a risk and criticality method; approved policies; an inventory of third parties by risk and criticality; and aggregation of exposures and trends.

**Criticality (2.1.1):** Weigh the severity of loss if a provider or subcontractor fails, how easily the service can be replaced, how far it supports [[critical operations]], and the impact of an exit.

**Risk (2.1.2):** Consider the probability of failure, the bank's ability to test controls, the provider's financial health and step-in risk, subcontracting, concentration, data and cyber practices, and other risks.
**No tiers:** B-10 uses descriptive labels such as critical and high-risk but sets no scale or thresholds. The bank must define its own, document them and apply them consistently.
deepDive.takeaway: The methodology is the bank's responsibility, and it will be judged on how consistently it is applied.

deepDive.heading: Assess and diligence through the lifecycle
deepDive.lede: Assessment starts before signing and repeats through renewal and material change.
points: **Before entry:** Assess risk and criticality before the arrangement starts and throughout its life, including at renewal and on material change. Count the risks it reduces as well as those it creates.
**Minimum content:** Each assessment shows alignment with risk appetite, documented criticality, an established risk level, and a monitoring and mitigation plan (2.2.1.1).
**Due diligence:** Scale it to risk and criticality. Annex 1 lists 17 factors for high-risk and critical arrangements, from financial strength and subcontractor reliance to portability and insurance.
**Foreign providers (2.2.2.3):** Where a provider or subcontractor operates abroad, review the foreign legal requirements and the political, legal, security, economic and social risks.

**[[concentration risk]] (2.2.3.1):** Assess it before contracting and on an ongoing basis, by geography, supplier, subcontractor, business unit and legal entity. Assess systemic concentration as far as possible.
deepDive.takeaway: A signed contract is the start of monitoring, not the end of assessment.

deepDive.heading: Subcontractors and the written agreement
deepDive.lede: Concentration often sits one layer down, in the provider's own suppliers.
points: **Before entry (Principle 5):** Identify the provider's subcontracting practices, including the number and criticality of its subcontractors and the effect on the bank's concentration.

**Subcontracting controls (2.2.4.2):** Depending on risk, the contract may prohibit subcontracting of certain functions, require written notice of new or replaced subcontractors, let the bank refuse one, and let the bank audit it.

**Written agreement (Principle 6):** Each arrangement should have a written contract or agreement, such as an SLA, setting out each party's rights and responsibilities and reviewed by legal counsel (2.3.1.1).
**Annex 2:** For high-risk and critical arrangements, include the 14 provisions in Annex 2, from scope and location to default, termination and insurance.

**[[Standardized contracts|standardized contract]] (3.1):** Take-it-or-leave-it terms, such as those of a utility, are allowed. The bank must still assess the residual risk and accept it formally where applicable, and plan redundancy and workarounds.

**External auditor (3.3):** Before buying management consulting from its external auditor, confirm the auditor meets Canadian independence standards. Do not obtain from the auditor actuarial services or internal audit services for accounting controls (B-10 3.3.2, with its stated carve-outs).
deepDive.takeaway: Ask for the subcontractor list before signing, not after an incident.

deepDive.heading: Access, audit, continuity and exit
deepDive.lede: The bank and OSFI need to see inside the provider, so the contract has to say so.
points: **Evaluation and audit (2.3.3.3):** OSFI expects the contract to let the bank and OSFI evaluate the provider's risk management, or appoint independent auditors to do so, and to give access to audit reports on the service. The bank should use a range of methods, including pooled audits and independent reports.

**Records (s.643(2)(a)):** OSFI's right of access reaches records held by or on behalf of the bank, so records a provider holds for the bank fall within it. The bank's records must generally be kept at its head office or another place in Canada (s.239(1)), with limited exceptions in s.239(3) and (3.1).

**Continuity (2.3.4.1):** The provider should set out its continuity measures, test its business continuity and disaster recovery plans regularly, share the results and fix material gaps. The bank plans for severe but plausible disruption.

**[[Exit plans|exit plan]] (2.3.5.1):** For high-risk and critical arrangements, set triggers and two playbooks, one for a stressed exit after provider failure and one for a planned exit. Check the notice and post-termination service terms in the contract.

**Resolution (CDIC Act s.39.15):** After an order under CDIC Act s.39.13(1), made by the Governor in Council, no one may terminate or amend the bank's agreement only because of insolvency, the order, a change of control or a monetary default that is remedied within 60 days after the order. Contrary terms have no effect (see stage 13).
deepDive.takeaway: Exit and resolution terms matter most when the bank is weakest, so draft them at signing.

deepDive.heading: Hong Kong and Canada compared
deepDive.lede: The core contract terms overlap; the regulatory trigger is what differs.
points: **SA-2 trigger:** SA-2 covers outsourcing generally but asks the bank to discuss outsourcing of a banking-related business area with the HKMA in advance (SA-2 1.3.2), and the Digital Bank Guideline expects advance discussion of material outsourcing. B-10 has no such gate: every arrangement is in scope, scaled to risk and criticality.
**B-10 trigger:** There is no advance discussion and no approval. B-10 applies to every third-party arrangement, scaled to risk and criticality, so the bank must classify all of them.
**Carried over:** Access, audit, subcontracting, continuity and exit terms appear in both regimes. Canada expects the same core terms, now set out in Annex 2.
**Canada adds statute:** Records location and access (Bank Act ss.238–245), related-party rules for vendors (Part XI), and consumer duties for agents who sell the bank's products (s.627.15).
**Reuse with care:** Hong Kong vendor templates can be reused, but each clause must be re-mapped to Annex 1, Annex 2 and the Canadian statutes.
deepDive.takeaway: Keep the Hong Kong advance-discussion habit as a judgment call, since B-10 does not require it.

provisions.instrument: OSFI Guideline B-10, Third-Party Risk Management
provisions.title: Risk and criticality assessment; due diligence
provisions.summary: The bank should assess risk and criticality before entering an arrangement, at renewal and on material change, and set due diligence in proportion to both. For high-risk and critical arrangements, Annex 1 lists 17 factors to consider.
provisions.counselNote: Keep each assessment on file with its criticality finding, risk level and monitoring plan. The Annex 1 factors double as a vendor due-diligence checklist.

provisions.instrument: OSFI Guideline B-10, Third-Party Risk Management
provisions.title: Provisions for third-party agreements
provisions.summary: Lists 14 provisions to include in agreements for high-risk and critical arrangements. The list is non-exhaustive, and the bank should consider the same provisions for other arrangements. They cover scope and location, subcontracting, performance measures, ownership and access, data security, notifications, default and termination, and insurance.
provisions.counselNote: Use Annex 2 as the drafting backbone of the vendor-contract toolkit. Where a provider refuses a provision, record the gap and who accepted the risk.

provisions.instrument: OSFI Guideline B-10, Third-Party Risk Management
provisions.title: Evaluation and audit rights for the bank and OSFI
provisions.summary: The agreement should let the bank and OSFI evaluate the provider's risk management practices, or appoint independent auditors to do so, and access audit reports on the service. The bank should use a range of audit and information methods.
provisions.counselNote: Draft audit rights in favour of OSFI expressly, not only the bank. The text does not say whether the right reaches subcontractors' premises, so check the position before drafting.

provisions.instrument: OSFI Guideline B-10, Third-Party Risk Management
provisions.title: Contingency and exit plans
provisions.summary: Plans should be proportionate to risk and criticality. For high-risk and critical arrangements they should set triggers, a stressed-exit and a non-stressed exit playbook, reference the contract's notice and post-termination terms, and cover severe but plausible scenarios.
provisions.counselNote: Build the exit plan with the business before signing, and test it. Notice periods and post-termination service obligations must be long enough to carry the plan out, so negotiate them early.

provisions.title: Examination of banks
provisions.summary: The Superintendent must examine each bank at least once a year, including whether it has adequate policies against threats to its integrity or security. The Superintendent also has a right of access to any records, cash, assets and security held by or on behalf of a bank.
provisions.counselNote: The access right reaches records a vendor holds for the bank, so contracts should not stop OSFI from reaching them. The examination also covers integrity and security policies, which vendor controls must support.

provisions.title: Requirement to maintain copies and process information in Canada
provisions.summary: The Superintendent must direct a bank not to keep copies of its records, or process related data, abroad where that is incompatible with OSFI's responsibilities or the Minister advises it is against the national interest. Where a bank exempt under s.239(3.1) or s.251(3) keeps records outside Canada, OSFI may order a Canadian copy if it lacks immediate, direct, complete and ongoing access, and the bank must comply without delay.
provisions.counselNote: Before a vendor hosts or processes record data outside Canada, check this section, and keep the contract able to deliver a Canadian copy quickly. The Canadian-copy power applies only to a bank exempt under s.239(3.1) or s.251(3).

provisions.title: Protection of records
provisions.summary: The bank and its agents must take reasonable precautions to prevent loss or destruction of records and falsification of entries, to facilitate detection of inaccuracies, and to keep unauthorized persons from accessing the information.
provisions.counselNote: Whether a particular vendor is an agent in law is a question for Legal. Either way, write the precautions into the contract as measurable controls.

provisions.title: Services
provisions.summary: A bank may buy services from a related party under a written contract if the services are used in the ordinary course of business. If such contracts leave all or substantially all management functions with non-employees, the Superintendent may order the bank to have employees exercise the integral functions.
provisions.counselNote: A vendor that is a related party, such as a shareholder with a significant interest or an entity a director controls, must fit this route or another Part XI route. Keep integral management functions with bank employees.

provisions.title: Market terms and conditions
provisions.summary: A transaction with a related party must be on terms at least as favourable to the bank as market terms. For a service the bank offers the public, market terms mean terms no more or less favourable than those the public receives.
provisions.counselNote: Group and related-party vendor contracts need evidence of market terms on file, such as benchmark quotes or an arm's-length comparison.

provisions.instrument: Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions Act
provisions.title: Office established; objects of the Office
provisions.summary: One object of OSFI is to supervise whether financial institutions have adequate policies and procedures against threats to their integrity or security, including foreign interference. If they do not, OSFI must promptly advise the board and management and require corrective measures.
provisions.counselNote: This is the statutory basis for OSFI's interest in vendor security and foreign-interference controls. It also means a vendor integrity problem can reach the board quickly.

provisions.instrument: OSFI Guideline E-21, Operational Risk Management and Resilience
provisions.title: Critical third parties in operational resilience
provisions.summary: Critical operations must be mapped end to end, including third parties, and a critical third party's resilience should be assessed. Scenario testing should cover critical third-party disruption and coordinate with those providers where possible. Sections 1 and 2 applied from 22 August 2024, section 4 was due by 1 September 2025, and full adherence was due by 1 September 2026, and testing of all critical operations is due by 1 September 2027.
provisions.counselNote: Keep the E-21 critical-operations map and the B-10 criticality ratings consistent with each other. OSFI said it would supervise selectively during the transition, and the full-adherence date has now passed.

provisions.instrument: OSFI Integrity and Security Guideline (issued 31 January 2024)
provisions.title: Third parties: equivalent controls and foreign interference
