The Bank Act sets the procedures, a prescribed 56-day period, seven-year records and disclosure duties, and the contract must route each complaint to the bank in time to meet them.
require: **Procedures and officers:** the bank must establish complaint procedures satisfactory to the Commissioner of the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada, designate officers to receive and deal with complaints, and file the procedures with the Commissioner (Bank Act s.627.43(1)(a)–(c) and (3), statute).

**Wide definition:** a complaint is any dissatisfaction, whether justified or not, expressed to an institution about a product or service or the way it is offered, sold or provided (s.627.01(1), statute). Whether a complaint made only to the Supplier is expressed to the Bank is for Legal to confirm (drafting inference). Contact with a partner's sales or call-centre team can be a complaint on that basis (drafting inference).

**56-day period:** the prescribed period is 56 days after the day the complaint is received (Financial Consumer Protection Framework Regulations s.14, statute). Whether receipt by a partner counts is for Legal to confirm, so forwarding must be fast enough to keep the clock (drafting inference).
**Acknowledgment and records:** the bank must acknowledge each complaint in writing and keep a record for at least seven years with the particulars listed in s.627.44 (ss.627.43(4), 627.44, statute).

**Disclosure and external body:** the bank must disclose its procedures, the external complaints body and the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada's (the Agency's) mailing address, website address and telephone number to customers and the public (s.627.65). Every bank must be a member of the external complaints body (s.627.48(3)). The body is reported as OBSI (reported; check the designation).

sources.label: Bank Act
Financial Consumer Protection Framework Regulations
sources.note: In force 30 June 2022.

drafting: **Shared channels:** the bank's complaint wording must appear in the partner's app, call scripts and written replies, not only on the bank's own site (s.627.65; drafting inference).
**Chain of custody:** each complaint record that the partner holds should show the time of receipt, so that the 56-day period can be shown to have run from the right date (drafting inference).
terms.cloud: Contact-centre and CRM platforms often set short retention or deletion cycles by default. Override them in the contract so that complaint records survive for at least seven years.

playbook.why: Bank Act Part XII.2 is statute. It requires complaint procedures, records and disclosure (ss.627.43, 627.44, 627.65), and the 56-day period is in regulations. A partner that takes complaints is inside the bank's process, so the contract must route them to the bank.
preferred: **Any dissatisfaction counts:** the Supplier logs every expression of dissatisfaction as a complaint, whether or not it considers it justified, and never screens it out (s.627.01(1)).

**Forward within [2] Business Days:** the Supplier passes each complaint, with the particulars required by s.627.44, to the Bank's complaint officers within [2] Business Days of receipt (the 56-day limit is in SOR/2021-181 s.14; the 2-Business-Day period is a drafting choice).
**Bank-led acknowledgment and disclosure:** the Bank sends the written acknowledgment under s.627.43(4). The Supplier gives customers the Bank's disclosure wording at first contact (s.627.65).
**Seven-year records:** the Supplier keeps a copy of each complaint record for at least seven years, in the form s.627.44 requires, and delivers it to the Bank on request.
**Trained front line:** call-centre and sales staff are trained to recognise and forward complaints, and never describe the Bank's procedures or staff in a misleading way (ss.627.02, 627.43(2)).
fallback: **Own complaints log:** accept that the Supplier keeps its own log, only if it copies each entry to the Bank within [2] Business Days and the log meets s.627.44.
**Longer forwarding for low volumes:** accept [5] Business Days for a partner with fewer than [ ] complaints a year, only if the Bank's reporting shows that the 56-day period is still met.

**Partner resolution of small complaints:** accept that the Supplier resolves some complaints itself, only if the Bank has approved that procedure in writing, the Bank receives each outcome, and the customer keeps access to the Bank's route (s.627.15(b)).
redLines: **Routing to the Bank:** no term that stops complaints reaching the Bank's designated officers or that sends them only to the Supplier, because the bank must run the procedures (s.627.43(1)(c)) and customers must have access to them (s.627.15(b)).
**Clock:** no forwarding period that could cause the bank to miss the 56-day period (SOR/2021-181 s.14).
**Records:** no deletion or destruction of complaint records before the end of the seven-year period (s.627.44).
model: (a) Scope. Each expression of dissatisfaction made to the Supplier about a product or service of the Bank, or about the way it is offered, sold or provided, whether or not the Supplier considers it justified, is a complaint for this clause.

(b) Routing. The Supplier shall tell each complainant how to use the Bank's complaint procedures, in the wording the Bank supplies, and shall refer each complaint to the Bank's designated complaint officers within [two] Business Days after receipt. The Supplier shall not resolve a complaint itself unless the Bank has approved that procedure in writing.

(c) Time limit. [The Supplier and the Bank agree that a complaint is received by the Bank when the Supplier receives it.] The Supplier acknowledges that the Bank must deal with each complaint within the prescribed period of 56 days after it is received, and shall not delay any referral in a way that puts that period at risk.

(d) Records. The Supplier shall keep a record of each complaint with the particulars required by section 627.44 of the Bank Act, including the original or recording, the names and contact details of the parties, the dates of receipt and resolution, the nature of the complaint, the actions taken and any compensation. It shall keep each record for at least seven years and deliver it to the Bank on request.

(e) Disclosure and information. The Supplier shall give each complainant the information the Bank specifies, including the Bank's complaint procedures and the contact details of the external complaints body. It shall not describe its own or the Bank's procedures or staff in a misleading way, including by use of the term ombudsman.

(f) External complaints body. The Supplier shall cooperate with the external complaints body in any complaint referred to it, and shall provide the information it needs within [ten] Business Days of request.
watchFor: **Narrow definition:** terms that treat only written, formal letters as complaints, so that calls and social-media messages are not logged. Section 627.01(1) covers any dissatisfaction.
**Silent resolution:** the Supplier resolves complaints and reports only closed cases, so the Bank misses the record and the clock (s.627.44).
**Long forwarding:** a forwarding period of [30] days, which uses most of the 56-day period (SOR/2021-181 s.14).
**Deletion on exit:** the Supplier deletes complaint records at termination, before the seven-year period has run (s.627.44; see the termination clause).
**Misleading names:** a 'customer ombudsman' desk, or a reviewer described as independent when it is part of the Bank's or the Supplier's own staff (s.627.43(2)).

pushback.says: Complaints go to our customer team, which resolves them quickly. Your forwarding is extra work.
pushback.reply: Dissatisfaction expressed to the bank is a complaint whether or not it is justified (s.627.01(1)), and the bank must run the procedures and keep the record for seven years (ss.627.43, 627.44). Forward within [2] Business Days and you may keep your own log as well.

pushback.says: Two Business Days is impossible for our call centre.
pushback.reply: The 56-day period is what the regulations prescribe (SOR/2021-181 s.14), and the bank must meet it. Our most generous position is [5] Business Days, and only for low-volume partners (see fallback).

pushback.says: We will not keep records after the contract ends.
pushback.reply: The bank must keep complaint records for at least seven years (s.627.44). We propose that the records, or a full copy, are handed over to the Bank at exit.

playbook.escalate: Suggested: the Head of Customer Complaints and the Head of Legal approve deviations, and any change to the forwarding period or to record-keeping goes to the Chief Compliance Officer.

terms.title: Deposit insurance statements by partners
terms.summary: Partners that show deposit products or hold customer money can imply that deposits are insured when they are not. The CDIC by-law sets the prescribed membership wording, the sign and badge placements and the brochure duty, and bars misleading representations by any person.
require: **Prohibition for everyone:** no person may make a false, misleading or deceptive representation about what is or is not a deposit, what is insured, or who is a member institution (SOR/96-542 s.2, statute). This binds the partner directly.

**Prescribed wording:** a membership representation in advertising uses one of the prescribed phrases, such as 'Member of the CDIC', and must not suggest that a non-member is a member or that an ineligible deposit is insured (ss.4(1), 4(2), statute).

**Sign and badge:** the membership sign appears on the home page of the bank's website (s.5(2)). The digital badge appears on the home page, each deposit product landing page, the first page after log-on that shows insured deposits, and each page showing the sign (s.7(1)).

**Shared home pages:** a member that shares its home page with a non-member must not display the badge there (s.7(3), statute). The membership sign must still not create a misleading impression (ss.5(3), 7(5)).

**Brochure:** when an eligible deposit account is opened, the depositor receives the brochure in digital or printed form as part of the process (s.6(2)). Ineligible deposit instruments carry the warning in s.9 (statute).

**CDIC's view (reported):** CDIC's April 2026 bulletin reportedly treats 'insured' or 'covered' as misleading and prefers 'eligible for deposit insurance' (reported; check). It reportedly expects members to inform fintech partners of the by-law duty.

sources.label: CDIC Deposit Insurance Information By-law
sources.note: SOR/96-542, current to 24 July 2025.

sources.label: CDIC bulletin
sources.ref: April 2026 bulletin on deposit insurance information
sources.note: Reported; check the current bulletin before relying on the wording point.

drafting: **Partner's own app:** the partner's app home page, product pages and first post-log-on screen are all within s.7(1) if they show deposits. Map each screen in the placement schedule (drafting inference).
**Brochure link:** the digital badge carries a hyperlink to the brochure, unless it is on an automated teller machine (s.7(4)). Keep that link working on partner screens (drafting inference).

playbook.why: The CDIC Deposit Insurance Information By-law is in-force subordinate legislation. Its prohibition in s.2 binds any person who speaks for the bank, and its wording and placement rules (ss.4, 5, 6, 7) bind the bank itself. A partner's app is a place where these rules can fail.
preferred: **Approved wording only:** the partner uses only the Bank's approved membership wording, sign and badge files, and does not describe a deposit as 'insured' or 'covered' where that would mislead (ss.2, 4(2)). CDIC reportedly prefers 'eligible for deposit insurance' (reported; check).
**Placement schedule:** a schedule lists each page or screen where the sign, badge and brochure appear, and the partner's pages follow it (ss.5(2), 6(2), 7(1)).

**No badge on shared home pages:** where the partner's app and the Bank share a home page, the badge is not displayed there, and the membership sign is placed so that it does not mislead (ss.5(3), 7(3), 7(5); drafting inference on placement).
**Brochure at onboarding:** the partner provides the Bank's brochure, digital or printed, as part of account opening for any eligible deposit (s.6(2)).

**Ineligible products flagged:** any instrument evidencing a deposit that is not eligible to be insured carries the s.9 warning, and no such product appears on a page showing insured deposits (ss.7(5), 9).
fallback: **Partner-written copy:** accept copy written by the partner, only if the Bank approves every representation about deposits and membership before it is published.

**Badge in a menu:** accept the digital badge in a navigation menu, only if it is visible on each required page (s.7(1)) and keeps its brochure hyperlink (s.7(4)). The April 2026 bulletin reportedly accepts this (reported; check).

**Non-deposit products on shared pages:** accept the partner's own non-deposit product on a shared page, only if no badge or membership sign is shown next to that product and the copy cannot suggest that it is insured (ss.5(3), 7(3), 7(5)).
redLines: **No misleading deposit-insurance claims:** no term that lets the partner make a false, misleading or deceptive statement about what is a deposit, what is insured or who is a member (SOR/96-542 s.2), or that shows an ineligible deposit as insured (s.4(2)). CDIC reportedly also treats 'insured' or 'covered' as misleading for eligible products (reported; check).
**No badge where barred:** no badge on a home page shared with a non-member, and no sign or badge on any page where it would give a misleading impression (s.7(3), s.7(5), s.5(3)).
**No eligible deposit without the brochure:** no account opening for an eligible deposit without the brochure given to the depositor (s.6(2)).
model: (a) Representations. The Supplier shall not make any false, misleading or deceptive representation about what constitutes, or does not constitute, a deposit, a deposit insured by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation (CDIC), or who is a member institution. It shall not describe any product as 'insured' or 'covered' by deposit insurance, and shall describe eligibility only in wording the Bank approves in writing.

(b) Membership statements. Any statement by the Supplier about the Bank's membership shall use only the wording the Bank supplies or approves, and shall not give the impression that the Supplier, or any product that is not eligible to be insured, is a member or is insured.

(c) Signs and badges. The Supplier shall display the membership sign and the digital badge only where [Schedule [ ] (Deposit Insurance Placements)] specifies, using the files the Bank supplies. Where a home page is shared with a person that is not a member institution, the Supplier shall not display the badge on that page.

(d) Brochure. As part of the account opening process for each deposit eligible to be insured, the Supplier shall give the depositor the Bank's brochure in the form the Bank specifies, digital or printed, and shall keep evidence of its delivery for [five] years.

(e) Ineligible instruments. Where the Supplier issues any instrument evidencing a deposit that is not eligible to be insured, or takes a telephone instruction to open such an account, it shall place on its face one of the warning statements in section 9(1) or 9(2) of the CDIC by-law and, for a telephone instruction or transaction, give the oral representation and written notice that section 9(3) requires.

(f) Notice and correction. The Supplier shall tell the Bank promptly of any inquiry from the Regulator, including CDIC, about its representations, and shall correct any non-compliant material within [two] Business Days of notice from the Bank.
watchFor: **Own-brand framing:** the partner's app calls the account 'protected', 'secure deposits' or 'insured' without explaining the term. That is misleading wording (SOR/96-542 s.2).
**Badge on shared pages:** the partner's home page carries the badge although it is shared with a non-member product (s.7(3)).
**Review after launch:** wording and screens go live before the Bank reviews them, or the partner changes them without notice to the Bank.
**Hidden placements:** the sign or badge appears only in a footer or a menu that the customer must open to find it, rather than on each required page (ss.5(2), 7(1)).
**Skipped brochure step:** the partner's onboarding flow omits the brochure because it sits outside the Bank's product page (s.6(2)).

pushback.says: Our users already know the bank is insured, so the wording does not matter.
pushback.reply: The by-law applies to any person who makes a representation about deposit insurance (s.2), and it prescribes the wording and placements (ss.4, 7). Your app must use the approved wording.

pushback.says: We have a navigation menu, so the badge can sit there.
pushback.reply: Only if it is visible on each of the required pages (s.7(1)). The April 2026 CDIC bulletin reportedly takes the same view (reported; check). We will confirm the placement before launch.

pushback.says: Calling it 'insured' is clearer for customers.
pushback.reply: CDIC reportedly treats 'insured' and 'covered' as misleading and prefers 'eligible for deposit insurance' (reported; check). Under s.2 this is a legal risk for both of us, not a style choice.

playbook.escalate: Suggested: the Chief Compliance Officer and the Head of Legal approve any deviation, and any deviation on a deposit-insurance representation goes to the Chief Risk Officer with the Head of Deposits.

terms.title: Electronic marketing by partners (CASL)
terms.homeNote: The partnership or referral agreement with the partner.
terms.summary: Partners who send marketing emails, texts or other commercial electronic messages for the Bank create liability for the Bank under Canada's anti-spam law (CASL). The agreement must put consent, sender identity, unsubscribe and record-keeping on the partner, and must give the Bank the evidence it needs to rely on the due diligence defence.
require: **Consent:** a commercial electronic message may be sent to an electronic address only if the recipient consented, expressly or impliedly (CASL s.6(1)(a)). Statute.

**Message content:** each message must identify the sender and the person on whose behalf it is sent, give contact details valid for at least 60 days, and carry an unsubscribe mechanism (CASL s.6(2)-(3)). Statute.

**Unsubscribe:** the mechanism must be free to the recipient and work by the same electronic means or another electronic means, and effect must be given without delay and in any event within 10 business days (CASL s.11(1), (3)). Statute.

**Aiding and vicarious liability:** no one may aid, induce, procure or cause a breach (CASL s.9). The Bank is liable for a breach by its agent acting within the scope of its authority (s.32), subject to a due diligence defence (s.33(1)). Statute.

**Penalties:** the maximum administrative monetary penalty is $10 million for a corporation (CASL s.20(4)). Officers and directors are liable if they directed, authorised, assented to, acquiesced in or participated in a violation (s.31). Statute.

**Partner arrangements:** the Bank may not cooperate with an agent or intermediary to sell or further the sale of its products unless the partner complies with the consumer provisions, gives customers access to the Bank's complaints procedures, allows whistleblowing and observes the anti-reprisal rule (Bank Act s.627.15(a)-(d)). Statute.

**Advertising and customer lists:** advertisements by the Bank in Canada must be accurate, clear and not misleading (Bank Act s.627.14), and sharing personal information needs knowledge and consent (PIPEDA Sch. 1, cl. 4.3). Statute. Partner marketing is the Bank's advertising in practice (drafting inference).

sources.label: PIPEDA
Bank Act

drafting: **Consent records:** the Supplier keeps, for each address, the type of consent, its date, its source and the notice given, so the Bank can show consent if challenged (drafting inference; CASL s.33(1) turns on due diligence).

**Unsubscribe in each message:** the unsubscribe link sits in every message, not only on a separate web page, so that the recipient can use the same channel the message came through (drafting inference from CASL s.11(1)(a)).
terms.cloud: Marketing platforms usually hold the subscriber list and apply their own unsubscribe and retention rules. Require the Bank's suppression list to be the master copy, with same-day export rights.

playbook.why: CASL is statute with administrative monetary penalties of up to $10 million for a corporation (s.20(4)) and vicarious liability for the Bank (s.32). The consent, identification and unsubscribe rules are the floor, and the Bank must be able to show due diligence (s.33(1)).
preferred: **Bank as named sender:** every message identifies the Bank as the person on whose behalf it is sent, and the Supplier as sender, with postal and electronic contact details that stay valid for at least 60 days (CASL s.6(2)(a)-(b), (3)).

**Consent and records:** express or implied consent recorded per address, with the notice given and its source, kept for [the Records period] and delivered to the Bank within [2] Business Days of request (drafting inference; CASL s.33(1) turns on due diligence, and s.10(1) sets what a request for express consent must state).

**Central unsubscribe:** unsubscribe requests passed to the Bank the same day and applied to the Supplier's lists without delay, and in any event within 10 Business Days of the request (CASL s.11(1), (3)).

**Approved templates and lists:** the Bank approves each template, offer and contact list in advance; the Supplier uses no address or list it has not shown the Bank the consent basis for (drafting inference).
fallback: **Spot checks:** accept spot checks of sent messages in place of approval of each message, only if templates and any new offer, price or condition are still approved in advance.
**Partner's own platform for suppression:** accept the Supplier's platform as the suppression store, only if the Bank's list is updated the same day and effect is given within the CASL period.

**Supplier-led sending for its own products:** accept the Supplier sending its own messages, only if the Bank is not named as a person on whose behalf the message is sent and the messages do not use the Bank's name or branding.
redLines: **Consent:** no message to an address without the recipient's express or implied consent (CASL s.6(1)(a)).
**Identity and unsubscribe:** no message that omits the sender or the person on whose behalf it is sent, or that lacks a working unsubscribe mechanism (CASL s.6(2)).
**Unsubscribe timing:** no unsubscribe process that costs the recipient money, requires more than the same or another electronic means, or gives effect later than the CASL period (CASL s.11(1), (3)).
model: (a) The Supplier shall send a commercial electronic message for the Bank only to a person who has given express or implied consent to receive it. The Supplier shall keep a record of each consent, its date, its source and the notice given, for [the Records period], and shall give the Bank a copy within [2] Business Days of request.

(b) Each such message shall identify the Supplier and the Bank as the persons on whose behalf it is sent, give contact details valid for at least 60 days after sending, and include an unsubscribe mechanism that is free to the recipient and works by the same electronic means or another electronic means.

(c) The Supplier shall give effect to each unsubscribe request without delay, and in any event within [10] Business Days after the request is sent, and shall pass the request to the Bank on the same Business Day. It shall not send further messages of the class unsubscribed from to that address.

(d) The Supplier shall not send, cause or assist the sending of any commercial electronic message that does not comply with Applicable Law, and shall use no address, list or content that the Bank has not approved in writing.

(e) The Supplier shall use Personal Information for marketing only as permitted by [the Personal Information clause] and Applicable Law, and shall not give any list it supplies to the Bank unless it was lawfully obtained.

(f) The Supplier shall tell the Bank promptly of any complaint, inquiry or notice from a Regulator about a message sent for the Bank, and shall cooperate in the response. [The Liability clause] applies to any breach of this clause.
watchFor: **Partner as sole sender:** messages sent in the partner's name only, so that the Bank is not identified as the person on whose behalf they are sent (CASL s.6(2)(a)).
**Unsubscribe by login only:** unsubscribe that needs an account login, a multi-step process, or a web form that lapses after a short period (CASL s.11(1), (2)).

**Consent by bundled terms:** consent treated as given by accepting general terms or a pre-ticked box. Express consent must be requested clearly and simply, with its purposes and the requester's identity (CASL s.10(1)).
**Bank indemnity for partner messages:** a clause requiring the Bank to indemnify the Supplier for CASL claims arising from the Supplier's own messages or lists.
**Data licence for partner marketing:** a licence to use customer contacts for the Supplier's own marketing, which needs its own consent and notice (see the Personal Information clause).

pushback.says: Our platform manages consent and unsubscribes for all our clients, so the Bank does not need to see the records.
pushback.reply: The Bank is liable for a violation by its agent acting within its authority (CASL s.32). Its only defence is due diligence (s.33(1)), which needs evidence that it can see. Records must be delivered on request.

pushback.says: We will process unsubscribes within a week as standard.
pushback.reply: CASL s.11(3) requires effect without delay, and within 10 business days at the latest. We require same-day passing to the Bank's suppression list, so a weekly batch does not meet our terms (drafting inference).

pushback.says: The customer relationship means we do not need consent for these messages.
pushback.reply: CASL s.6 applies to commercial electronic messages to any electronic address. Implied consent counts only where a case listed in s.10(9) applies, such as an existing business relationship, and the regulations define those cases further. We need the consent basis recorded for each address before any message is sent (drafting inference).

playbook.escalate: Suggested: the Chief Privacy Officer and Head of Legal approve deviations on consent or records; any departure from the unsubscribe or sender-identity terms goes to the Chief Compliance Officer.

terms.title: Contests and promotions run with partners
terms.homeNote: The partnership or referral agreement with the partner.
terms.summary: Partners often run prize draws, contests and loyalty promotions for the Bank. The Criminal Code restricts paid chance-based games, the Competition Act requires fair disclosure of prizes and odds, and the Bank Act bars undue pressure and misleading advertising. The agreement must fix the rules and give the Bank approval and control.
require: **Disclosure:** the promotion must make adequate and fair disclosure of the number and approximate value of prizes, the areas they relate to and any fact that materially affects the chances of winning (Competition Act s.74.06(a)). Statute. Breach is reviewable conduct.

**Timing and selection:** prizes must not be unduly delayed, and participants must be selected on the basis of skill or at random in each area to which prizes are allocated (Competition Act s.74.06(b), (c)). Statute.

**Paid chance games:** a game of chance or mixed chance and skill in which the entrant pays money or other valuable consideration is an offence (Criminal Code s.206(1)(f)). Free entry and a skill-testing question are common practice to stay outside it (drafting inference; check the current Competition Bureau position).

**Pressure:** the Bank may not impose undue pressure to obtain a product or service as a condition for obtaining another product or service from it or an affiliate (Bank Act s.627.04(a)). Statute. Making a purchase a condition of a prize is treated as undue pressure in the Bank's policy (drafting inference).
**Messages about contests:** a contest message sent electronically is a commercial electronic message and needs consent and an unsubscribe mechanism (CASL s.6). Statute.
**Quebec:** Quebec has its own rules for publicity contests, overseen by the Régie des alcools, des courses et des jeux (reported; check).

sources.label: Criminal Code
sources.note: The offence turns on whether the entrant pays and whether the game is one of chance or of mixed chance and skill; how courts treat the mixed form is a question for Legal.

sources.label: Competition Act
Bank Act

drafting: **Official rules:** the Bank approves written rules covering eligibility, entry method, prizes, odds, regions, closing date, selection method and how winners are notified, and the rules sit in a schedule that changes only by agreement (drafting inference).
**Release forms:** avoid a release that waives all claims against the Bank or the partner as a condition of receiving a prize; the Bank's own redress rights must survive (drafting inference).

playbook.why: The Criminal Code, the Competition Act and the Bank Act are statute, and each sets a floor for contests: no paid chance-based game, fair disclosure of prizes and odds, and no undue pressure or misleading advertising. The Bank is the party whose advertising and product sales are affected, so it must control the terms.
preferred: **Bank approval of rules:** written official rules approved by the Bank before launch, covering prizes, values, regions, odds and any fact that affects the chances of winning (Competition Act s.74.06(a)).

**Free entry and skill question:** entry without purchase, and a skill-testing question before any prize where the format is intended to be one of skill (practice only: s.206(1)(f) turns on payment, not on a skill question; the Competition Bureau position is for Legal to check).

**Disclosure in the advertisement:** the prize, its approximate value, the regions and the odds, or a clear link to the rules, in every promotional message and advertisement (s.74.06(a); Bank Act s.627.14).

**Selection and prize delivery:** selection by the published method, with audit records; prizes delivered within [30] days of winner confirmation and any delay reported to the Bank at once (s.74.06(b), (c)).
fallback: **Chance elements:** accept a format with a random element, only if it is free to enter, Legal has cleared it under the Criminal Code, and the rules disclose the chances.
**Regional prizes:** accept different prizes by region, only if the rules disclose each region's prizes, values and odds (Competition Act s.74.06(a)).
**Fulfilment by a third party:** accept delivery by the partner's fulfilment vendor, only if the Bank remains responsible for the timing and the delay limits apply.
redLines: **Paid chance games:** no contest, game of chance or game of mixed chance and skill in which entrants pay money or other valuable consideration (Criminal Code s.206(1)(f)).

**Disclosure and selection:** no promotion without adequate and fair disclosure of prizes, values, regions and chance-affecting facts, or with selection that is neither skill-based nor random in each prize area (Competition Act s.74.06(a), (c)).

**Undue pressure:** no promotion that uses undue pressure to make a customer buy a product or service as a condition of getting another from the Bank or an affiliate (Bank Act s.627.04(a)). A purchase made a condition of a prize is treated as undue pressure under the Bank's policy (drafting inference).
model: (a) The Supplier shall run a Promotion only under written rules approved in advance by the Bank. The rules shall state eligibility, the entry method, the number and approximate value of prizes, each area to which prizes relate, any fact that materially affects the chances of winning, the closing date, the selection method and how winners will be notified.

(b) Entry to a Promotion shall not require payment of money or other valuable consideration. Any other format requires the Bank's prior written approval, given only after its legal function confirms that the format complies with Applicable Law.

(c) The Supplier shall select participants and distribute prizes only on the basis of skill or on a random basis in each area to which prizes are allocated, using the method in the rules, and shall keep records of each selection and give them to the Bank on request.
(d) The Supplier shall distribute each prize without undue delay after the winner is confirmed, and in any event within [30] days, and shall tell the Bank at once of any delay or failure.

(e) Every promotional material and message about a Promotion shall be accurate, clear and not misleading, shall state the material rules, and shall comply with Applicable Law, including the consent and unsubscribe requirements in [the Marketing Messages clause]. [The French-language clause] applies to any Promotion offered to Quebec customers.
(f) The Supplier shall not make a Promotion conditional on the purchase of a product from the Bank, the Supplier or any affiliate, or use it to apply undue pressure to make a sale.
watchFor: **Unlimited discretion:** a right to change or cancel prizes, odds or closing dates at will, or to select winners by a process the Bank cannot see.
**Paid entry by another name:** a 'processing fee', a donation requirement or a product purchase as the price of entry.
**Token skill question:** a skill question so easy that it does not decide the outcome, or used on a draw that is otherwise random.
**Rules in a link only:** the prize, odds and regions shown only in a terms page, not in the advertisement itself.
**Release that waives claims:** winners must sign a release waiving all claims against the Bank or the partner before any prize is paid.

pushback.says: A skill question makes any contest legal everywhere, so we do not need your approval of the format.
pushback.reply: A skill question helps only where the outcome genuinely depends on skill. Criminal Code s.206(1)(f) turns on whether entry is paid and whether the game is one of chance or of mixed chance and skill, so the design decides the question, not the question. Legal must clear each format.

pushback.says: We cannot publish the odds because they are commercially sensitive.
pushback.reply: Competition Act s.74.06(a) requires adequate and fair disclosure of the number and approximate value of prizes and any fact that materially affects the chances of winning. We need at least that in the rules and the advertisement.

pushback.says: Our standard terms let us change prizes at any time.
pushback.reply: A change after launch would make the disclosure inaccurate, and advertising that is not accurate, clear and not misleading breaches Bank Act s.627.14. Changes need the Bank's written approval and notice to entrants.

playbook.escalate: Suggested: the Head of Marketing and the Head of Legal approve each Promotion's rules; any paid-entry or chance-based format goes to the General Counsel before launch.

terms.title: Quebec: French-language contracts, terms and interfaces
terms.summary: The Charter of the French Language sets language rules for standard-form contracts, customer-facing terms, software and interfaces, and commercial publications aimed at Quebec. The Supplier's standard terms and products must support those rules for Quebec customers, and the Bank needs control over the French versions.
require: **Standard-form contracts:** a contract of adhesion and its related documents must be drawn up in French first, and an English version may follow only where the customer has expressly chosen it (Charter of the French Language, as amended in 2022; reported; check).
**Customer-facing terms and interfaces:** software, screens, menus, notices and help text presented to Quebec customers must be in French, subject to the Charter's exceptions (reported; check).

**Commercial publications and advertising:** advertising and publications aimed at Quebec customers must be in French, with any other language permitted only on the Charter's conditions (reported; check).

**Scope for a federal bank:** how the Charter applies alongside federal rules to a federally regulated bank in Quebec is a question for Legal (reported; check). Supplier-provided materials and standard-form contracts offered in Quebec are covered in practice (drafting inference).

**Advertising accuracy:** any advertisement in Canada made by the Bank, in French or English, must be accurate, clear and not misleading (Bank Act s.627.14). Statute. Quebec advertising must also meet the Charter rules above (reported; check).

sources.label: Charter of the French Language (CQLR c C-11)
sources.note: Amended in 2022 (Bill 96). In-force dates and section numbers are reported only; check the current consolidated text before relying on them.

sources.label: Bank Act

drafting: **French master:** make the French version the authoritative text for Quebec, with the English version as a courtesy copy, and state that rule in the agreement (drafting inference).
**Governing law:** a governing-law clause does not by itself displace the Charter's language rules for Quebec customers (reported; check).

playbook.why: The Charter is statute, so its language rules set the floor for Quebec-facing terms, screens and documents. The 2022 amendments and their scope are reported and need checking against the current text (reported; check).
preferred: **French master versions:** the French text of every Quebec-facing term, screen, notice and contract is the master, reviewed by a French-language reviewer, and updated together with the English version (drafting inference).
**French first by default:** Quebec customers see French first, and any English choice is recorded as the customer's express request (reported; check).
**Delivery before go-live:** French versions of each update are delivered before the change takes effect, and the Bank can reject a release that is not French first (drafting inference).
**Interfaces and partner apps:** Quebec screens, menus, help and error messages are in French by default, with Bank review before release (drafting inference).
fallback: **Technical strings:** accept English for developer logs, error codes and technical identifiers that Quebec customers never see, only if no customer-facing text is affected.
**Bilingual screens:** accept bilingual screens only where Legal confirms the Charter allows them and French is given the prominence the Charter requires (reported; check).
**Customers outside Quebec:** accept English-only interfaces outside Quebec, only if Quebec customers are routed to the French version and their language setting is respected.
redLines: **French first for Quebec contracts:** no Quebec standard-form contract offered in English only, or with English first, unless Legal confirms the Charter allows it (reported; check).
**Quebec interfaces:** no customer-facing screen, notice or term for Quebec customers left in English only where the Charter requires French (reported; check).
**Bank control:** no term that leaves the French versions to the Supplier's discretion without Bank review and approval.
model: (a) The Supplier shall provide, for each Quebec customer, every standard-form contract, term, notice and related document needed for the Services in French first, in a form the Bank approves. An English version may be provided alongside it only where Applicable Law allows and, for a contract of adhesion, only at the customer's express request.

(b) The Supplier shall make each screen, menu, help text, notice, message and error message presented to a Quebec customer available in French, and shall not present an English-only version to a Quebec customer except where Applicable Law permits.

(c) The French version of each document the Supplier provides for Quebec shall be the master text and shall be no less complete or accurate than the English version. The Supplier shall update the French and English versions together, and shall deliver the French version before any change takes effect.

(d) The Supplier shall use only French-language materials for commercial publications and advertising aimed at Quebec customers, save as Applicable Law permits, and shall submit each such material to the Bank for review before publication.

(e) The Supplier shall tell the Bank promptly of any complaint, inquiry or notice from a Regulator about the French-language compliance of the Services, and shall cooperate in the response. [The Liability clause] applies to any breach of this clause.
watchFor: **English-first templates:** standard terms written in English, with a French translation 'for convenience' that is not the authoritative version or that lags behind.
**Bilingual by default:** bilingual terms in which the French is shorter, smaller or placed after the English.
**Language choice bundled:** English selected by default, or by a pre-ticked box, in the sign-up flow.
**Third-party screens:** the Supplier disclaims responsibility for third-party or embedded screens shown to Quebec customers.
**Translation on request:** French versions produced only when a customer asks, rather than delivered with each release.

pushback.says: Our platform is English-only and global; a French layer is too expensive for one province.
pushback.reply: The Bank needs its Quebec screens and documents in French whatever the platform's default. Cost must be priced in. Whether and how the Charter applies to a federal bank is for Legal (reported; check).

pushback.says: The English contract governs, so the French is a courtesy.
pushback.reply: The Charter's rules on contracts of adhesion generally require French first, whatever a governing-law clause says (reported; check). A separate English version is only for a customer who expressly asks for it.

pushback.says: We will translate on request.
pushback.reply: Quebec materials must be in French from the outset, not on request. French versions must be delivered with each release (reported; check).

playbook.escalate: Suggested: the Head of Legal and the Head of Quebec operations approve deviations; any English-only Quebec interface goes to the General Counsel before launch.

intro: **How to use it:** for each clause in a provider's draft, check the stance first, then mark up towards the model wording, and use the pushback lines for common objections. The tags on each clause show which contracts it applies to.

**Three stances:** must-have means the core comes from a statute or regulation, a binding order, or from OSFI saying the bank or OSFI must have it. Do not sign without it. Expected means an OSFI guideline or agency guidance expects it. Negotiable means good practice only.

**Standardized contracts:** where a provider offers take-it-or-leave-it terms, OSFI expects the bank to assess inherent risk and mitigating controls, and to formally accept residual risk where applicable, with mitigants such as redundancy, workarounds and business continuity (B-10 3.1.1). Risk acceptance is a formal decision to accept residual risk after the mitigants have been assessed (B-10 3.1.1). Record it, with the mitigants and a review date.

**Brackets and deviations:** square brackets mark a choice for the bank to complete. A departure from a must-have follows the escalation route below. OSFI expects prompt notice only of substantive issues affecting critical operations, not of every variation in a contract.

definitions.meaning: the Bank, a bank under the Bank Act (S.C. 1991, c. 46) that is a party to this Agreement.
the party that provides the Services under this Agreement.
the services, software, platform or other deliverables that the Supplier provides under this Agreement and each Order.
any person to whom the Supplier delegates any part of the Services or handling of Bank Data, at any level.

OSFI and the Superintendent, FCAC and the Commissioner, FINTRAC, the Privacy Commissioner, the Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec, CDIC, the Bank of Canada, and any other authority with jurisdiction over the Bank.
every statute, regulation, by-law, binding order and binding requirement of a Regulator that applies to the Bank or the Supplier in relation to the Services.
all data and information, in any form, that the Bank or a person for the Bank provides to the Supplier, or that the Supplier creates or holds for the Bank under this Agreement.
Bank Data that identifies, or relates to, a customer of the Bank or a prospective customer.
information about an identifiable individual within the meaning of PIPEDA s.2(1) and, for an individual in Quebec, of the Act respecting the protection of personal information in the private sector.
the records the Bank must keep under Bank Act ss.238-239 and other Applicable Law, in whatever form they are held.
a Service that supports a critical operation of the Bank, as the Bank identifies it under its risk and criticality assessment.
any event or series of events that affects, or may affect, the confidentiality, integrity or availability of the Services, Bank Data or Records, or that is a breach of security safeguards.
the period of [ ] months, starting on notice of termination or expiry, during which the Supplier continues the Services and assists the Bank to move them to another provider.
a day other than a Saturday, Sunday or a holiday on which banks are open in [Toronto, Ontario].
CDIC and the Superintendent, each acting under the Bank Act or the CDIC Act.
a bridge institution or any person to whom the Bank's business or this Agreement is transferred under the CDIC Act.

escalation: **Who proposes a deviation:** the business owner and third-party risk propose it together, with the clause's specialist owner (such as the Chief Information Security Officer or the Chief Privacy Officer) where the clause is theirs.
**Must-have or expected:** the General Counsel and the Chief Risk Officer decide. A must-have departure should not be approved below that level.

**Critical arrangements:** we suggest that the board risk committee approve any deviation on a critical arrangement, and any formal risk acceptance for a standardized contract. This is a suggested governance practice, not an OSFI requirement.
**Record:** enter each decision in the third-party inventory and the risk acceptance log, with the mitigants and a review date.

process.heading: Before you sign
process.lede: Most of the regulatory exposure is created, or avoided, before the contract exists.
points: **Inventory:** list every third-party arrangement, including group companies and agents. B-10 applies to all of them, so the list is the starting point (A3).
**Risk and criticality:** set the bank's own method for risk and criticality, and assess each arrangement before entry (B-10 2.1.1, 2.1.2, 2.2.1.1). B-10 leaves the scale to the bank.

**Due diligence:** for high-risk and critical arrangements, work through the Annex 1 factors (2.2.2). Check foreign legal and political risks where a third party or subcontractor operates outside Canada (2.2.2.3).
**Concentration:** assess concentration by geography, supplier and subcontractor before contracting, and keep assessing it (2.2.3.1).
**Quebec privacy impact assessment:** before communicating personal information of Quebec residents outside Quebec, carry out an assessment and a written agreement (reported; check: P-39.1 s.17).

**Group companies:** a services contract with a group company or other related party must meet Part XI, including the market-terms rule in s.501. The conduct review committee oversees the bank's Part XI procedures and reviews its related-party practices (s.195(3)).

**Partners:** the bank must not arrange for a partner or other intermediary to sell its products unless (a) the intermediary complies with the consumer provisions as if it were an institution, (b) customers can use the bank's complaint procedures, (c) its employees can use the whistleblowing channels, and (d) it observes s.979.4 as if it were a bank (Bank Act s.627.15).

**Identity verification by a vendor:** where a vendor verifies customers' identity for the bank, the bank may rely on those measures only under a written agreement with the vendor, and must be satisfied that the information is valid and current (PCMLTFR s.106(1), (3)). FINTRAC Guide 11 (guidance) says the bank remains responsible when it uses an agent.

**Deposit and core systems:** a vendor running deposit or core systems must support the bank's CDIC obligations under SOR/2010-292 s.2, including producing depositor data as of the determination time within the deadlines in s.2(2), and stopping withdrawals within six hours of a CDIC instruction (s.2(1)(b)).

process.heading: During the contract
process.lede: Monitoring is where the bank shows that the contract works in practice.
points: **Monitoring:** confirm delivery, financial soundness and performance against the agreed measures (B-10 Principle 10, 2.4.1.1).
**Reporting:** agree the type and frequency of reports, including risk measures and timely notice of events that may materially affect risk or service (2.3.3.1, 2.3.3.2).
**Reassessment:** reassess risk and criticality on a material change and at renewal (2.2.1.1, 2.2.2.2).
**Continuity testing:** test business continuity and disaster recovery with the vendor, and require fixes for any deficiency (B-10 2.3.4.1; B-13 2.9.3).
**Scenario testing:** E-21 3.3 expects the bank to coordinate scenario testing of critical operations with critical third parties where possible, on a best-effort basis.
**Subcontractors:** keep the subcontracting list current and use the audit right over subcontractors where the risk warrants it (2.2.4.2).

process.heading: When it goes wrong
process.lede: A vendor incident starts the bank's own clocks, often before the vendor has finished its investigation.
points: **Incident report:** under OSFI's 2021 advisory the bank should report a reportable technology or cyber incident within 24 hours, or sooner if possible, in writing, to the Technology Risk Division and the Lead Supervisor. Events at a vendor count (for example a vendor-declared disaster or a third-party breach that affects the bank). OSFI expects regular updates, e.g. daily, until the details are complete.
**Precautionary reports:** when in doubt, report. OSFI expects the bank to report as a precaution rather than wait for certainty.

**Privacy:** where a processor is breached, the personal information is still under the bank's control, and the Privacy Commissioner treats the bank as the organization that reports (OPC position, not in the statute). The bank reports to the Privacy Commissioner, and notifies individuals, where a breach creates a real risk of significant harm (PIPEDA s.10.1(1), (3)).
**Substantive issues:** OSFI expects prompt notice of substantive issues affecting critical operations because of a third-party arrangement (B-10, Overview).
**Exit plans:** keep stressed and non-stressed exit plans, with defined triggers and tested playbooks (B-10 2.3.5.1).

**Resolution:** once an order under s.39.13(1) is made, a contract term that lets a vendor terminate only because of the bank's insolvency or the making of the order has no force (CDIC Act s.39.15(1)(e), (2)).

vendorKit.caveat: This kit is built from the statute text as consolidated on Justice Laws, for the Bank Act, PIPEDA, the PCMLTFR, the CDIC Act and its by-laws, and the Financial Consumer Protection Framework Regulations. It also draws on OSFI Guideline B-10 (issued April 2023, effective 1 May 2024), B-13, E-21, E-23 (effective 1 May 2027), the Technology and Cyber Security Incident Reporting Advisory (2021) and the Integrity and Security Guideline (2024), and on Privacy Commissioner, FINTRAC and CDIC material. OSFI and agency material is summarised, not reproduced. The Critical Cyber Systems Protection Act is enacted but not in force, so check its commencement and whether a banking class is designated. Check current versions before relying on a point, and treat Quebec points as reported.

intro: **Why this matters:** B-10 has no materiality test. Every third-party arrangement is in scope, and the bank sets its own method for risk and criticality (B-10 1.2.2, 2.1.1, 2.1.2). Unlike SA-2 in Hong Kong, there is no advance discussion with the regulator and no approval step, so this tool is a screen to route work, not OSFI's method.

**What the texts say:** A2 asks the bank to apply B-10 in proportion to the risk and criticality of each arrangement and to its own size, complexity and risk profile. For high-risk and critical arrangements, Section 2 sets minimum expectations. OSFI expects prompt notice of substantive issues affecting critical operations, but it does not approve arrangements in advance.

**How to use this:** answer the questions for one arrangement. The result shows which outcome applies, what to do before signing and after go-live, and why. Answers stay in this browser; download the result as a note for the third-party inventory.

labels.conditionTitle: Signing before the assessments are finished
labels.unsureNote: “Not sure” is treated as yes for this screen, as a conservative default. B-10 2.2.1.1 expects risk and criticality to be assessed before the bank enters into the arrangement, so an unresolved answer should be assessed, not assumed away.
steps: Step 1 · Is it a third-party arrangement?
Step 2 · Does it touch a critical operation, the bank's data, systems, records or customers?
Step 3 · Is it high-risk or critical? Any yes makes it so on this screen
labels.pending: Answer the remaining questions: one yes would make it high-risk or critical.

gates.ask: Is there a business or strategic arrangement with an outside entity or individual, including a group company? (Do not count contracts with customers or employment contracts.)
gates.help: B-10 defines a third-party arrangement widely: any business or strategic arrangement, by contract or otherwise, with an entity or individual. It includes outsourcing, cloud and other technology providers, consultants, and services from a parent, affiliate or subsidiary (B-10 A3). Contracts with customers and employment contracts are excluded. If the answer is no, B-10 does not apply.

gates.ask: Does it support a critical operation, or touch Bank Data, the bank's systems, Records or customers?
gates.help: A yes means the arrangement may be critical or high-risk, so the bank must assess its risk and criticality before entry and scale the assessment to them (B-10 2.2.1.1, 2.1.1). The bank decides what is critical using its own methodology, but E-21 expects critical operations to be identified and mapped, including dependencies on third parties (E-21 3.1). Records are the records the bank must keep under Bank Act ss.238-239. “Not sure” is treated as yes.

factors.ask: Would its failure disrupt a critical operation or the bank's tolerance for disruption?
factors.help: Criticality factors include the severity of loss if the provider fails and the degree to which it supports a critical operation (B-10 2.1.1). E-21 expects the bank to set tolerances for disruption of critical operations and to test them against severe but plausible scenarios, including critical third-party disruptions, which the bank coordinates with those providers where possible (E-21 3.2, 3.3).

factors.ask: Would it be hard to replace, move or bring back in-house without disruption?
factors.help: Substitutability, including portability and the time needed to transfer, is a criticality factor, and so is the impact on operations if the bank must exit (B-10 2.1.1). For cloud arrangements, portability should be considered at entry and in design (B-10 4.4).

factors.ask: Will the provider hold Records, core deposit data or Bank Data?
factors.help: Records must be kept in Canada unless the statute allows otherwise, and OSFI must have access to them (Bank Act ss.238-239, s.643). The Superintendent must direct a bank not to keep copies of records, or process related data, abroad where that is incompatible with OSFI's responsibilities or the Minister advises it is not in the national interest (Bank Act s.245(1)). For an exempt bank that keeps records abroad, OSFI may order a copy kept in Canada if it lacks immediate, direct, complete and ongoing access (s.245(1.1)). CDIC requires certain deposit data to be produced on demand (SOR/2010-292).

factors.ask: Will services be delivered, or data stored or accessed, outside Canada, or by foreign subcontractors?
factors.help: Where a third party or subcontractor has a presence outside Canada, the bank reviews foreign legal requirements and political, legal and security risks (B-10 2.2.2.3). The Integrity and Security Guideline adds foreign-interference factors, including where the provider and its subcontractors operate and who owns them (Principle 9).
factors.ref: B-10 2.2.2.3; Integrity and Security Guideline, Principle 9

factors.ask: Does it rely on subcontractors, or add concentration on one provider?
factors.help: Subcontracting practices are identified before entry, and concentration risk is assessed across suppliers, subcontractors and geographies (B-10 2.2.4.1, 2.2.3.1). Contracts may prohibit subcontracting for some functions, require notice of it, or give the bank a right to refuse a subcontractor (B-10 2.2.4.2).

factors.ask: Will it handle personal information at scale, or sensitive personal information?
factors.help: Transferring information for processing does not remove the bank's responsibility. PIPEDA requires comparable protection through contract or other means (PIPEDA Sch. 1, cl. 4.1.3). Quebec residents' information may also need a privacy impact assessment before it is communicated outside Quebec (reported; check).

factors.ask: Will the provider deal with the bank's customers, for example by selling products or verifying identity?
factors.help: The bank must not arrange with its representatives, agents or intermediaries to sell or further the sale of its products unless they comply with the consumer provisions as if they were an institution, customers can use the bank's complaint procedures, their employees can use the whistleblowing channels, and they observe s.979.4 as if they were a bank (Bank Act s.627.15). For identity verification by an agent, the bank needs a written agreement, must be satisfied that the information is valid and current, and must be satisfied that the agent verified identity by a method in PCMLTFR s.105(1)(a) to (d) (PCMLTFR s.106(3)(a), (c)).

factors.ask: Is the provider a related party, such as a significant shareholder or an entity that shareholder controls?
factors.help: Part XI restricts transactions with related parties. A written contract to buy services used in the ordinary course of business is allowed (Bank Act s.495(1)(a)), but a related-party transaction must, subject to the exceptions in s.496(4) to (6), be on terms at least as favourable to the bank as market terms (s.501(1)). If such contracts, taken together, leave all or substantially all of the bank's management functions with non-employees, the Superintendent may, if he or she considers that inappropriate, order the bank to have those functions exercised by employees (Bank Act s.495(2)).

factors.ask: Will it have technology or cyber access to bank systems, such as remote or privileged access?
factors.help: B-10 Section 4 recognizes that technology and cyber risks in third-party arrangements present elevated vulnerabilities. B-13 expects risk-based identity and access controls, including multi-factor authentication for third-party access where feasible (B-13 3.2.7).

procurement.label: Outside B-10
procurement.verdict: On these answers the bank has no third-party arrangement in B-10's sense, or the relationship is a customer or employment contract, which B-10 excludes. Other rules may still apply, including privacy and consumer protection law.
steps: **Record why:** note the reason (B-10 A3) in the procurement file, so the answer can be shown to an examiner.
**Other rules:** check the privacy and consumer rules that still apply, for example PIPEDA for customer information.
**Look again if it changes:** if the provider later takes a role in the bank's operations or gets access to bank data, run this screen again.

non-banking.label: Low-risk arrangement
non-banking.verdict: B-10 applies, but on these answers the arrangement is not high-risk or critical. OSFI expects it to be managed in proportion to its risk, with standard terms or a documented risk acceptance (B-10 A2, 3.1.1).
steps: **Inventory:** record the arrangement in the third-party inventory, with its risk and criticality (B-10 1.2.2).
**Proportionate due diligence:** check the provider's soundness and controls to a depth that matches the risk (B-10 2.2.2.2).
**Terms:** use standard terms, or document a formal risk acceptance for take-it-or-leave-it contracts (B-10 3.1.1).
**Exit:** an exit or contingency plan may not be needed for a low-risk arrangement (B-10 A2), but the bank should keep the option of moving the service.

banking.label: Elevated risk: apply B-10 proportionately
banking.verdict: B-10 applies, with the assessment, contract and monitoring steps scaled to the risk and criticality of the arrangement and to the bank's size, complexity and risk profile (B-10 A2). On these answers the arrangement is not yet high-risk or critical, but the bank should decide that on its own methodology (B-10 1.2.2, 2.1.1).
steps: **Assess:** document criticality and the risk level, and what the arrangement reduces as well as what it creates (B-10 2.2.1.1).
**Contract:** use a written agreement that sets out each party's rights and responsibilities, reviewed by legal counsel (B-10 2.3.1.1).
**Information and audit rights:** the bank and OSFI can evaluate the provider's risk management practices, or appoint auditors to do so (B-10 2.3.3.3).
**Monitor:** confirm delivery against the contract and that the provider remains financially sound (B-10 2.4.1.1).
**Escalate:** if a factor later makes the arrangement high-risk or critical, run the full set of Section 2 minimums.

material.label: High-risk or critical arrangement
material.verdict: Apply the Section 2 minimum expectations, the Annex 1 due diligence factors and the Annex 2 contract provisions (B-10 2.2.2.2, 2.3.1.2). OSFI expects to be promptly notified of substantive issues affecting critical operations.
steps: **Section 2 minimums:** apply the expectations for each principle, including subcontracting controls, business continuity testing and the exit plan (B-10 Section 2).
**Due diligence:** cover the Annex 1 factors before entry and again on material change (B-10 2.2.2.2, Annex 1).
**Contract:** include the Annex 2 provisions, plus the evaluation and audit rights of the bank and OSFI (B-10 2.3.1.2, 2.3.3.3).
**Exit plan:** write stressed and non-stressed exit playbooks, with triggers and enough detail to act on (B-10 2.3.5.1).

**Senior management:** report residual third-party risk against risk appetite, individually and in aggregate (B-10 2.4.1.2). Report to the board as well under the governance expectations (Corporate Governance Guideline; E-21 2.4.2 for operational risk).
**OSFI:** tell OSFI promptly of substantive issues affecting critical operations (B-10 Overview).
**Quebec and related parties:** complete any Quebec privacy impact assessment, and check Part XI approvals where they apply (reported; check).

intro: **Before entry, not after signing:** B-10 expects due diligence before the bank enters the arrangement, at renewal, periodically and on material change, scaled to risk and criticality (B-10 2.2.2.2). Annex 1 lists the factors for high-risk and critical arrangements.

**Keep the file:** record the evidence, the open points and how each was closed, for the approver and the third-party inventory. Areas marked Material apply to high-risk and critical arrangements. B-10 sets no tiers, so the depth is the bank's own judgement (B-10 1.2.2).

areas.title: Capability, capacity and experience
checks: Technical competence and capacity for the service, including the bank's volumes and growth
Experience of providing similar services to regulated financial institutions
Dependence on a few key people, and staff turnover in the service team
Compliance with Canadian laws and OSFI guidance, and with the laws of other relevant jurisdictions
evidence: Client references, ideally from other federally regulated institutions
redFlags: Key functions resting on one or two people
No experience with regulated clients
Capacity not tested at the bank's volumes

areas.title: Financial strength and insurance
checks: Audited accounts for the last [two to three] years, and the parent's where the contracting entity is thin
Going-concern position, profitability and funding runway for a young provider
Financial health and step-in risk, as part of the risk level assessment (B-10 2.1.2)
Insurance cover and limits, including cyber cover, and whether they fit the bank's exposure
redFlags: Qualified audit opinion or going-concern note
Less than [12] months' runway
Refusal to share financial information

areas.title: Legal, regulatory and reputation
checks: Litigation, investigations and complaints, pending or recent, over the last [five] years
Political and legal risk in the provider's jurisdiction and in the jurisdictions of its subcontractors
Regulatory actions and data breaches involving the provider or its group
Sanctions and adverse-media screening, under the bank's own policies
redFlags: Unresolved regulatory action
Undisclosed investigations
Owners or key operations in a high-risk jurisdiction

areas.title: Risk management, controls and culture
checks: Strength of the provider's risk management programme, internal controls and reporting, and how well they align with the bank's
Values, code of conduct and culture, and how they fit the bank's
Whether the provider runs its own third-party risk programme, and how it oversees its subcontractors
redFlags: No documented controls for the service
Conduct concerns raised in reviews or by former staff
Controls the provider will not share with the bank

areas.title: Technology, cyber and information security
checks: Scope of ISO/IEC 27001 or SOC 2 Type II reports, and whether they cover this service
Penetration testing, vulnerability management, encryption and key management, privileged access
Capacity to give the bank timely information for its incident reporting under OSFI's Advisory (Annex 1, item 7)
Multi-factor authentication and background checks for people with access, where feasible (B-13 3.2.7)
redFlags: Exceptions in key controls
Assurance scope that excludes the service
No notice terms for technology or cyber incidents

areas.title: Continuity and disaster recovery testing
checks: Recovery time and recovery point objectives against the bank's tolerance for disruption for each critical operation (E-21 3.2)
Business continuity and disaster recovery plans, with the quality, frequency and results of recent tests (Annex 1, item 9)
Architecture: regions, failover and single points of failure
Willingness to join broader scenario exercises with the bank, where appropriate (E-21 3.3)
evidence: Recovery commitments in the draft contract
redFlags: Recovery times beyond the bank's tolerance
Untested disaster recovery
A single region or data centre for a critical service

areas.title: Subcontractors, concentration and location
checks: Subcontractors, their criticality, and the provider's oversight of them (B-10 2.2.4.1)
Where data is stored, processed and accessed, including for support, and where each subcontractor is (Annex 1, item 12)
Concentration on this provider across the bank, including through its group (B-10 2.2.3.1)
Records kept in Canada, or the statutory conditions met for keeping them elsewhere (Bank Act ss.238-239, 245)
redFlags: Locations the provider will not name
Subcontractors that cannot be audited
The provider already runs several of the bank's critical services

areas.title: Substitution and portability
checks: Ability and ease of substitution, and the effect on the bank's operations (Annex 1, item 13)
Portability of applications and data to another provider or to the bank (Annex 1, item 14)
Exit assistance, including the period of continued service after termination notice (B-10 2.3.5.1)
For cloud services, a design such as multi-cloud to limit provider concentration (B-10 4.4)
evidence: Exit plan the provider will support
redFlags: No portable export format
Exit assistance only at the provider's discretion
Lock-in through proprietary features with no path out

areas.title: Integrity, security and ownership
checks: Ownership chart to the ultimate beneficial owners, and the location of the provider's headquarters and operations
Foreign-interference factors: connections to foreign governments and ownership, for the provider and its subcontractors
Risk-based background checks on responsible persons, employees and contractors, including people supplied through another entity
Protective measures at the provider that are equivalent and proportionate to the bank's (Principle 9)
redFlags: Ownership or key operations linked to a state the bank cannot assess
Refusal to disclose ownership
No background checks on people with access

friction.caption: B-10 covers every third-party arrangement, so the screen runs before the contract, and the assessments should be finished before the bank signs (B-10 2.2.1.1).

frictionPoints: **Scope:** B-10 covers every third-party arrangement, including cloud and group services, so the screen catches more than vendors that look like outsourcing. The bank sets how much work each one needs (B-10 A3, 2.1.3).

**Hyperscaler terms:** cloud and SaaS providers usually offer standard paper. B-10 3.1.1 covers take-it-or-leave-it terms: the bank's risk assessment should consider inherent risk and mitigating controls, and OSFI expects the bank to formally accept residual risk where applicable.

**Regulator and CDIC terms:** Ask early for OSFI access and audit rights (B-10 2.3.3.3; Bank Act s.643). The CDIC stay is statutory, not a term to request: once an order under s.39.13(1) is made, no person may terminate or amend an agreement with the bank by reason only of the listed resolution events, and contrary stipulations have no force (CDIC Act s.39.15(1)(e), (2)). Check that the contract does not conflict with them.

**Records and Quebec:** records must be kept in Canada unless the statute allows otherwise, and OSFI needs access to them (Bank Act ss.238-239, 245). Quebec residents' data can add a privacy impact assessment before it leaves Quebec (reported; check).
**Leverage:** a small bank has less leverage with a large provider. Take the Annex 2 list into the request for proposal, so the gaps are visible before the provider is chosen.
condition: (a) The Bank shall not implement the Services, or transfer any Bank Data to the Supplier, until the Bank has completed its risk and criticality assessment and due diligence on the Supplier, any privacy impact assessment required under Quebec law, security testing, and any approval required for a transaction with a related party under Part XI of the Bank Act.
(b) Until then, the Supplier shall give the Bank the information the Bank reasonably requests for those steps, including about its controls, the locations of Bank Data and its Subcontractors.

(c) The Supplier shall tell the Bank promptly if it becomes aware of a substantive issue that affects the Services and could affect a critical operation of the Bank, so that the Bank can keep the Regulator promptly informed.
(d) If the condition in paragraph (a) is not met by [date], the Bank may terminate this Agreement by notice without liability, and the Supplier shall refund any fees paid in advance.

materialityKit.caveat: This is a screen for triage, not a legal opinion or OSFI's method: the bank's own risk and criticality methodology governs (B-10 1.2.2). The factors are built from the B-10 Overview, A2, A3, Sections 2 to 4, Annexes 1 and 2, E-21 3.1-3.3, B-13 3.2.7 and the Integrity and Security Guideline, with the Bank Act and PIPEDA points following the official text. OSFI material is expectations, not law, and the Quebec points are reported and need checking. Check current versions before relying on the result, including B-10 (effective 1 May 2024).

title: Technology, cyber & operational resilience
oneLiner: OSFI expects the bank to govern technology risk, stay within disruption tolerances and report vendor-driven incidents within 24 hours.
keyPoints: **Three guidelines, one system:** B-13 sets technology and cyber expectations, E-21 sets operational resilience, and B-10 governs the vendor relationship. OSFI expects them to be run together, not as separate projects.

**Vendors are in scope:** B-13 reaches third-party assets, incident processes, disaster recovery tests and access controls. It has no cloud-specific rules; cloud expectations sit in B-10, ss.4.3 and 4.4.

**E-21 deadlines:** Full adherence was due by 1 September 2026, and testing of all critical operations is due by 1 September 2027. Critical third parties are part of the mapping, and the bank coordinates testing with them where possible, on a best-effort basis.

**Incident reporting:** OSFI expects written notice within 24 hours, or sooner if possible, to its Technology Risk Division and the Lead Supervisor. Vendor incidents can be reportable, and precautionary reporting is encouraged.

**Integrity and security:** The Integrity and Security Guideline says accountability for security cannot be contracted out. Under the Bank Act, the Superintendent can direct a bank that lacks adequate integrity or security policies (s.645(1.1)).

**Coming law:** The Critical Cyber Systems Protection Act lists banking systems as a vital service and caps incident reporting to the Communications Security Establishment at 72 hours. It was enacted in June 2026 but, as at November 2026, its commencement must be checked.
