deepDive.heading: Technology and cyber risk under B-13
deepDive.lede: B-13 sets OSFI's expectations in three domains: governance, technology operations and cyber security.

visual.caption: Three domains, one risk framework. Each domain has its own outcome.

items.label: Governance and risk management
items.note: Accountability, strategy and a risk framework

items.label: Technology operations and resilience
items.note: Architecture, asset inventory, change, incidents and DR

items.label: Cyber security
items.note: Identify, defend, detect, respond and recover

points: **Three domains, 17 principles:** The guideline sets an outcome for each domain and a principle for each area within it. It applies to all federally regulated financial institutions, including banks.
**Proportionality:** B-13 says there is no one-size-fits-all approach. It asks banks to apply it according to size, complexity and risk profile.

**Vendor assets:** The technology asset inventory may include third-party assets that store or process bank information or provide critical services (2.2.2). Acquired software needs a security risk assessment and SDLC controls (2.4.4).
**Access and baselines:** MFA and privileged access controls reach third parties where feasible (3.2.7). Security configuration baselines cover tools provided by third parties (3.2.8).

**Incidents with third parties:** B-13 expects incident processes to include third parties and to be tested with them (2.7.2), and Principle 17 covers incidents that originate at third-party providers. Background checks on persons with access are expected where feasible (3.2.7).
**Cloud:** The word cloud does not appear in B-13. Read it with B-10, ss.4.3 and 4.4, which cover cloud arrangements.
deepDive.takeaway: Ask each vendor whether its services, data or tools belong in the bank's technology inventory, and whether the bank's controls reach them.

deepDive.heading: Operational resilience under E-21
deepDive.lede: E-21 assumes disruption will happen and asks the bank to keep critical operations running within set tolerances.

visual.caption: The resilience cycle, in the order E-21 describes it.

items.label: Identify critical operations
items.note: Assess ability to withstand disruption

items.label: Map dependencies
items.note: Include people, technology, facilities and third parties

items.label: Set tolerances
items.note: Maximum disruption across severe but plausible scenarios

items.label: Test against tolerances
items.note: Scenario testing for all critical operations by 1 September 2027

points: **Critical operations:** Services or products whose disruption would put the bank's safety and soundness at risk, or harm other institutions through interconnectedness. The bank identifies and reviews them regularly.
**Mapping:** Map each critical operation end to end. Where a third party is critical, the bank should obtain enough information to assess its resilience (3.1).

**Tolerances:** A tolerance is the most disruption the bank can withstand. Tolerances are usually greater than risk appetite, and the bank should consider the impact on critical third-party suppliers (3.2).

**Scenario testing:** Test a range of severe but plausible scenarios, including critical third-party service disruptions. Coordinate with critical third parties where possible, on a best-effort basis (3.3).
**Continuity plans:** Business continuity tests should cover critical third-party disruption, and critical third parties should show robust continuity plans of their own (4.1.3).
deepDive.takeaway: Put the critical vendors into the resilience map before a scenario test exposes the gap.

deepDive.heading: Incident reporting to OSFI
deepDive.lede: OSFI's 2021 advisory sets a 24-hour outer limit and treats some vendor events as reportable.

visual.caption: Three clocks run from the same event. The OSFI notice is a supervisory expectation; the PIPEDA report is a statutory duty already in force; the CCSPA report applies once Part 2 is in force.

items.label: OSFI technology or cyber notice
items.note: Or sooner if possible, in writing on OSFI's form

items.label: PIPEDA breach report
items.note: Real risk of significant harm; keep records for 24 months

items.label: CSE incident report (CCSPA)
items.note: Period set by regulation; Act not yet in force

points: **Window:** A reportable incident must be notified within 24 hours, or sooner if possible. The advisory says the notice must be in writing.
**Recipients:** Notify OSFI's Technology Risk Division and the Lead Supervisor. Telephone followed by paper is a fallback only where electronic means fail.

**Vendor triggers:** An incident is reportable where a third party's impact affects the bank, or where a third-party vendor declares a disaster that affects it. Appendix I gives a material third party's breach as an example.
**Updates:** Expect regular updates, for example daily, situation updates until containment, and a post-incident report.
**Precaution:** When in doubt, report as a precaution. Failure to report can lead to more supervision, including watch-listing or staging of the bank.
deepDive.takeaway: Write the vendor's notice duty so the bank can meet its own 24-hour clock without waiting for the vendor's root-cause analysis.

deepDive.heading: Integrity, security and foreign interference
deepDive.lede: The Integrity and Security Guideline treats vendors as part of the bank's security perimeter.
points: **Equivalent measures:** Third parties should be subject to equivalent and proportional measures against threats (P9). Accountability for security stays with the bank.
**Technology and data:** Technology assets and data should be protected in proportion to threat, and data classification should consider vulnerability to foreign interference (P7, P8).
**Due diligence:** Before engagement and during it, assess the vendor's threat exposure, its security policies and its background-check processes. Include subcontractors.
**Foreign-interference factors:** Consider where the vendor operates and is headquartered, any connections to foreign governments, and its ownership structure.
**Reporting:** Report suspected foreign interference promptly. OSFI should be told immediately when the bank reports to CSIS or the RCMP (P10).
**Statutory hooks:** The OSFI Act makes adequate integrity and security policies a supervisory objective (s.4(2)(a.1)), and Bank Act s.645(1.1) lets the Superintendent direct remedial measures.
deepDive.takeaway: Add foreign-interference questions to vendor onboarding and repeat them when a vendor's ownership or location changes.

deepDive.heading: Coming law: the CCSPA and E-23
deepDive.lede: Two instruments are not yet fully in effect, but they change what the vendor file should contain now.
points: **CCSPA:** Enacted by Bill C-8 (S.C. 2026, c. 9). Schedule 1 lists banking systems as a vital service. Designated operator classes are set by order, and no banking class is listed in the Act as enacted; whether one is added by order, and which regulator applies, is not yet settled.

**Designated operator duties:** Keep a cyber security program that covers supply-chain risk, notify the regulator of material changes to third-party products and services, mitigate supply-chain risk, and report incidents to the CSE within a period set by regulation of no more than 72 hours.
**E-23 (effective 1 May 2027):** OSFI expects the bank to identify vendor and third-party models, including AI, rate them on a standalone basis, review their components and plan decommissioning.
**Status:** Check the commencement orders and any regulations for the CCSPA as at November 2026 before relying on the dates.
deepDive.takeaway: Prepare a supply-chain register and a 72-hour incident route now, and confirm the commencement date before the bank relies on either.

deepDive.heading: Hong Kong comparison
deepDive.lede: The HK regime uses similar ideas with different triggers and clocks.
points: **Technology risk:** TM-G-1 sets the HKMA's technology risk expectations. B-13 is the closer match, but the structure differs, so map the controls one by one.
**Clock:** OSFI sets a 24-hour outer limit for written notice of technology or cyber incidents.
**Resilience:** OR-2 is the closest HK analogue to E-21, and it also expects dependency mapping and tolerances for critical services.
**Critical infrastructure:** Cap. 653 is the nearest HK analogue to the CCSPA. Check its designations before comparing scope.

provisions.title: Technology and Cyber Risk Management
provisions.summary: Sets OSFI's expectations for technology and cyber risk in three domains: governance, technology operations and resilience, and cyber security. It has 17 principles, including vendor-facing expectations on inventories, incident processes with third parties, DR tests of critical third-party technologies, and access controls for third parties. The guideline is risk-based and does not state an enforcement mechanism.
provisions.counselNote: This is the main technology file for vendor contracts. Map each vendor to the inventory, incident, DR and access expectations and record how the contract supports them.

provisions.title: Operational Risk Management and Resilience
provisions.summary: Sets expectations for operational risk management and operational resilience. It requires the bank to identify critical operations, map internal and external dependencies, set tolerances for disruption and test them through scenarios. Section 4.6 treats threats from critical third-party arrangements as a resilience risk.
provisions.counselNote: E-21 turns vendor dependency into a resilience question. Ask critical vendors for the information needed to assess their resilience, and build their outages into the scenario tests.

provisions.instrument: OSFI Guideline B-10, Third-Party Risk Management
provisions.title: Third-Party Risk Management
provisions.summary: Covers third-party arrangements, including cloud and other technology providers, and sets the expectations that apply to contracts with them. Sections 4.3 and 4.4 address cloud arrangements. B-13 and E-21 refer back to it for vendor expectations.
provisions.counselNote: B-13 has no cloud rules of its own, so the cloud points come from B-10. Read the technology contract terms against B-10 as well as B-13.

provisions.instrument: OSFI Technology and Cyber Security Incident Reporting Advisory
provisions.ref: Advisory (13 August 2021), reporting window and criteria
provisions.title: Technology and Cyber Security Incident Reporting
provisions.summary: Requires written notice of a technology or cyber incident within 24 hours, or sooner if possible, to OSFI's Technology Risk Division and the Lead Supervisor. Lists criteria for reporting, including third-party impacts and vendor disaster declarations, and encourages precautionary reporting. It describes watch-listing or staging as a consequence of failing to report.
provisions.counselNote: Write vendor notice duties so the bank can meet the 24-hour clock, and keep the OSFI form and recipients in the incident playbook. Report when in doubt.

provisions.title: Integrity and Security
provisions.summary: Expects the bank to protect itself against threats to integrity and security, including foreign interference. Third parties should face equivalent and proportional measures, and accountability for security cannot be contracted out. Suspected foreign interference should be reported, and OSFI informed immediately of reports to CSIS or the RCMP.
provisions.counselNote: Add foreign-interference factors and background-check questions to vendor due diligence. Make the contract require reporting of suspected interference that affects the bank's services.

provisions.instrument: OSFI Guideline E-23, Model Risk Management
provisions.ref: E-23, C.1, C.2, D.2 and Appendix 1
provisions.title: Model Risk Management
provisions.summary: Applies from 1 May 2027. It covers vendor and third-party models, including AI, and expects the bank to identify them, rate them on a standalone basis, review third-party components and plan decommissioning. Vendor models in the inventory must record their origin and dependencies (Appendix 1), and the inventory covers models with non-negligible inherent risk.
provisions.counselNote: Ask vendors that supply models to disclose components, data sources and update practices. Plan for a vendor model's decommissioning before signing a long-term contract.

provisions.title: Superintendent's directions to bank
provisions.summary: The Superintendent may direct a bank to stop an unsafe or unsound practice and to take remedial steps. A separate power covers a bank that lacks adequate policies against threats to its integrity or security, or does not follow them. The bank must have a reasonable opportunity to make representations first, with limited exceptions.
provisions.counselNote: The Bank Act backs OSFI's guideline expectations with a direction power. A vendor failure that exposes weak integrity or security policies can lead to a direction against the bank.

provisions.title: Protection of records
provisions.summary: A bank and its agents must take reasonable precautions to prevent loss or destruction of records, falsification of entries, and unauthorized access to them. The duty binds the bank's agents as well as the bank.
provisions.counselNote: Section 244 binds the bank and its agents. Whether a vendor is an agent is a question of fact and contract, so the bank should not assume the record-keeping duty passes to the vendor; write the records terms into the contract either way.

provisions.instrument: Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions Act
provisions.title: Objects of Office: financial institutions
provisions.summary: Sets OSFI's objects in respect of financial institutions, including supervising whether they have adequate policies and procedures against threats to their integrity or security, including foreign interference.
provisions.counselNote: This is the statutory basis for OSFI's integrity and security supervision. Expect OSFI to ask how vendors are assessed against it.

provisions.instrument: Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act
provisions.title: Report to Commissioner
provisions.summary: An organization must report to the Privacy Commissioner a breach of security safeguards involving personal information under its control if there is a real risk of significant harm. The report is due as soon as feasible after the organization determines the breach occurred, and individuals must also be notified.
provisions.counselNote: A breach at a vendor that holds personal information can trigger this duty for the bank. Build the PIPEDA clock into the same incident playbook as the OSFI 24-hour notice.

provisions.instrument: Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act
provisions.title: Principle 1: Accountability
provisions.summary: The organization stays responsible for personal information transferred to a third party for processing. It must use contractual or other means to give a comparable level of protection while the third party processes the information.
provisions.counselNote: This is the contractual baseline for processing agreements with vendors. The bank cannot pass accountability for personal information to a vendor.

provisions.instrument: Critical Cyber Systems Protection Act (S.C. 2026, c. 9, Part 2)
provisions.title: Critical Cyber Systems Protection Act
provisions.summary: Enacted by Bill C-8 with Royal Assent on 15 June 2026. Schedule 1 lists banking systems as a vital service. Designated operators must run a cyber security program covering supply-chain risk, notify the regulator of material third-party changes, and report cyber incidents to the CSE within a period set by regulation of no more than 72 hours. Part 2 comes into force on a day fixed by order.
provisions.counselNote: Prepare now: keep a supply-chain register, a route for material-change notices and a 72-hour incident path to the CSE. Confirm whether a banking class has been designated and when Part 2 commences.

checklist: **Inventory vendor-hosted assets:** Include third-party assets that store bank information or provide critical services in the technology inventory (B-13, 2.2.2).
**Contract for fast incident notice:** Require vendor notice quick enough for the bank to meet the 24-hour OSFI clock, with regular updates and root-cause cooperation.
**Test with critical vendors:** Include critical third-party disruption in DR and scenario tests, with the vendor's participation where possible (B-13, 2.9.3; E-21, 3.3).
**Map critical operations:** Record which vendors each critical operation depends on, and where they operate (E-21, 3.1; B-13, 2.9.2).
**Apply access controls to vendors:** Require MFA and privileged access controls for vendor access where feasible (B-13, 3.2.7).
**Run foreign-interference diligence:** Record locations, ownership and government connections for the vendor and its subcontractors (Integrity and Security, P9).
**Prepare for the CCSPA:** Keep a supply-chain register and a process for material-change notices, and confirm the banking designation status before relying on either.
**Calendar the dates:** E-21 full adherence was due 1 September 2026, testing of all critical operations is due 1 September 2027, and E-23 applies from 1 May 2027.
itAngle: **Incident clock in the tooling:** Build the 24-hour OSFI notice into the incident platform, with a timestamp at detection, an OSFI criteria checklist and a field for the vendor's notice time.
**Dependency maps as live data:** E-21 mapping works best as a maintained data set linking services, systems, vendors and locations, so the bank can update it after each change.
**Vendor telemetry:** Ask vendors for security logs and alerts that feed the bank's monitoring, and for configuration baselines that cover their tools (B-13, 3.2.8).
**Model inventory:** Record vendor models and AI components in the E-23 model inventory, with their origin, data sources and dependencies (E-23, Appendix 1).
virtualBankNotes: **Concentrated dependencies:** A digital bank often relies on a small number of cloud, core and payment providers. E-21 expects those single points of failure to be mapped and tested against tolerances.
**Customer-facing outages:** For an app-only bank, a vendor outage is a customer outage. Set tolerances in customer terms, such as outage time, diminished service and customer impact (E-21, A5).

**No branch fallback:** A digital bank has no branch network to fall back on, so it should consider a customer channel that does not depend on the same vendor. E-21 asks for crisis communication protocols (4.3).
**Incident criteria are broad:** Customer impact, reputational harm and reports to senior management are all reporting triggers. App incidents can meet them quickly, so start the 24-hour clock early.
pitfalls: **Treating B-13 as silent on vendors:** The word cloud does not appear in B-13, but the guideline still reaches third-party assets, incident processes and DR tests.
**Waiting for vendor confirmation before reporting:** The advisory expects notice within 24 hours, and precautionary reporting is encouraged when the bank is unsure.
**Ignoring the CCSPA because it is not yet in force:** Enacted law can be brought into force by order. Contracts signed now should allow the supply-chain information the Act may need.

**Sharing supervisory findings with vendors:** Ratings, intervention stages and findings are prescribed supervisory information. Vendors are not among the permitted recipients, so keep them out of vendor exercises.

glossary.definition: A service or product whose disruption would put the bank's continued operations or safety and soundness at risk, or harm other institutions because of its interconnectedness. E-21 requires the bank to identify and review them.

The maximum disruption, including outage time, diminished service, data loss or customer impact, that the bank can withstand under severe but plausible scenarios. It is usually greater than risk appetite.
The ability to keep delivering operations, especially critical operations, through disruption. E-21 assumes disruption will happen and focuses on response and recovery.

Something tangible or intangible that supports technology services and needs protection, such as hardware, software, data or information. B-13 allows third-party assets to be included in the inventory.
The OSFI supervisor assigned to the bank. The incident advisory requires notice to the Lead Supervisor as well as to OSFI's Technology Risk Division.
Undue influence or activity by foreign actors that threatens the bank's integrity or security. OSFI's Integrity and Security Guideline asks banks to assess it for vendors and their subcontractors.
A third party whose failure would disrupt a critical operation. E-21 does not define the term separately, so the bank sets its own test and documents it.
A service listed in Schedule 1 to the CCSPA, such as banking systems. Operators of critical cyber systems that support a vital service may be designated under the Act.
An operator of a critical cyber system that is placed in a class by order under the CCSPA. Designated operators must run a cyber security program and report incidents.

intro: **The scenario:** a critical SaaS vendor goes down, or reports a breach. Several clocks start at once, owed to different bodies, with different legal force. Answer the questions to see who must be told, and by when.

**The vendor's notice must arrive early:** OSFI expects a reportable technology or cyber incident to be reported within 24 hours, or sooner if possible (OSFI Technology and Cyber Security Incident Reporting Advisory). The bank can only meet that if its vendor contract requires prompt notice (OSFI Guideline B-10, 2.4.2.2). The bank stays responsible for privacy reporting when a processor is breached (PIPEDA Sch. 1, cl. 4.1.3).

**Most of these clocks are not statute:** the OSFI Advisory and the Integrity and Security Guideline set OSFI's expectations, and OSFI can act through its supervisory ratings. The privacy duties in PIPEDA s.10.1 to s.10.3 are the binding ones, with the Quebec and Real-Time Rail rules to check where they apply.

questions.ask: Does the incident meet an OSFI Advisory criterion, such as an impact on operations, data or systems, a third-party impact on the bank, or a disaster declared by a third-party vendor that affects the bank?
questions.help: The Advisory lists several criteria, and any one is enough. When in doubt, report: OSFI encourages a precautionary notice where an incident does not match a criterion or the bank is unsure.

questions.ask: Does a third-party arrangement affect, or threaten, the bank's ability to deliver a critical operation?
questions.help: OSFI expects to be promptly told of substantive issues of this kind (OSFI Guideline B-10, Overview). The bank's own list of critical operations, set under OSFI Guideline E-21, decides the answer.

questions.ask: Is there a breach of security safeguards involving personal information under the bank's control, including information held by a processor?
questions.help: PIPEDA s.10.1(1) sets the trigger. The bank is accountable for information its processor handles (PIPEDA Sch. 1, cl. 4.1.3), and the Privacy Commissioner treats the bank as the organization in control, so it reports.

questions.ask: Is there a real risk of significant harm to an individual?
questions.help: Weigh the sensitivity of the information and the probability that it is misused (PIPEDA s.10.1(8)). Significant harm includes financial loss, identity theft and humiliation (s.10.1(7)). The bank decides and should record its reasons.

questions.ask: Does the incident involve personal information of Quebec residents with a risk of serious injury?
questions.help: The Quebec private-sector Act, as amended by Law 25, uses a serious injury test, which differs from the PIPEDA test (reported; check). Most banks comply with both regimes, so answer both questions.

questions.ask: Is the bank a Real-Time Rail (RTR) participant, and is the incident a Severity 1 or Severity 2 incident?
questions.help: RTR launched on 9 November 2026. Payments Canada's rules set the phone call and the detailed report. The severity levels are defined in the rules (reported; check the current version).

questions.ask: Is there suspected foreign interference, undue influence or malicious activity that the bank reports to CSIS or the RCMP?
questions.help: Integrity and Security Guideline, Principle 10. The bank is encouraged to report to CSIS or the RCMP where it has reasonable grounds. OSFI should be told immediately when it does.

questions.ask: Is the bank a designated operator under the Critical Cyber Systems Protection Act, and is it a cyber security incident on a critical cyber system?
questions.help: The Act is enacted (S.C. 2026, c. 9). Part 2 comes into force on a day fixed by order of the Governor in Council; check whether an order has brought it into force. The reporting period is set by regulation, and may be no more than 72 hours. Check commencement and whether a banking class has been designated.

tracks.when: Within [2] hours (contract clock, set by the bank)
tracks.what: Prompt notice of any technology or cyber incident at the vendor or its subcontractors, to the bank's named contact, with the information the bank needs for its own report. Then regular updates and a root cause analysis.
tracks.basis: The contract. The bracketed figure is a model clause for the bank to set, not a rule. The bank needs it shorter than its own 24-hour clock.

sources.label: OSFI Guideline B-10, Third-Party Risk Management
OSFI Technology and Cyber Security Incident Reporting Advisory

tracks.who: OSFI, Technology Risk Division and the Lead Supervisor
tracks.when: Within 24 hours, or sooner if possible
tracks.what: Initial report in writing on OSFI's incident form, sent to the Technology Risk Division and to the Lead Supervisor. Mark missing facts as not yet available, give best estimates and say when more will follow. Then regular updates (OSFI expects, for example, daily), situation updates until containment, and a post-incident report with lessons learned.
tracks.basis: The Advisory is OSFI's supervisory expectation, not a statute. Failure to report may lead to closer supervision, including watch-listing or staging.

sources.label: OSFI Technology and Cyber Security Incident Reporting Advisory

tracks.what: Notice of substantive issues affecting the bank's ability to deliver a critical operation because of a third-party arrangement. Good practice is to give the facts known so far and update as the issue develops.
tracks.basis: OSFI Guideline B-10, Overview. A guideline, so OSFI expects this rather than the law requires it. No advance approval is needed.

sources.label: OSFI Guideline B-10, Third-Party Risk Management

tracks.when: As soon as feasible after the bank determines that the breach occurred
tracks.what: Written report to the Privacy Commissioner with the circumstances and cause of the breach, the dates, the personal information involved, the number of individuals, the steps taken to reduce harm, the steps to notify individuals, and a contact person.
tracks.basis: PIPEDA s.10.1(1) and (2). The content and form come from the Breach of Security Safeguards Regulations s.2.

sources.label: PIPEDA
Breach of Security Safeguards Regulations

tracks.when: As soon as feasible after the bank determines that the breach occurred
tracks.what: Direct and conspicuous notice to each affected individual, with enough information to understand what the breach means for them and what steps they can take to reduce or mitigate the harm.
tracks.basis: PIPEDA s.10.1(3) to (6). Notice may be given indirectly only in the circumstances the regulations prescribe.

sources.label: PIPEDA

tracks.when: As soon as feasible after the bank determines that the breach occurred

marks.label: Notify others that can reduce harm

tracks.what: Notice to any other organization or government body that may be able to reduce or mitigate the risk of harm from the breach.
tracks.basis: PIPEDA s.10.2(1) and (2). Section 10.2(3) allows the disclosure needed for that purpose.

sources.label: PIPEDA

tracks.when: Keep for 24 months after the bank determines that the breach occurred
tracks.what: A record of every breach of security safeguards involving personal information under the bank's control, including breaches that do not meet the real risk of significant harm test. The record must let the Commissioner check compliance with the notice duties, and be given to the Commissioner on request.
tracks.basis: PIPEDA s.10.3, and the Breach of Security Safeguards Regulations s.6 (24 months).

sources.label: PIPEDA
Breach of Security Safeguards Regulations

tracks.who: Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec, and affected persons
tracks.when: Promptly, on a risk of serious injury (reported; check)

marks.label: Written notice on the CAI form

tracks.what: Written notice to the Commission on its prescribed form where there is a risk of serious injury, with prompt updates, and notice to each affected person. The bank also keeps a register of every confidentiality incident, including those below the threshold, and gives it to the Commission on request.
tracks.basis: The Quebec private-sector Act as amended by Law 25 (CQLR c P-39.1), section numbers commonly cited (reported; check).

sources.label: Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec, incident guidance
sources.note: Reported; check the current form and section numbers.

tracks.who: Payments Canada Real-Time Payments Support Centre
tracks.when: Phone within 5 minutes of determining a Severity 1 or 2 incident; detailed report within 10 business days from the incident date
tracks.what: A phone call to the Real-Time Payments Support Centre, immediately and in any event within 5 minutes of determining that a Severity 1 or 2 incident has occurred, and a detailed report within 10 business days from the incident date.
tracks.basis: RTR Rule 9, as reported from Payments Canada's rules: the detailed report is due within 10 business days from the incident date (reported; check the current version). The participant also stays responsible for any activity it contracts out (RTR By-law s.2(3)).

sources.label: Canadian Payments Association By-law No. 10 (RTR)
Payments Canada RTR Rules
sources.note: Reported from Payments Canada's PDF; check the current version.

tracks.when: Immediately, when the bank reports to CSIS or the RCMP
tracks.what: Tell OSFI immediately when the bank reports suspected foreign interference, undue influence or malicious activity to CSIS or the RCMP. Record suspicions below the reporting threshold in the internal inventory for senior management.
tracks.basis: Integrity and Security Guideline, Principle 10 (31 January 2024). OSFI expects the immediate notice; the report to CSIS or the RCMP is encouraged where there are reasonable grounds.

sources.label: OSFI Integrity and Security Guideline

tracks.who: Communications Security Establishment, then the appropriate regulator
tracks.when: Within the period set by regulation, not more than 72 hours; then notify the regulator immediately
tracks.what: Report the cyber security incident to the Communications Security Establishment within the period the regulations set. Immediately after reporting, notify the appropriate regulator that the report was made and give it a copy.
tracks.basis: Critical Cyber Systems Protection Act, enacted (S.C. 2026, c. 9); confirm its commencement and whether a banking class has been designated before relying on it. The period is set by regulation.

sources.label: Critical Cyber Systems Protection Act (S.C. 2026, c. 9)
sources.note: Sections 17 and 18 of Bill C-8 as enacted (S.C. 2026, c. 9). Check commencement and the regulations.

notes: **One clock sheet:** keep one incident clock sheet for the plan, with a named owner for each track. Several tracks can start on the same day, and the bank should not rely on one team to remember them.

**The vendor clock sits inside the OSFI clock:** a vendor notice at [2] hours leaves the bank time to assess and report within 24 hours. If the vendor waits, the bank has less time to report within the 24-hour window.

**Who decides real risk of significant harm:** the bank does, on the PIPEDA factors. Record the reasons for each decision, since the breach record must let the Commissioner check compliance (SOR/2018-64 s.6(2)).
**Precautionary reports:** where an incident does not clearly meet an OSFI criterion, the Advisory encourages a precautionary notice. Decide early and record the decision.

**Root cause comes from the vendor:** B-10 2.4.2.4 expects the bank to request a root cause analysis proportionate to severity, and to carry out its own where appropriate. Put that right in the contract.
**Keep the evidence:** keep the vendor's notices, timestamps and updates, so the bank can show what it knew and when, to OSFI, the Commissioner and any Quebec authority.
incidentKit.caveat: Built from the official text of PIPEDA ss.10.1 to 10.3, the Breach of Security Safeguards Regulations (SOR/2018-64), the RTR By-law (SOR-2026-133) and the Critical Cyber Systems Protection Act, whose points rest on the text of Bill C-8 and need a check of commencement and the regulations. OSFI's Technology and Cyber Security Incident Reporting Advisory (13 August 2021), Guideline B-10 (2023, effective 1 May 2024) and the Integrity and Security Guideline (31 January 2024) are summarised in the bank's own words, not reproduced. The Quebec clocks, the RTR Rule 9 timings and the CAI guidance rest on agency and industry material and are reported; check the current texts before relying on them. The 24-hour clock is OSFI's expectation, not a statute, and the vendor clock is a model figure.

title: Data, privacy & records
oneLiner: The bank keeps its records in Canada or under OSFI's access, and it stays accountable for personal data its vendors handle.
keyPoints: **Records:** The Bank Act requires the bank to keep prescribed records at its head office or another place in Canada, and the bank and its agents must protect them.

**Records abroad:** The Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) must direct a bank to keep copies or process data only in Canada where that is incompatible with OSFI's responsibilities, or the Minister advises it is not in the national interest. For an exempt bank, OSFI may order a copy kept in Canada if it lacks immediate, direct, complete and ongoing access.
**Accountability:** PIPEDA keeps the bank responsible for personal information it transfers to a vendor for processing, and the bank must use contracts or other means to protect it.

**Breaches:** A breach that creates a real risk of significant harm must be reported to the Privacy Commissioner and to affected individuals as soon as feasible, and every breach must be recorded for 24 months.
**Quebec:** Quebec's private-sector Act adds a privacy impact assessment and a written agreement before data leaves Quebec, and its own incident regime (reported; check).
**Hong Kong contrast:** Canada has no adequacy test for transfers abroad. The question is whether the bank can still reach its records and still answers for them, not whether a country is approved.

deepDive.heading: Bank Act records: where they are kept
deepDive.lede: The Bank Act fixes where the bank's core records sit and who may look at them.
points: **Place of records:** Records under s.238 are kept at the head office or at another place in Canada that the directors choose (s.239(1)). Records of a branch outside Canada are excluded (s.239(3)).

**Daily records:** The bank must keep, for each customer, a daily record of transactions and balances (s.238(2)(c)). Records of this kind are not open to directors in the same way as other records (s.239(4)).

**Protection:** The bank and its agents must take reasonable precautions against loss, falsification and unauthorized access to its records (s.244). Whether a vendor is an agent depends on the contract and the facts, so the contract should say how this duty applies to it.
**Access:** The Superintendent has a right of access to any records held by or on behalf of a bank (s.643(2)(a)). This reaches records a cloud or outsourcing vendor holds for the bank.

**OSFI expectations:** OSFI expects records to be current at the end of each business day, and expects complete electronic copies on servers at the places the statute requires (OSFI Guideline B-10, Third-Party Risk Management, 2.3.2.2). OSFI also expects exempt banks to give it immediate, direct, complete and ongoing access to records held outside Canada.
deepDive.takeaway: Write vendor contracts so that OSFI can reach every record the statute covers, wherever the vendor stores it.

deepDive.heading: Records and processing abroad
deepDive.lede: Offshore hosting is allowed, but the Superintendent can order it stopped or copied back to Canada.
points: **Direction to stop:** If the Superintendent considers foreign copies or processing incompatible with OSFI's responsibilities, the Superintendent must direct the bank to keep copies or process data only in Canada (s.245(1)).
**National interest:** The same direction is required where the Minister advises that foreign holding is not in the national interest (s.245(1)).

**[[Exempt banks|exempt bank]]:** A subsidiary of a foreign bank from a Schedule IV country, or of a regulated foreign entity, may keep records abroad (s.239(3.1)), subject to s.245(1.1). OSFI may then order a copy kept in Canada if it lacks immediate, direct, complete and ongoing access.
**Compliance:** The bank must comply without delay with any order under s.245(1) or (1.1) (s.245(2)).

**Practical test:** For an exempt bank, OSFI's access test under s.245(1.1) decides whether it may order a copy kept in Canada. For other banks, the question is whether the Superintendent is of the opinion that foreign holding is incompatible with OSFI's responsibilities (s.245(1)). A contract with no access or audit rights makes the access test hard to meet (B-10, 2.3.3.3).

visual.caption: For an exempt bank, a foreign-held record stays lawful only while OSFI keeps its access.

deepDive.heading: PIPEDA: accountability for vendors
deepDive.lede: PIPEDA treats a vendor's processing as the bank's own responsibility.
points: **Accountability:** The bank stays responsible for personal information [[transferred to a third party for processing|transfer for processing]], and must use contractual or other means to give comparable protection (Sch. 1, cl. 4.1.3).
**Safeguards:** Protection must match the sensitivity of the information and apply whatever the format of storage (Sch. 1, cl. 4.7.1, 4.7.2).
**Retention:** Personal information is kept only as long as needed for its purposes (Sch. 1, cl. 4.5).

**Openness:** The bank must make its policies and practices on personal information readily available (Sch. 1, cl. 4.8). The OPC expects that to cover notice of processing abroad (OPC 2009 guidelines).

**Transfers abroad:** The OPC's 2009 guidelines treat a transfer for processing as a use, not a disclosure. No adequacy test applies, but the bank should tell customers that data may be processed abroad and may be accessed by foreign authorities (reported; check the 2009 guidelines).

**Consent:** Under cl. 4.3 the bank needs an individual's knowledge and consent for its purposes. The OPC's draft says that if a provider wants to use data for its own purposes, such as model training, the bank should assess whether consent is needed (OPC draft, proposed).
deepDive.takeaway: A vendor's privacy failure is the bank's privacy failure in law, so vendor diligence is a privacy control too.

deepDive.heading: Breach notices and records
deepDive.lede: A vendor breach starts the bank's own clock, and the bank must keep a record of it.
points: **Trigger:** A breach of security safeguards involving personal information under the bank's control must be reported where it creates a [[real risk of significant harm]] (s.10.1(1)).

**Control:** The Office of the Privacy Commissioner (OPC) treats the bank as in control of data its processor holds, so the bank reports and notifies even when a vendor was breached (OPC breach guidance).
**Timing:** Reports and notices are due as soon as feasible after the bank determines the breach occurred (s.10.1(2), (6)). The Act sets no fixed number of hours.
**Other organizations:** The bank must also notify any organization that can reduce the harm (s.10.2).
**Records:** Every breach must be recorded for 24 months, whether or not it met the reporting threshold (s.10.3(1); SOR-2018-64 s.6). The OPC may ask to see the record (s.10.3(2)).

deepDive.heading: Quebec and the wider privacy picture
deepDive.lede: Federal rules are not the only layer, and reform is still moving.
points: **Quebec transfers:** Before communicating personal information outside Quebec, a business must carry out a [[privacy impact assessment]] and conclude a written agreement (reported; check s.17).
**Quebec service providers:** A written contract must set confidentiality measures, limit use and require deletion when the mandate ends (reported; check s.18.3).

**Quebec incidents:** A confidentiality incident with a risk of serious injury must be reported to the CAI and to affected persons, and every incident must go in a register (reported; check ss.3.5 to 3.8).
**Supervisory information:** Ratings, stages and directions are [[prescribed supervisory information]] that the bank may not disclose to a vendor (SOR-2001-59 s.2).
**Reform:** Bill C-27 died in January 2025. Bill C-36 (Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act) was introduced on 15 June 2026. As at November 2026 it was reported at second reading (check status).

**Consumer-driven banking:** The Consumer-Driven Banking Act (S.C. 2026, c. 3) makes the Bank of Canada its administrator and lets it accredit third-party service providers. Most of it depends on an order, so confirm the commencement status before relying on it.

deepDive.heading: Draft OPC guidance on third-party providers
deepDive.lede: The OPC's 2026 draft shows what it will look for in a vendor assessment.
points: **Assess first:** The assessment should happen before the bank uses a provider or signs an agreement with it.
**Map the data:** Identify subcontractors, storage locations and any use the provider makes of the data for its own purposes, such as model training.
**Put it in the contract:** The OPC suggests recording the provider's role under PIPEDA, the roles of subcontractors and the best practices as contract terms.
**Exit:** Consider data portability, deletion (including backups) and return of data on termination.
**Status:** This is a draft with comments open to 4 December 2026, so cite it as proposed.

provisions.title: Bank records and their place
provisions.summary: The bank must maintain prescribed records, including daily customer transaction records, at its head office or another place in Canada chosen by the directors. A subsidiary of a foreign bank from a Schedule IV country or a regulated foreign entity is exempt from the in-Canada rule, subject to s.245(1.1).
provisions.counselNote: Map each record to its location before the vendor is chosen. Daily transaction records are the ones most likely to be held by a core banking or cloud vendor.

provisions.title: Protection of records
provisions.summary: The bank and its agents must take reasonable precautions to prevent loss, destruction and falsification of records, to facilitate detection of inaccuracies, and to keep unauthorized persons away from them.
provisions.counselNote: The duty reaches the bank's agents. Whether a vendor is one depends on the contract and the facts, so set the security and access terms in the contract either way, and test them.

provisions.title: Requirement to maintain copies and process information in Canada
provisions.summary: The Superintendent must direct a bank to keep copies of records, or to process data, only in Canada where that is incompatible with OSFI's responsibilities or the Minister advises it is not in the national interest. Where an exempt bank (s.239(3.1) or s.251(3)) keeps records abroad, the Superintendent may order a copy kept in Canada if OSFI lacks immediate, direct, complete and ongoing access. The bank must comply without delay.
provisions.counselNote: For an exempt bank, this is the basis for OSFI's copy-back order where OSFI lacks immediate, direct, complete and ongoing access. Keep the access rights in the vendor contract strong enough to meet it at short notice.

provisions.title: Examination of banks and access to records
provisions.summary: The Superintendent examines each bank at least once a year, including whether it has adequate policies against threats to its integrity or security. The Superintendent has a right of access to any records, cash, assets and security held by or on behalf of a bank.
provisions.counselNote: The words 'held by or on behalf of' reach records a vendor holds. The bank cannot contract out of OSFI's access, so the vendor must give access on request.

provisions.instrument: OSFI Guideline B-10, Third-Party Risk Management
provisions.title: Record keeping requirements
provisions.summary: OSFI expects records under the Bank Act to be current at the end of each business day, reproducible in intelligible form, and kept in the places the statute requires. For exempt banks, OSFI expects immediate, direct, complete and ongoing access to records held outside Canada.
provisions.counselNote: This is OSFI's expectation, not law. Use it to set record-location and access terms for every high-risk or critical arrangement.

provisions.instrument: Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act, S.C. 2000, c. 5
provisions.title: Accountability for information transferred to a third party
provisions.summary: An organization is responsible for personal information in its possession or custody, including information transferred to a third party for processing. It must use contractual or other means to give comparable protection while a third party processes it.
provisions.counselNote: The bank cannot shift privacy liability to a vendor by contract. Use the contract to pass down controls, audit rights and breach-notice duties.

provisions.instrument: Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act, S.C. 2000, c. 5
provisions.title: Safeguards
provisions.summary: Safeguards must protect personal information against loss, theft, unauthorized access, disclosure, copying, use and modification, whatever the format. The level of protection rises with the sensitivity of the information.
provisions.counselNote: Set the security standard in the contract by the sensitivity of the data, not by a single template. Confirm it is met in testing, not only on paper.

provisions.instrument: Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act, S.C. 2000, c. 5
provisions.title: Report and notify breaches of security safeguards
provisions.summary: An organization must report a breach of security safeguards to the Privacy Commissioner, and notify affected individuals, where it is reasonable to believe the breach creates a real risk of significant harm. Both must be done as soon as feasible after the breach is determined. Sensitivity and probability of misuse are the main factors.
provisions.counselNote: A vendor breach is usually the bank's reportable breach. Agree in the contract how fast the vendor tells the bank, so the bank can meet the as soon as feasible standard.

provisions.instrument: Breach of Security Safeguards Regulations, SOR/2018-64
provisions.title: Record of every breach for 24 months
provisions.summary: An organization must keep a record of every breach of security safeguards for 24 months after it determines the breach occurred. The record must allow the Privacy Commissioner to verify compliance with the reporting and notification duties.
provisions.counselNote: The record covers breaches that did not meet the reporting threshold. Make sure vendor incident logs feed it, because the bank must produce it on request.

provisions.instrument: OPC, Guidelines for Processing Personal Data Across Borders (2009)
provisions.title: Processing personal data across borders
provisions.summary: PIPEDA does not bar transfers for processing abroad. A transfer for processing is a use, not a disclosure, and the transferring organization stays accountable. Organizations should be open with customers that data may be processed abroad and accessed by foreign authorities.
provisions.counselNote: These guidelines are not binding, but the OPC relies on them. Use the customer notice to set expectations about foreign processing and foreign access.

provisions.instrument: OPC, draft guidance on assessing third-party service providers (2026)
provisions.title: Assessing third-party service providers
provisions.summary: The draft sets out what an organization should assess before engaging a provider, including subcontractors, storage locations, training data, breach handling, data portability and destruction at the end of the contract. Comments are open to 4 December 2026.
provisions.counselNote: This is a draft and is cited as proposed. Build the vendor questionnaire to it now, and check the final text when it is issued.

provisions.instrument: Act respecting the protection of personal information in the private sector, CQLR c P-39.1 (as amended by Law 25)
provisions.title: Quebec private-sector privacy Act
provisions.summary: Reported from the Commission d'acces a l'information's guidance: before communicating personal information outside Quebec, a business carries out a privacy impact assessment and concludes a written agreement. Service-provider contracts must be written and limit use. Confidentiality incidents with a risk of serious injury must be reported to the CAI and to affected persons, and recorded in a register.
provisions.counselNote: Whether and how this Act applies alongside PIPEDA to a federally regulated bank needs Legal's review. Most banks comply with both. Confirm the section numbers before relying on them.

provisions.instrument: Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act, S.C. 2000, c. 5
provisions.title: Breach records
provisions.summary: An organization must keep a record of every breach of security safeguards involving personal information under its control, in accordance with any prescribed requirements. It must give the Privacy Commissioner access to, or a copy of, the record on request.
provisions.counselNote: The record covers breaches below the reporting threshold. Set the duty out in the vendor contract so that incident details reach the bank's record in time.

provisions.title: Prohibited disclosure of supervisory information
provisions.summary: A bank must not, directly or indirectly, disclose prescribed supervisory information, subject to the exceptions in ss.3 and 4.
provisions.counselNote: Keep OSFI ratings, stages and directions out of vendor assessments and data rooms, and disclose them only within the listed exceptions.

checklist: **Map every record** to its location, owner and vendor, and confirm that each location lies within the s.238–239 rules or an exemption.
**Write OSFI access into every vendor contract** for records held by or on behalf of the bank (s.643(2)(a)), with a short response time.

**Assess offshore hosting** against s.245: for an exempt bank, can OSFI obtain immediate, direct, complete and ongoing access, failing which it may order a copy kept in Canada (s.245(1.1))? For any other bank, would foreign holding be incompatible with OSFI's responsibilities (s.245(1))?
**Set contract terms under PIPEDA cl. 4.1.3**: purpose limits, safeguards by sensitivity, subcontractor flow-down, retention and deletion, and breach notice.
**Agree vendor breach notice times** short enough for the bank to report as soon as feasible to the OPC and to affected individuals.
**Keep one breach register** covering all breaches, reportable or not, for 24 months (SOR-2018-64 s.6), fed by vendor incident logs.

**Run a privacy impact assessment** before personal data leaves Quebec (reported; check s.17). Put a written contract in place before entrusting data to a Quebec service provider (reported; check s.18.3).
**Keep supervisory information away from vendors**: ratings, stages and directions must not go to them (SOR-2001-59 s.2).
itAngle: **Data location map:** Keep a current map of where each record and copy sits, including backups, logs and vendor sub-processors. OSFI and the OPC will ask for it first.
**Access drills:** Test that the bank can pull a full, intelligible copy of its records from a vendor within a set time. A s.245 order gives no time to build the capability.
**Breach detection across vendors:** Feed vendor security alerts into the bank's own incident process, so that the 'determination' date and the 24-month record are set by the bank, not by the vendor.
**Contract evidence:** Keep the signed contract, the latest vendor assessment and the record-location map in one place, so that a s.643 request can be answered quickly.
virtualBankNotes: **No branches to hold records:** A digital bank's records sit almost entirely with its core banking, cloud and app vendors, so record location and access are vendor-contract questions from day one.
**Customer data flows:** Every app feature that sends data to a vendor is a processing decision under PIPEDA cl. 4.1.3. Map them before launch, and update the openness notice when they change.
**Breach volume:** Digital channels produce more incidents to assess. The register of every breach, including those below the reporting threshold, becomes a larger task.
**Customer notices:** Tell app users in plain terms that data may be processed abroad and may be accessed by foreign authorities, in line with the OPC's 2009 guidelines.
pitfalls: **Offshore by default:** Choosing a foreign cloud region without checking OSFI's access, so the bank meets s.245 only by luck.
**Vendor breach, bank silence:** Waiting for the vendor's report before starting the bank's own clock. The bank is treated as in control, so the clock runs from when it determines the breach.
**Contract without access:** Relying on the vendor's standard terms, which give the bank no audit, access or record-return rights.
**Sharing supervisory material:** Giving a vendor OSFI ratings, letters or intervention stages to help with an assessment.

glossary.term: immediate, direct, complete and ongoing access
glossary.definition: The standard in Bank Act s.245(1.1) for OSFI's access to an exempt bank's records kept outside Canada. If OSFI lacks it, OSFI may order a copy kept in Canada.
A subsidiary of a foreign bank from a Schedule IV country, or of a regulated foreign entity, which is exempt from the in-Canada record rule in Bank Act s.239(3.1), subject to s.245(1.1).
Passing personal information to a third party to handle on the organization's behalf. Under PIPEDA the organization stays responsible for it (cl. 4.1.3).
PIPEDA's first principle (Sch. 1, cl. 4.1): an organization is responsible for personal information under its control, including information held by a third party.

Loss of, unauthorized access to or unauthorized disclosure of personal information resulting from a breach of security safeguards under clause 4.7 of Schedule 1, or from a failure to establish them (PIPEDA s.2(1)).
The PIPEDA threshold for reporting a breach to the Privacy Commissioner and notifying individuals (s.10.1). It is judged by sensitivity and the probability of misuse (s.10.1(8)).
OSFI ratings, intervention stages, orders, prudential agreements and directions. The bank may disclose them only to listed persons who keep them confidential (SOR-2001-59 s.2).
The Quebec assessment (EFVP) a business must carry out before communicating personal information outside Quebec, to check the information will get adequate protection.

Under Quebec's private-sector Act, unauthorized access, use or disclosure of personal information, or its loss. Serious injury risk triggers notice to the CAI and to affected persons (reported; check).

title: Partners, agents & distribution
oneLiner: A digital bank's partners sell, verify, market and process for it, and the bank answers for them under Part XII.2, CASL and CDIC rules.
keyPoints: **Who counts:** Marketing affiliates, referral and co-brand partners, white-label fintechs, deposit brokers, payment partners and identity agents are each a [[third-party arrangement]] under OSFI Guideline B-10.

**Sellers:** Part XII.2 reaches anyone who sells the bank's products, for training (s.627.02) and pay (s.627.07). The bank's own statements, and partner statements it is responsible for, must be accurate and not misleading (s.627.03, s.627.14).

**Sales arrangements:** Under s.627.15 the bank may not arrange for an [[intermediary|intermediary]] to sell its products unless four conditions are met, including that the partner complies with the consumer provisions as if it were an institution (s.627.15(a)).

**Limits:** Networking is permitted (s.411), but a bank may not act in Canada as agent for anyone placing insurance (s.416(2)). SOR/92-330 further limits promotion and the sharing of customer information with insurers.

**Deposit insurance statements:** Anyone, partners included, must not make a false, misleading or deceptive representation about what is a deposit, what is insured or who is a member (SOR/96-542 s.2). The membership wording, sign and badge rules bind the bank (ss.4-7), and CDIC's bulletin expects members to tell fintech partners about the s.2 duty (reported; check).

**Marketing and contests:** CASL makes the bank answerable for messages sent for it (s.32) unless it shows due diligence (s.33). Contests need adequate disclosure and selection by skill or at random (Competition Act s.74.06).

deepDive.heading: Who counts as a partner
deepDive.lede: Partners differ in what they do for the bank, and that decides which rule bites.
points: **Scope:** OSFI Guideline B-10, Third-Party Risk Management (effective 1 May 2024), covers any business or strategic arrangement with an outside entity, by contract or otherwise, including brokers and joint ventures.
**Marketing affiliates:** Their messages and adverts may be the bank's communications. Check who sends each message and who is named as the sender (CASL s.6(2)(a)).
**Referral and co-brand partners:** Referral is allowed under s.411. If the partner also sells, s.627.15 applies to that sale.

**White-label and [[banking-as-a-service]] fintechs:** Check whether the bank acts as an intermediary for another entity's product (s.627.16). The prescribed requirements for that agreement are in the regulations, so check them before signing.
**Deposit brokers, payment and identity partners:** Each is a third-party arrangement under B-10. Non-bank payment partners register under the RPAA, and identity agents work under PCMLTFR s.106.
**Scope rule:** B-10 applies to every partner arrangement, scaled to risk and criticality. Unlike SA-2, it has no materiality gate and no advance discussion with the regulator.

deepDive.heading: Sellers under Part XII.2
deepDive.lede: The consumer rules reach the people who sell the bank's products, not only the bank's own staff.
points: **Training and pay:** Anyone who offers or sells the bank's products must be trained on its consumer policies (s.627.02). Pay and benefits must not undermine appropriateness (s.627.07).

**The four conditions:** Under s.627.15 the bank may use a partner only if the partner complies with the consumer provisions as if it were an institution, give customers access to the bank's complaint procedures, let its staff use the whistleblowing channels, and observe the anti-reprisal rule.
**Undue pressure:** The bank must not coerce anyone, and must not impose undue pressure to tie one product to another (s.627.04). A partner's bundled offer can breach this.

**Complaints:** The bank's complaint procedures must satisfy the Commissioner, and must not be presented as independent of the bank (s.627.43(1)-(2)). Partner customers reach the same route (s.627.15(b)).
**Penalties:** The FCAC Act (s.19(2)) allows an administrative monetary penalty of up to $10 million for a violation by a financial institution.

visual.caption: The same training and pay rules apply to bank staff and to partner sellers.

deepDive.heading: Networking, insurance and customer data
deepDive.lede: Referral and agency are allowed, but insurance and customer data are tightly limited.
points: **Networking (s.411):** A bank may act as agent for, or refer people to, other financial institutions and permitted entities, subject to s.416. Regulations may require disclosure of the principal and of any commission.
**Insurance agency (s.416(2)):** A bank may not act in Canada as agent for anyone placing insurance. This bar applies whatever the channel, so app-based insurance sales face it too.
**Authorized types (SOR/92-330, ss.2, 4, 5):** A bank may administer and advise on authorized types of insurance, such as credit card-related, creditors', mortgage and travel insurance.

**Customer information (SOR/92-330 s.8):** A bank may not give an insurer, agent or broker information about its customers in Canada, directly or indirectly. Subsidiaries may not pass on such information either.

**Promotion (SOR/92-330 ss.6-7):** A bank may promote an insurer, agent or broker only within the regulation's exceptions, such as where it deals only in authorized types. For app and web promotion, s.7.1 lets the bank promote on a bank web page only where the insurer, agent or broker deals only in authorized types, and the bank may not link on its web pages to promotion of any other insurer, agent or broker.
deepDive.takeaway: Map every insurance touchpoint in a partner journey before launch, and keep customer data out of any insurer feed.

deepDive.heading: Deposit insurance, AML and identity
deepDive.lede: Partners must not blur what CDIC insures, and the bank stays answerable for identity checks.
points: **Membership statements (SOR/96-542 s.4):** The bank, as a member, must use the prescribed membership wording in its advertising (SOR/96-542 s.4(1)), and its displays must not suggest that a non-member is a member or that an ineligible deposit is insured (s.4(2)).

**[[CDIC badge]] (s.7):** The digital badge goes on the home page, deposit landing pages and the first page after log-on. A member that shares its home page with a non-member must not show the badge there (s.7(3)).
**Ineligible products:** Warnings are required on deposit instruments that CDIC does not insure (s.9).

**Identity checks by a [[mandatary]] (PCMLTFR s.106):** The bank may rely on an agent to verify identity only under a written agreement. It must obtain the information as soon as feasible and be satisfied that it is valid and current.
**Reliance on others (PCMLTFR s.107):** Reliance on another reporting entity, or on a similar affiliated foreign entity, needs a written agreement to obtain the information on request.

**Responsibility:** FINTRAC's guidance (Guide 11) says the bank stays responsible for its client identification when it uses an agent (reported; check). Records are kept at least five years (PCMLTFR s.148).

deepDive.heading: Marketing, contests and payments
deepDive.lede: Marketing rules follow the message, and contest rules follow the prize.
points: **CASL content (s.6):** A commercial electronic message needs consent, must identify the sender and the person on whose behalf it is sent, and must carry an unsubscribe mechanism.

**[[vicarious liability|Vicarious liability]] (s.32):** The bank answers for messages sent by an agent or mandatary acting within its authority, whether or not the agent is identified or proceeded against.
**Due diligence (s.33):** This is a defence only if the bank can show it exercised due diligence to prevent the violation, so keep the evidence from onboarding and monitoring.
**Aiding (s.9):** Aiding, inducing, procuring or causing a partner's non-compliant message is itself prohibited.

**Contests (Competition Act s.74.06):** Prize numbers and approximate values, the areas, and any fact that materially affects the chances of winning must be adequately and fairly disclosed, prizes must not be unduly delayed, and selection must be by skill or at random. Criminal Code s.206 also reaches some chance-based draws that require payment. Quebec has its own rules for publicity contests open to Quebec residents (reported; check before running a contest there).
**Payments (RPAA s.9(a)):** The Act does not apply to a bank's own retail payment activities. A non-bank payment partner must register and carry its own framework and incident duties (ss.17-18).
**Consumer-driven banking:** S.C. 2026, c. 3 adds accreditation for third-party service providers. Most of it comes into force by order, so confirm the commencement status before relying on it.
deepDive.takeaway: Route every partner campaign and contest through counsel, with sender identity, consent and prize terms settled first.

deepDive.heading: Onboarding a partner
deepDive.lede: A workable sequence settles the legal conditions before the launch date.
points: **Classify:** Decide whether the arrangement is a third-party arrangement under B-10, and whether it is high-risk or critical.
**Map the rules:** Identify which rule bites for each activity, from s.627.15 for sellers to s.416 for insurance and PCMLTFR s.106 for identity.
**Contract:** Build in the s.627.15 conditions, the B-10 Annex 2 terms and any PCMLTFR s.106 agreement before anything goes live.
**Train and approve:** Train sellers (s.627.02), approve scripts and adverts (s.627.14), and test remuneration (s.627.07).
**Launch and monitor:** Check partner pages for CDIC badge use, and confirm that complaints reach the bank's procedures.

provisions.title: Arrangements with affiliates, etc.
provisions.summary: The bank may not arrange with its representatives, agents or other intermediaries to sell or further the sale of its products unless four conditions are met. The partner must comply with the consumer provisions as if it were an institution, give customers access to the bank's complaint procedures, let its staff use the whistleblowing channels, and observe the anti-reprisal rule. The same applies to certain affiliate finance entities.
provisions.counselNote: This is the core clause for every sales partner. Write the four conditions into each agreement, and check that the partner can meet them. The prohibition binds the bank.

provisions.title: Training
provisions.summary: The bank must ensure that its officers and employees in Canada, and anyone who offers or sells its products or services in Canada, are trained on its consumer-protection policies and procedures.
provisions.counselNote: Partner sales staff count even though they are not the bank's employees. Keep training records, and test that partners deliver the training in practice.

provisions.title: Remuneration, payment or benefit
provisions.summary: Remuneration of the bank's staff, and of anyone who offers or sells its products, and any payment or benefit offered to them, must not interfere with their ability to comply with the appropriateness policies in s.627.06.
provisions.counselNote: Test commission and bounty structures for partners against the appropriateness policies, especially where pay rises with sales volume.

provisions.title: Advertisements
provisions.summary: Any advertisement in Canada made by a bank must be accurate, clear and not misleading.
provisions.counselNote: Partner adverts the bank has made or approved should be treated as made by the bank for s.627.14; whether approval alone makes an advert one made by the bank is a question for counsel. Approve partner copy before it runs and keep a record.

provisions.title: Networking
provisions.summary: Subject to s.416, a bank may act as agent for any person in providing a service of a financial institution or permitted entity, and may refer any person to such an institution or entity. Regulations may require disclosure of the principal and of any commission the bank earns.
provisions.counselNote: Referral and agency arrangements are permitted, but they sit under the insurance bar in s.416 and any disclosure regulations. Check both before launch.

provisions.title: Restriction on insurance business
provisions.summary: A bank may not act in Canada as agent for anyone in the placing of insurance, and may not lease or provide space in its Canadian branches to anyone placing insurance. Further limits are set by regulation.
provisions.counselNote: A digital bank's app-based insurance offers face the same agency bar as a branch network. Confirm that each insurance feature is within the permitted activities before launch.

provisions.instrument: Insurance Business (Banks and Bank Holding Companies) Regulations (SOR/92-330)
provisions.title: Prohibited activities
provisions.summary: A bank may not provide an insurer, agent or broker, directly or indirectly, with information about its customers in Canada. A bank may not permit its subsidiaries to pass on information they receive from the bank in the same way.
provisions.counselNote: Customer data sent to insurers, including through a partner's data feed, is a hard stop. Design partner data flows so that no customer information reaches an insurer or broker.

provisions.title: Display of badge
provisions.summary: A member must prominently display the digital CDIC badge on its home page, on each deposit product landing page and on the first page after log-on that shows insured deposits. A member that shares its home page with a non-member must not display the badge on that page.
provisions.counselNote: A partner's app or site that shares the bank's home page must not carry the badge. Map every page where deposits are sold before go-live, and test each one.

provisions.instrument: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Regulations (SOR/2002-184)
provisions.title: Measures for verifying identity
provisions.summary: A reporting entity may rely on an agent or mandatary to verify identity, but only under a written agreement or arrangement entered into for that purpose. It must obtain the information as soon as feasible, and be satisfied that the information is valid and current and that the agent verified the person's identity by a method in s.105(1)(a) to (d).
provisions.counselNote: Identity checks by partners need a written agreement in place before the partner starts work. FINTRAC's guidance (Guide 11) says the bank remains responsible for identity checks it has an agent perform (PCMLTFR s.106 sets the reliance conditions) (reported; check).

provisions.title: Vicarious liability
provisions.summary: A person is liable for a violation committed by its employee acting within the scope of employment, or by its agent or mandatary acting within the scope of authority, whether or not that employee, agent or mandatary is identified or proceeded against.
provisions.counselNote: The bank can be liable for messages its partners send for it. Build due diligence evidence (s.33) into onboarding and monitoring, so that the defence is available if needed.

provisions.title: Promotional contests
provisions.summary: A person who conducts a contest to promote a product or business interest engages in reviewable conduct where prize disclosure is not adequate and fair, prize distribution is unduly delayed, or selection is not made by skill or at random.
provisions.counselNote: Partner-run contests must disclose prizes, odds and areas adequately and fairly, and selection must be by skill or at random. Review every partner contest before launch.

provisions.title: Payment service providers
provisions.summary: The Act does not apply to a bank or to the other entities listed in s.9 (for example certain credit unions, insurers, trust and loan companies). Other payment service providers that perform retail payment activities are within the Act.
provisions.counselNote: The bank's own payment activities sit outside the Act, but a non-bank payment partner must register and carry its own framework and incident duties. Write notice terms into the partner agreement.

checklist: **Classify every partner:** Record whether each arrangement is a third-party arrangement under B-10, and whether it is high-risk or critical, before any contract is signed.
**Put the s.627.15 conditions in each sales contract:** Include consumer-provision compliance, complaint access, whistleblowing and the anti-reprisal rule.
**Confirm training and pay:** Evidence that sellers are trained (s.627.02) and that their remuneration does not undermine appropriateness (s.627.07).
**Approve every partner advert and script:** Check each against s.627.14 and s.627.03 before it is used, and keep the approvals.
**Clear insurance features against s.416 and SOR/92-330:** Confirm the activity is permitted, and that no customer information reaches an insurer.
**Check CDIC wording and badge placement:** On each partner page and app screen, test the membership statement and the badge rules (SOR/96-542 ss.4, 7).
**Sign PCMLTFR s.106 agreements first:** No partner verifies identity until the written agreement is in place.
**Review marketing and contests:** Check CASL sender identity, consent and unsubscribe (s.6), and contest disclosure and selection (Competition Act s.74.06).
itAngle: **Complaint routing:** Partner-sourced complaints must reach the bank's designated procedures and be recorded for at least seven years (s.627.44). Build the routing and record-keeping into the partner interface.
**Consent and sender evidence:** Store consent records and the sender identity for each partner message. These records support the CASL due diligence defence (s.33).
**Partner page controls:** Automate checks on deposit pages and the home page so that the CDIC badge appears only where the rules allow.
**Identity data flows:** Partner identity checks must return the information the bank relied on, and do so as soon as feasible (PCMLTFR s.106). Build the data feed and its audit trail before go-live.
virtualBankNotes: **No branches:** The branch-lease limb of s.416(2) has little effect on a digital bank, but the agency bar still applies to app-based insurance sales.

**Partner apps:** A partner app that shares the bank's home page cannot display the CDIC badge on that home page if the partner is a non-member (SOR/96-542 s.7(3)). The badge rules for the first page after log-on (s.7(1)(c)) still apply.
**Digital onboarding:** Identity-check partners and reliance arrangements under PCMLTFR ss.106-107 need written agreements in place before the first customer is onboarded.

**Partner links and content:** Where the bank sends or approves links in partner content, treat them as the bank's communications (s.627.14), with CASL consent and sender identity recorded for each message.
pitfalls: **Commission on volume alone:** Paying partners by sales volume without testing it against the appropriateness policies (s.627.07).

**Unreviewed partner copy:** Partner adverts that use the bank's name without the bank's approval create a risk under CASL and the misleading-advertising rules where the bank is responsible for them (s.627.14 if the bank made the advert).
**Badge on a shared page:** Showing the CDIC badge on a home page shared with a non-member (SOR/96-542 s.7(3)).
**Chance-based contests:** A prize draw with paid entry, or with undisclosed odds, which can breach s.74.06 and may fall within Criminal Code s.206.

glossary.definition: Under OSFI Guideline B-10, any business or strategic arrangement with an entity or individual, by contract or otherwise, other than with customers or under employment contracts. It includes outsourcing, brokers, cloud providers, affiliates and joint ventures.
A representative, agent or other intermediary of a bank, as the term is used in Bank Act s.627.15. Whether a particular partner is one depends on the facts and the contract.
An affiliate controlled by a bank or bank holding company that is a finance entity under Bank Act s.464(1). Section 627.15 covers its sales as well as those of the bank.
The power in Bank Act s.411 for a bank to act as agent for, or refer people to, other financial institutions and permitted entities, subject to the insurance bar in s.416.
A person who acts for another under a mandate. PCMLTFR s.106 lets a reporting entity rely on an agent or mandatary to verify identity, under a written agreement.
A person or entity listed in section 5 of the PCMLTFA, including banks. PCMLTFR s.107 allows reliance on another reporting entity or on certain affiliated foreign entities.
Liability for another person's violation because of the relationship, here an employee, agent or mandatary acting within the scope of employment or authority (CASL s.32).
The digital badge that a CDIC member must display on prescribed pages under the CDIC Deposit Insurance Information By-law (SOR/96-542, s.7).
A model in which a non-bank partner offers banking products under its own brand, with a licensed bank providing the regulated account or deposit product behind it.

title: Capital, liquidity & deposit insurance
oneLiner: Capital, liquidity and deposit insurance run on one statute, OSFI guidelines and CDIC by-laws, and each one reaches the vendors that hold the data.
keyPoints: **Statutory duty:** Bank Act s.485(1) requires a bank to maintain adequate capital and adequate, appropriate liquidity, and to comply with the regulations that apply to them.
**Guidelines:** OSFI sets the detail in its Capital Adequacy, Leverage and Liquidity Adequacy guidelines. OSFI expects compliance; the guidelines are not themselves law.
**Superintendent's direction:** Under s.485(3) the Superintendent can order a bank to increase capital or provide more liquidity, even when the bank complies with the rules.

**Proportionality:** The SMSB guideline places non-D-SIB banks in three categories by total assets, loans and derivatives, so a new digital bank is categorised from its business plan, and an existing one from the threshold tests.
**Deposit insurance:** CDIC insures each eligible deposit only up to $100,000 per category, and the bank must produce depositor data and stop withdrawals within hours of a CDIC instruction.
**Counsel's role:** Tie capital headroom, dividend policy and data-processing contracts to these duties, and confirm that core banking and deposit vendors can meet the CDIC timetable.
