deepDive.heading: The statutory duty
deepDive.lede: Capital and liquidity are a statutory duty of the bank, not only an OSFI guideline matter.
points: **Duty:** s.485(1) requires adequate capital and adequate, appropriate liquidity, and compliance with any regulations on them. The directors manage the bank's business, so they own this duty in practice (s.157).
**Rule-making:** s.485(2) lets the Governor in Council make regulations and the Superintendent make guidelines on capital, liquidity and, for D-SIBs, loss-absorbing capacity.

**Direction:** s.485(3) lets the Superintendent order a bank to increase capital or provide additional liquidity, even while it complies with the guidelines. The bank must comply within the time the order sets (s.485(4)).

**Rule form:** Canada's main capital and liquidity standards are OSFI guidelines made under s.485(2), not Governor in Council regulations. The Superintendent's direction power under s.485(3) is the backstop.

deepDive.heading: Capital, leverage and liquidity rules
deepDive.lede: Three OSFI guidelines set the minimum ratios, and an internal assessment sits on top of them.
points: **Capital Adequacy Requirements (CAR):** sets the risk-based capital ratios a bank must meet. Check the current CAR text and its effective dates before setting a headroom target.
**Leverage Requirements:** a non-risk-based ratio that supplements the CAR.
**Liquidity Adequacy Requirements (LAR):** sets the liquidity measures, including the liquidity coverage ratio and net cumulative cash flow. Check the current LAR text for its effective dates.
**Basel III:** these guidelines carry Basel III reforms into Canada. State the ratio levels only from the current guideline text.
**ICAAP (E-19):** OSFI expects a capital assessment process (ICAAP); check the current E-19 guideline text.

deepDive.heading: SMSB categories and proportionality
deepDive.lede: The SMSB guideline sorts banks that OSFI has not designated as D-SIBs into three categories.

visual.caption: Categories narrow as the requirements get lighter; average total assets and total loans are tested over twelve month-ends.

items.label: Category I
items.note: Total assets; subsidiaries of D-SIBs are Category I

items.label: Category II
items.note: Any one loan, derivative or off-balance-sheet test is met

items.label: Category III
items.note: None of the Category II tests is met

points: **Scope:** SMSBs are banks, bank holding companies and trust and loan companies that OSFI has not designated as D-SIBs, applied on a consolidated basis.
**Category II tests:** total loans above $100 million, interest rate or FX derivatives above 100% of total capital, other derivatives, or other off-balance-sheet exposure above 100% of total capital.
**Notice:** the bank must notify OSFI within 60 days of its fiscal year end when the thresholds are crossed. Category changes take effect after OSFI confirms them, in the following fiscal year.

**Derivatives (Category III):** notify OSFI within 60 days of a quarter-end if derivative or off-balance-sheet exposures exceed the thresholds. The bank then stays in Category II for at least two years (reported; check).
**New banks:** a new SMSB is categorised from its business plan at the Order to Commence and Carry on Business stage. A Category III bank can ask in writing to be moved to Category II.
**Legal status:** the SMSB guideline is a reference tool, not a guideline under s.485(2). The minimum standards sit in CAR, LR and LAR, and s.485(3) still applies.

deepDive.heading: Deposit insurance and CDIC data
deepDive.lede: CDIC coverage is capped, and the bank must be able to hand CDIC its depositor data on a short clock.

visual.caption: Clock runs from the determination time or CDIC's instruction; the 4 p.m. outer limits are noted on the data and interest items.

items.label: Stop withdrawals
items.note: After CDIC's instruction

items.label: Depositor data
items.note: Earlier of this and 4 p.m. the next day

items.label: Interest accrued
items.note: Earlier of this and 4 p.m. on day two

points: **Cap:** s.12(c) of the CDIC Act means CDIC insures a deposit only up to $100,000. Coverage is per category per depositor at each member institution.
**Not covered:** mutual funds, stocks, bonds, ETFs and crypto-assets, including stablecoins, are outside coverage.

**Data by-law:** SOR-2010-292 s.2 requires the bank to produce depositor data, identify insurance categories and stop withdrawals within six hours of CDIC's instruction. The bank must also keep policies to ensure these capabilities.
**Disclosure:** SOR-96-542 s.6 governs brochure delivery at account opening. Location and display must not suggest that the bank is a member when it is not, or that an ineligible deposit is insured.

**Resolution:** CDIC Act s.39.15(1)(e) stops anyone from ending or amending an agreement with a member merely because of insolvency, the order or a change of control, so vendor termination-on-resolution clauses may not bite.

deepDive.heading: Early losses, dividends and capital planning
deepDive.lede: A digital bank with early losses should plan its capital before it plans payouts.

items.label: Plan capital
items.note: Stress test losses against the business plan

items.label: Notify before a dividend
items.note: Notice to the Superintendent before payment (s.79(2))

items.label: Dividend bar
items.note: No payment where there are reasonable grounds to believe it would breach a s.485 rule or direction

items.label: Direction to add capital
items.note: Superintendent may order more capital or liquidity

points: **Dividend bar:** s.79(4) stops the directors declaring or the bank paying a dividend where there are reasonable grounds to believe the payment would breach a s.485 regulation or a s.485(3) direction.
**Director exposure:** the Bank Act makes directors liable for a dividend paid contrary to s.79 (s.207(2)(c)), so the capital test belongs in the board paper.
**Business plan:** an early-stage bank should show how losses reduce capital and liquidity over the planning period, and what it does if the plan misses.
deepDive.takeaway: Put a capital and liquidity trigger into the dividend policy before the first profitable quarter, not after.

provisions.title: Adequacy of capital and liquidity
provisions.summary: Requires a bank to maintain adequate capital and adequate, appropriate liquidity, and to comply with regulations on both. The Governor in Council may make regulations, the Superintendent may make guidelines, and the Superintendent may order a bank to add capital or liquidity even when it complies. The bank must comply with such an order within the time the order sets.
provisions.counselNote: Treat capital and liquidity as a statutory duty. Because OSFI can order an increase, plan headroom against the business plan, not the bare minimum.

provisions.title: Declaration of dividend or patronage allocation
provisions.summary: Directors must notify the Superintendent at least 15 days before a dividend is paid. They must not declare or pay a dividend if there are reasonable grounds to believe the payment would breach a s.485 regulation or a s.485(3) direction.
provisions.counselNote: Build the Superintendent notice into the dividend calendar, and record the capital and liquidity test in each declaration.

provisions.title: Duty to insure
provisions.summary: CDIC must insure each deposit with a member institution, except the part of any one deposit that exceeds $100,000. Deposits not payable in Canada and deposits where the Crown is a preferred claimant are excluded.
provisions.counselNote: The per-deposit cap drives product design, including how a bank structures accounts for a single customer. Explain the limit accurately in marketing and in the brochure.

provisions.title: Stay of proceedings
provisions.summary: After a CDIC resolution order, no person may terminate or amend an agreement with the member, or accelerate it, merely because of insolvency, the order, a change of control, a prior non-monetary default, or a monetary default cured within 60 days. Contrary terms have no force.
provisions.counselNote: Vendor and group agreements that let the counterparty walk away on resolution may be unenforceable in that event. Confirm the position in contracts that run to the core banking and deposit services.

provisions.instrument: CDIC Data and System Requirements By-law
provisions.title: Capabilities
provisions.summary: A member must be able to produce specified depositor data as of the determination time, give it to CDIC within set deadlines, and stop withdrawals within six hours of CDIC's instruction. The member must also have policies and procedures that secure these capabilities.
provisions.counselNote: Core banking and deposit vendors must support this clock. Test the data extract and the withdrawal freeze end to end, and keep evidence for CDIC's annual certification.

provisions.title: Display and Provision of Brochure
provisions.summary: A member must give depositors the CDIC brochure as part of account opening for an eligible deposit. The display of the brochure must not give the impression that a non-member is a member, or that an ineligible deposit is insured.
provisions.counselNote: Map the brochure and the membership statements into the app flow at account opening, and check that the screens where they appear do not imply coverage for products outside it.

provisions.instrument: OSFI SMSB Capital and Liquidity Requirements Guideline (2026)
provisions.title: Small and Medium-Sized Deposit-Taking Institutions (SMSBs) Capital and Liquidity Requirements
provisions.summary: Sorts banks and trust and loan companies that are not D-SIBs into Categories I to III by total assets, total loans and derivative or off-balance-sheet exposure. It sets the threshold tests, the 60-day notice rule and the opt-up route for Category III banks. It is a reference tool; the minimum standards sit in the CAR, LR and LAR guidelines.
provisions.counselNote: Model the category from the business plan at the OCCB stage, and diarise the 60-day notice and the quarterly derivative test. The category decides which capital and liquidity measures apply.

provisions.title: Capital Adequacy Requirements (CAR)
provisions.summary: Sets the risk-based capital ratios a bank must meet, including its treatment of credit, market and operational risk. Check the current text and its effective dates.
provisions.counselNote: Map each capital ratio to the business plan and the stress scenarios. Check the current CAR chapters and their effective dates before setting a headroom target.

provisions.title: Leverage Requirements
provisions.summary: Sets a non-risk-based leverage ratio that supplements the risk-based CAR.
provisions.counselNote: A digital bank with a large balance sheet relative to capital can breach the leverage ratio even with low risk weights. Run this test in the capital plan.

provisions.ref: Liquidity coverage and net cumulative cash flow
provisions.title: Liquidity Adequacy Requirements (LAR)
provisions.summary: Sets the liquidity measures a bank must hold, including the liquidity coverage ratio and net cumulative cash flow. Check the current LAR text for its effective dates.
provisions.counselNote: Deposit runs are the main liquidity risk for an app-only bank. Model outflows from app-based deposits and check that liquidity data can be produced daily.

provisions.instrument: OSFI E-19, ICAAP for Deposit-Taking Institutions
provisions.title: Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP) for Deposit-Taking Institutions
provisions.summary: Expects the bank to have a capital assessment process (ICAAP) that covers the capital its risks require. Check the current E-19 text before relying on it.
provisions.counselNote: Keep the ICAAP current with the business plan and the vendor risk register. OSFI reads it as evidence that management understands the bank's risks.

checklist: **Map the s.485 duty:** Assign a named executive to capital and liquidity, with a documented headroom target above the CAR, LR and LAR minimums.
**Confirm the SMSB category:** Record the category, the test date and the 60-day notice deadline, and diarise the quarterly derivative test.
**Test the CDIC clock:** Run a timed test of depositor data and of a withdrawal freeze, against the six-hour and 30-hour limits.
**Check the CDIC coverage message:** Review every screen that shows deposit or membership statements, and avoid 'insured' claims for ineligible products.
**Set the dividend test:** Record the s.79(2) 15-day notice and the s.79(4) capital and liquidity test in each declaration.
**Review vendor contracts for resolution:** Check whether core banking, deposit and data vendors can terminate on resolution, given s.39.15.
**Update the ICAAP:** Include vendor concentration and early-stage loss scenarios in the stress tests.
**Confirm CDIC wording:** Check the membership statements, brochure and data delivery against the current text of the CDIC by-laws.
itAngle: **Depositor data:** The bank's core banking and deposit ledgers must produce the depositor, category and accrued-interest data as of a fixed determination time, in a usable format.
**Withdrawal freeze:** Build a tested way to stop withdrawals by account type within six hours of a CDIC instruction, including when the app and card channels run through vendors.
**Capital and liquidity reporting:** The SMSB category is calculated from the M4 monthly balance sheet return, so data lineage from the ledger to that return needs controls.
**Stress and scenario data:** The ICAAP and liquidity tests need feeds from payment, deposit and lending vendors, with reconciliation and change control on the models.
virtualBankNotes: **No branches to fall back on:** A digital bank must produce the CDIC data and freeze withdrawals from its own systems, so the clock and the vendor support must be tested as part of the core platform.
**App-based deposit disclosure:** The brochure and membership statements must appear at account opening and in the app's display locations, without implying coverage for partner products.

**Early losses:** OSFI's incorporation guide expects initial paid-in capital to keep the bank above its target ratios for the longer of three years or until profitable (reported; check), so the capital plan and the dividend bar must be built into the business plan from the start.

**Partner products:** Where a fintech partner offers a product, the bank must check how the deposit and coverage statements read in that partner's app, since the bank remains responsible for the disclosure.
pitfalls: **Treating the SMSB category as fixed:** Categories change with the thresholds, and the notice clock runs from the fiscal year end. Missing it can leave the wrong measures applying.
**Assuming coverage follows the product:** Mutual funds, crypto-assets and stablecoins are outside CDIC coverage even when they sit in a bank-branded app near deposits.

**Declaring dividends during a capital squeeze:** s.79(4) bars a payment where there are reasonable grounds to believe it would breach a s.485 rule or direction, and directors can be exposed for an unlawful payment.
**Confusing guidelines with law:** The CAR, LR, LAR and E-19 texts are OSFI expectations, enforced through supervision and s.485(3), not free-standing offences.

glossary.definition: A small or medium-sized deposit-taking institution: a bank, bank holding company or trust and loan company that OSFI has not designated as a D-SIB. OSFI sorts SMSBs into Categories I to III.
A domestic systemically important bank, designated by OSFI. D-SIBs must also hold a minimum capacity to absorb losses under Bank Act s.485(1.1).
The OSFI guideline (CAR) that sets the risk-based capital ratios a bank must meet, based on the risk of its assets and off-balance-sheet exposures.
The OSFI guideline (LR) that sets a non-risk-based leverage ratio. It supplements the risk-based capital ratios.
The OSFI guideline (LAR) that sets liquidity measures, including the liquidity coverage ratio and net cumulative cash flow.
The internal capital adequacy assessment process, in which the bank assesses the capital its risks require. OSFI's E-19 guideline sets expectations for it.
An order under Bank Act s.485(3) requiring a bank to increase its capital or provide additional liquidity, even when it complies with the rules.
A class of deposit for CDIC coverage, such as one name, joint, RRSP or TFSA. CDIC covers up to $100,000 for each category, for each depositor, at each member institution.
The point in time that the CDIC data by-law uses to fix the deposit position that the bank must report to CDIC.

title: AML, sanctions & fraud
oneLiner: A digital bank's onboarding, vendor ID checks and sanctions screening all sit inside a federal compliance program that FINTRAC reviews.
keyPoints: **Who is caught:** Banks to which the Bank Act applies are [[reporting entities|reporting entity]] under PCMLTFA s.5(a). The full regime applies to the bank itself, not only to its partners.

**Compliance program:** PCMLTFA s.9.6 requires a risk-based [[compliance program]]. PCMLTFR s.156 sets its parts: a responsible person, written policies, a documented risk assessment, training and a periodic review.

**Remote identity checks:** PCMLTFR s.105 lists the approved verification methods. Agents and vendors may verify identity under s.106, but only under a written agreement and by a method in s.105(1)(a) to (d). FINTRAC guidance says the bank remains responsible.

**Reports and records:** [[Suspicious transactions|suspicious transaction report]] go to FINTRAC under PCMLTFA s.7, including suspected sanctions evasion. Records are kept for at least five years under PCMLTFR s.148.

**Sanctions and fraud:** Sanctions reporting and laundering risk run on separate tracks. Criminal Code s.462.31 makes laundering an offence. Banks must check for, and report, property of listed persons under the Criminal Code and the sanctions regulations. Responsibility for receiving these reports is reported to have moved from OSFI to FINTRAC in 2025 (reported; check FINTRAC's current instructions).

**Penalties:** FINTRAC can impose up to $20 million per violation on an entity under PCMLTFA s.73.1, with a cumulative cap, for all violations on one notice of violation, of the greater of $20 million and 3% of gross global revenue.

conceptMap.caption: The bank's AML duties run to FINTRAC and to the vendors and entities it relies on. A Minister's directive can add measures.

items.note: Suspicious transaction reports

items.label: Identity verification agents
items.note: Written agreement required

items.label: Other reporting entities

deepDive.heading: Who is caught and what the program must do
deepDive.lede: Banks are reporting entities, and the compliance program is the core obligation.

visual.caption: Each layer rests on the one above it, so the risk assessment drives the rest.

items.label: Risk assessment
items.note: Clients, products, channels, geography (s.156(1)(c))

items.label: Written policies
items.note: Approved by a senior officer (s.156(1)(b))

items.label: Training and review
items.note: Biennial auditor review (s.156(3))

points: **Scope:** PCMLTFA s.5(a) covers authorized foreign banks in respect of their business in Canada, and banks to which the Bank Act applies.
**Program:** s.9.6(1) requires a program to ensure compliance. Under s.9.6(1.1) it must be reasonably designed, risk-based and effective.
**Responsible person:** PCMLTFR s.156(1)(a) requires a person to run the program, and s.156(1)(b) requires written policies approved by a senior officer.

**Risk assessment:** s.156(1)(c) requires a documented assessment of clients, products, delivery channels and geography. Under s.156(2), a new technology that may affect these must be assessed before it is introduced.
**Review:** s.156(3) requires a review every two years by an internal or external auditor. Under s.156(4), findings go to a senior officer within 30 days of completion.
deepDive.takeaway: Complete the risk assessment before launch, not after the first audit finds the gap.

deepDive.heading: Identifying customers without branches
deepDive.lede: A digital bank must verify identity without meeting the customer, using only the methods the regulations approve.

visual.caption: Three of the approved routes for a remote customer, each with its own conditions.

items.label: Government photo ID
items.note: Authentic, valid and current (s.105(5))

items.label: Canadian credit file
items.note: At least three years old, more than one source

items.label: Two independent sources
items.note: Sources must differ (s.105(4))

points: **Approved methods:** PCMLTFR s.105(1) lists government photo ID, government information, a credit file, two independent sources, and reliance on an affiliated entity's earlier check (s.105(1)(e)).
**Document quality:** Under s.105(5), any document used must be authentic, valid and current. Other information must be valid and current.
**Credit file rule:** The file must be in Canada and at least three years old, and the information must come from more than one source (s.105(1)(c)).

**Agents:** A vendor may verify identity under s.106. The bank needs a written agreement, must obtain the information as soon as feasible, and must be satisfied it is valid and current and was verified by a method in s.105(1)(a) to (d) (s.106(3)).
deepDive.takeaway: Map each product to its approved method in the compliance policy, and test that the vendor follows it.

deepDive.heading: Reports, records and ministerial directives
deepDive.lede: Suspicion, large cash and records drive the reporting cycle, and the Minister can add targeted measures.

items.label: Reasonable grounds to suspect
items.note: Money laundering, terrorist financing or sanctions evasion

items.label: Report to FINTRAC
items.note: Completed or attempted transactions

items.label: Keep records
items.note: At least five years from the relevant trigger

points: **Suspicious transactions:** PCMLTFA s.7 requires a report of any completed or attempted transaction where there are reasonable grounds to suspect a money laundering, terrorist financing or sanctions evasion offence.
**No tipping off:** Under s.8, nobody may disclose a report, or its contents, with intent to prejudice a criminal investigation, whether or not one has begun.

**Large cash:** PCMLTFR s.10 requires a record of each cash receipt of $10,000 or more in a single transaction. The FINTRAC reporting rules for these transactions, and for electronic funds transfers, should be confirmed against FINTRAC's current guidance.
**Retention:** s.148(1) sets at least five years, counted from account closure, the last business transaction or creation, depending on the record type.

**Ministerial directives:** Under s.11.42 the Minister may require measures for certain transactions linked to foreign states or entities, such as verification, due diligence, monitoring and reporting. The Minister may act only on the grounds in s.11.42(4).
deepDive.takeaway: Record every suspicion decision and its reasons, including decisions not to report.

deepDive.heading: Sanctions screening and reporting
deepDive.lede: Sanctions duties run alongside the AML regime, and the reporting route needs confirming before the procedure is written.
points: **Listed persons:** Regulations under the United Nations Act, the Special Economic Measures Act and the Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act name persons whose property must be frozen (reported; check each regulation).

**Reporting route:** Banks must check for, and report, property of listed persons under the Criminal Code and the sanctions regulations. Responsibility for receiving these reports is reported to have moved from OSFI to FINTRAC in 2025 (reported; check FINTRAC's current instructions).
**Who receives the reports:** confirm with FINTRAC and OSFI which body receives the bank's listed-person reports, and in what form, before writing the procedure.
**Terrorist property:** The Criminal Code is reported to require disclosure of property of a terrorist group to the RCMP and CSIS, with immunity for good-faith disclosure (reported; check).
**Screening:** Screen at onboarding and again when a list changes, since a customer may be listed after the account opens.
deepDive.takeaway: Confirm the current reporting route with FINTRAC and OSFI before writing the sanctions procedure.

deepDive.heading: Laundering, fraud and the criminal law
deepDive.lede: Criminal liability reaches the bank's staff and customers, and fraud is a separate operational problem.
points: **Laundering offence:** Criminal Code s.462.31(1) covers dealing with property or its proceeds, intending to conceal or convert them, knowing or reckless that they come from a designated offence.
**Penalty:** The offence carries up to ten years' imprisonment on indictment (s.462.31(2)(a)), or up to 14 years where it is committed for a criminal organization (s.462.31(2.1)).

**No need to prove the predicate offence:** Where the accused is not also charged with the designated offence, the prosecutor need not prove the accused knew the specific designated offence (s.462.31(2.2), subject to (2.4)).

**Inference:** Where the accused is not also charged with the designated offence, a court may infer knowledge where dealings are markedly unusual or inconsistent with lawful activity typical of the sector (s.462.31(2.3), subject to (2.4)). Mule accounts often fit this pattern.
**Fraud and scams:** Scams draw attention from consumer regulators and industry (reported; check current FCAC guidance). The bank's fraud tools are practice, not a statutory requirement.
deepDive.takeaway: Review fraud losses and laundering risk together, since the same accounts often show both.

deepDive.heading: Penalties and accountability
deepDive.lede: [[FINTRAC]] penalties are large and tied to revenue, so the number of failed controls matters as much as any single failure.

visual.caption: Maximum amounts under PCMLTFA s.73.1. Each is a ceiling, not a set penalty.

items.label: Cumulative cap, entity
items.note: Greater of the two, on gross global revenue (s.73.1(3)(b))

points: **Per violation:** Up to $20 million for an entity and $4 million for a person under s.73.1(2). Each prescribed violation is classed as minor, serious or very serious (s.73.1(1)(b)).
**Cumulative cap:** For one notice, the greater of $20 million and 3% of gross global revenue for an entity (s.73.1(3)(b)). Affiliated entities use the group's revenue (s.73.1(4)).
**Designation:** The regulations decide which provisions are penalised (s.73.1(1)(a)). Check the amounts in those regulations before relying on them.
**Accountability:** Responsibility for the program sits with an appointed person (s.156(1)(a)). Regulators look at governance as well as at controls.

**Comparison:** The HKMA can reprimand, order remedial action and impose penalties under AMLO s.21 (see stage 12). In Canada the penalty regime sits in the PCMLTFA with FINTRAC as the penalty authority.

**Hong Kong comparison:** Hong Kong's statutory customer due diligence duties sit in AMLO Schedule 2, supported by the HKMA AML/CFT Guideline, which is a statutory guideline (reported; check the section numbers). Canada's equivalent is the PCMLTFA and PCMLTFR, with FINTRAC guidance such as Guide 11 setting out how the Regulations are read.
deepDive.takeaway: Penalty exposure is per violation, so a board should see the count of control failures, not just the total.

provisions.instrument: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act
provisions.title: Application of Part
provisions.summary: Applies the Part to authorized foreign banks in respect of their business in Canada, and to banks to which the Bank Act applies, among other persons and entities.
provisions.counselNote: The bank is a reporting entity in its own right. Partners that are not reporting entities may still be bound by contract, so map each product to the regime.

provisions.instrument: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act
provisions.title: Compliance program
provisions.summary: Requires a compliance program that is reasonably designed, risk-based and effective, including a risk assessment and special measures where the risk is high.
provisions.counselNote: The program is the first document an examiner asks for. Keep it approved, current and tied to the bank's actual products and channels.

provisions.instrument: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Regulations
provisions.title: Compliance programs and special measures
provisions.summary: Requires a named responsible person, written policies approved by a senior officer, a documented risk assessment, training for employees and agents, and a review every two years by an auditor, reported within 30 days.
provisions.counselNote: Assess a new technology or development before launch (s.156(2)). For a digital bank, a new onboarding flow or vendor is the usual trigger, so build it into product approval.

provisions.instrument: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Regulations
provisions.title: Measures for verifying identity
provisions.summary: Lists the approved identity methods: government photo ID, government information, a Canadian credit file at least three years old from more than one source, two independent sources, and reliance on an affiliate's earlier check. Documents must be authentic, valid and current.
provisions.counselNote: Remote onboarding must map each method to a product. A method the regulation does not list cannot support verification, however convenient it is for the customer.

provisions.instrument: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Regulations
provisions.title: Measures for verifying identity: agents
provisions.summary: Allows a reporting entity to rely on an agent or mandatary for identity checks, if there is a written agreement, the information is obtained as soon as feasible, and the entity is satisfied it is valid and current and was verified by an approved method.
provisions.counselNote: A vendor's check counts as the bank's check only if the contract meets s.106(3). FINTRAC's guidance says the bank remains responsible, so vendor oversight belongs in the program.

provisions.instrument: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Regulations
provisions.title: Record-keeping
provisions.summary: Requires records to be kept for at least five years, counted from account closure, the last business transaction or the creation of the record, depending on the record type.
provisions.counselNote: Set retention by record type rather than one period for all data. Records a vendor holds for the bank should follow the same periods under the contract.

provisions.instrument: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act
provisions.title: Transactions if reasonable grounds to suspect
provisions.summary: Requires a report to FINTRAC of any completed or attempted transaction where there are reasonable grounds to suspect a money laundering, terrorist financing or sanctions evasion offence.
provisions.counselNote: Suspicion turns on the facts the bank knows. Document the reasons for each decision, including a decision not to report. Check the reporting timing in the regulations.

provisions.instrument: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act
provisions.title: Minister's written directive
provisions.summary: Lets the Minister require specified measures, such as verification, due diligence, monitoring and reporting, for transactions linked to certain foreign states or entities, where the grounds in s.11.42(4) are met.
provisions.counselNote: Directives come from the Minister, not FINTRAC. Monitor them and build the ability to apply a targeted measure quickly to a defined transaction class.

provisions.instrument: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act
provisions.title: Regulations: penalties for prescribed violations
provisions.summary: Sets maximum penalties of $20 million per prescribed violation for an entity and $4 million for a person, with cumulative caps tied to revenue. The regulations designate the violations and set the penalties.
provisions.counselNote: Exposure is per violation, so count control failures across the program. Confirm the amounts in the regulations before relying on them.

provisions.instrument: FINTRAC Guidance: Methods to verify the identity of persons and entities (Guide 11)
provisions.title: Methods to verify identity, including agents
provisions.summary: Explains the approved identity methods and the conditions for using agents and for relying on another reporting entity, as FINTRAC reads the Regulations. Its agent guidance took effect on 1 October 2025.
provisions.counselNote: Guidance is not binding, but it sets out how FINTRAC reads the Regulations. Use the version in force for each onboarding flow, and check that the vendor contract matches the agent conditions.

provisions.title: Laundering proceeds of crime
provisions.summary: Makes it an offence to deal with property or its proceeds with intent to conceal or convert them, knowing or reckless that they come from a designated offence. Knowledge may be inferred from markedly unusual dealings.
provisions.counselNote: Staff who handle unusual flows may be exposed. Train front-line, payments and fraud teams on the knowledge test, since courts may infer it from the pattern of dealings.

checklist: **Map each product to an identity method:** Record the s.105 method used for every account type, and test that onboarding follows it.
**Contract vendors under s.106:** Use a written agreement that covers the information to be delivered, the timing and the validity checks.
**Run the new-technology assessment:** Document the risk before launching any new onboarding flow, vendor or model (s.156(2)).
**Schedule the biennial review:** Plan the auditor review and the 30-day report to a senior officer (s.156(3) and (4)).
**Build a suspicion workflow:** Log alerts, decisions and reasons, and write the no-tipping-off rule of s.8 into the procedure.
**Confirm the sanctions reporting route:** Confirm with FINTRAC and OSFI which body receives listed-person reports, and check FINTRAC's current instructions, before setting procedures.
**Set retention by record type:** Apply the s.148 periods, and mirror them in vendor contracts.
**Brief the board on penalty exposure:** Explain the per-violation maximum under s.73.1 and the cumulative cap.
itAngle: **Screening data:** Name matches, list updates and alert logs are evidence. Keep them time-stamped and retrievable for a FINTRAC examination.
**Vendor integration:** Identity vendors often return data through APIs. Confirm which fields the bank stores and for how long under s.148.
**Model governance:** Monitoring rules and any machine-learning model fall within the s.156 risk assessment and testing. Document the rule logic and each change.
**Access and secrecy:** Restrict access to suspicion records. Under s.8, tooling must not expose reports to staff or vendors who do not need them.
virtualBankNotes: **Remote onboarding is the whole process:** With no branches, the identity method is the main control. Each approved method and each vendor needs its own evidence file.
**Vendors as agents:** An identity vendor may act as an agent under s.106. FINTRAC's guidance says the bank remains responsible. Build vendor oversight into the program, not only into the contract.
**Partners that are reporting entities:** A partner that is itself a reporting entity may supply checks under s.107, under a written agreement to produce the information on request.
**Launch gate:** A new app feature or channel triggers the s.156(2) assessment before launch, so product teams need a compliance sign-off step.
pitfalls: **Vendor as the responsible party:** Assuming the identity vendor carries the obligation. The bank stays responsible; FINTRAC's guidance says so, and the vendor's check counts only if it meets s.106(3).
**Credit file shortcut:** Using a credit file under three years old, or one drawn from a single source, which fails s.105(1)(c).
**Informal disclosure:** Telling a customer or a partner about a suspicion in a way that could prejudice an investigation (s.8).
**One-time screening:** Screening customers only at onboarding and not again when sanctions lists change.

glossary.definition: A person or entity listed in PCMLTFA s.5, such as a bank to which the Bank Act applies. It must meet the Act's program, record and reporting duties.
The Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada. It receives reports under the PCMLTFA and can impose administrative monetary penalties.
A report to FINTRAC under PCMLTFA s.7 of a completed or attempted transaction where there are reasonable grounds to suspect a listed offence.
The risk-based program required by PCMLTFA s.9.6 and PCMLTFR s.156, covering the risk assessment, policies, training and review.
A person or entity acting for the bank under a written agreement, which may verify identity under PCMLTFR s.106.
Using identity checks made earlier by another reporting entity or an affiliate, under PCMLTFR s.107 or s.105(1)(e).
A record of each receipt of $10,000 or more in cash in a single transaction, which financial entities must keep under PCMLTFR s.10.
A written direction under PCMLTFA s.11.42 requiring specified measures for certain transactions linked to foreign states or entities.
A person or entity named under a sanctions regulation, whose property must be frozen and may have to be reported.

title: Customers, conduct & complaints
oneLiner: Part XII.2 of the Bank Act sets the consumer rules for sales, consent, cancellation and complaints, and FCAC enforces them.
keyPoints: **Statute, not guidance:** Part XII.2 of the Bank Act (the Financial Consumer Protection Framework, in force 30 June 2022) binds the bank directly. OSFI guidelines are expectations; these are legal duties.
**Conduct:** The bank must not use undue pressure, coerce people or take advantage of them, and products sold to individuals other than for business purposes must suit their circumstances.
**Consent and disclosure:** Express consent and an agreement come before a product is provided. Key terms, charges and cancellation rights must be disclosed.

**Complaints:** The bank runs its own procedure, deals with complaints within the 56-day prescribed period, keeps records for seven years, and refers unresolved complaints to the external complaints body.
**Enforcement:** FCAC examines each bank every year, can impose administrative monetary penalties of up to $10 million, and must publish violations.
**Counsel's role:** Map every customer touchpoint, including partner apps and call centres, against these duties before launch.

conceptMap.caption: The bank carries the consumer duties for its own staff, agents and partners, and answers to FCAC and the external complaints body.

centre.label: The bank
centre.note: Responsible for its own sales and its partners' sales

items.label: Partners and agents
items.note: Sell or further the bank's products
items.rel: must meet the consumer rules for

items.label: Customers' complaints
items.note: Received by the bank or a partner

items.label: Customers
items.note: Consent and an agreement first; a copy for ongoing products

items.label: Complaint records
items.note: Kept for at least seven years

items.label: External complaints body
items.note: Every bank must be a member

items.label: FCAC
items.note: Examines each bank at least yearly

items.label: FCAC penalties
items.note: Up to $10 million for a bank

deepDive.heading: The statutory framework
deepDive.lede: The bank's consumer duties are in the Bank Act, not in a voluntary code.

visual.caption: The consumer rules narrow from statute to voluntary commitments, but the bank can be held to its own promises.

items.label: Bank Act Part XII.2
items.note: Consumer provisions in force 30 June 2022

items.label: SOR/2021-181
items.note: Prescribed periods and requirements, such as s.14

items.label: Codes and public commitments
items.note: Must be disclosed (s.627.66); breach is wrongdoing (s.979.1)

points: **Part XII.2:** The [[consumer provisions]] apply to banks and authorized foreign banks. They are statutory duties, enforced by FCAC.
**Regulations:** The Financial Consumer Protection Framework Regulations (SOR/2021-181) add prescribed periods and requirements, including the 56-day complaint period in s.14.
**Codes and commitments:** A voluntary code or public commitment that protects customers must be disclosed (s.627.66). Breaching one counts as wrongdoing for whistleblowing (s.979.1(b)).

**Wide complaint test:** A complaint is any dissatisfaction, whether justified or not, expressed to the bank about a product or service (s.627.01). Treat every expression of dissatisfaction as a complaint until it is logged.
**Compared with Hong Kong:** The Code of Banking Practice in Hong Kong is non-statutory. Canada puts the core customer rules in statute, with penalties and an annual examination.
deepDive.takeaway: Treat the consumer provisions as law, and treat the bank's public commitments as promises it can be held to.

deepDive.heading: Responsible conduct and sales
deepDive.lede: The bank is responsible for how its products are sold, including by partners.
points: **No undue pressure:** The bank must not pressure or coerce a person, tie one product to another, or take advantage of them (s.627.04).
**Appropriate products:** Policies must ensure products sold to individuals for non-business purposes suit their circumstances, including their financial needs (s.627.06).
**Pay does not override suitability:** Pay and benefits for staff, and for anyone who sells the bank's products, must not undermine suitability (s.627.07).
**Training:** Staff, and anyone who offers or sells the bank's products, must be trained on the consumer policies (s.627.02).
**Advertising:** Advertisements made by the bank must be accurate, clear and not misleading (s.627.14). Check how far 'made by' reaches to partner material the bank issues.
deepDive.takeaway: Commission and incentive plans for partners need the same suitability review as the product itself.

deepDive.heading: Consent, disclosure and cancellation
deepDive.lede: A product should not be provided until the customer has consented, agreed to terms and received a copy.

visual.caption: Cancellation windows run from the day the agreement is entered into or the account is opened.

items.label: Mail or telephone
items.note: Ongoing agreements (s.627.1(1)(a))

items.label: Any other manner
items.note: Other agreements (s.627.1(1)(b)); deposit accounts have prescribed periods (SOR-2021-181 s.3, s.5), so check app sign-ups

items.label: Retail deposit account
items.note: From opening (SOR-2021-181 s.5; s.627.11)

points: **Express consent:** Obtain [[express consent]], enter into an agreement and give a copy for ongoing products (s.627.08(1)). Using the product is not consent (s.627.08(3)).
**Oral consent:** Confirm oral consent in writing without delay (s.627.08(2)).
**Clear requests:** Any request for consent must be clear, simple and not misleading (s.627.09).

**Cancellation refunds:** The bank must waive cancellation charges and refund what it received. It may recover only use-related amounts, expenses it reasonably incurred in providing the product, and any prescribed amount (s.627.1(3)).

**Disclosure before agreement:** Before an ongoing agreement, disclose the features, every charge and penalty, and the customer's rights and obligations (s.627.59). No charge may be imposed without express consent, a contract term and disclosure (s.627.12(1)).

**Promotional offers:** For a non-business offer of more than 30 days, disclose the post-offer rate, charges, rights and cancellation period 21 and 5 days before it ends. For shorter offers, disclose 5 days before (s.627.61).
deepDive.takeaway: Build consent, disclosure and cancellation into onboarding as legal steps, each with a timestamp and a record.

deepDive.heading: Complaints handling
deepDive.lede: Complaints run on a fixed statutory clock, with an external escalation route at the end.

items.label: Written acknowledgement
items.note: Date received and how to escalate (s.627.43(4))

items.label: Resolve within 56 days
items.note: Prescribed period, counted from receipt

items.label: Refer to the external body
items.note: Sole external complaints body (OBSI, reported; check)

items.label: Annual public figures
items.note: Publish within 135 days after the financial year ends, on each website, with counts, average handling time and resolution rate

points: **Procedures:** The bank must set procedures satisfactory to the [[Commissioner]], designate a Canadian officer to run them, and designate staff to receive complaints (s.627.43(1)). It must file the procedures and keep the filing current (s.627.43(3)).
**No 'ombudsman':** The bank must not use misleading terms, including ones suggesting its complaint staff are independent, such as 'ombudsman' (s.627.43(2)).
**Records:** Keep a record of each complaint for at least seven years, including the original complaint or recording and the date received (s.627.44).
**Quarterly reporting:** Report each complaint received in a quarter to the Commissioner within 60 days after the quarter ends (s.627.46).

**External body:** Every bank must be a member of the [[external complaints body]] (s.627.48(3)). It must give that body all relevant information without delay after it notifies the bank that a complaint has been received (s.627.52). OBSI is reported to recommend up to $350,000 per complaint (reported; check).
deepDive.takeaway: The complaint clock starts on receipt, so route every channel, including partner call centres and app forms, into the bank's own process from day one.

deepDive.heading: Supervision and penalties
deepDive.lede: FCAC supervises the consumer provisions and can impose penalties through its own administrative process.
points: **Annual examination:** The Commissioner must examine each bank at least once each calendar year to see that the consumer provisions are being complied with (s.659).
**Maximum penalty:** The maximum penalty for a violation by a financial institution is $10 million, and $1 million for a natural person (FCAC Act s.19(2)).
**Designated violations:** Regulations choose which consumer provisions are violations that FCAC can penalise (FCAC Act s.19(1)(a)). Check the current designations before rating the bank's exposure.
**Publication:** The Commissioner must make public the nature of a violation, the name of the person and the amount of the penalty, subject to regulations (FCAC Act s.31(1)).
deepDive.takeaway: Treat the annual FCAC examination as the test, and keep evidence of every consent, disclosure, training and complaint step.

deepDive.heading: Partners, whistleblowing and Quebec
deepDive.lede: The bank stays responsible when partners sell to or handle complaints from its customers.
points: **Partner conditions:** The bank must not arrange for agents or intermediaries to sell its products unless they comply with the consumer provisions as if they were a bank, customers can reach the bank's complaint process, their staff can use the whistleblowing channels, and they observe s.979.4 as if they were a bank (s.627.15(a)-(d)).

**Call centres:** Partners must give customers access to the bank's complaint procedures, or the bank cannot use them to sell (s.627.15(b)). Script the hand-off and record the complaint under s.627.44.
**Whistleblowing:** Part XVI.1 protects staff who report wrongdoing. Wrongdoing includes breach of a voluntary code or public commitment the bank has adopted (s.979.1).
**Quebec customers:** Quebec's Charter of the French Language sets language rules for consumer contracts and documents (reported; check the current text of the Charter before launch in Quebec).
**Customer data:** Customer information shared with partners must also meet the privacy rules covered in stage 7 (data).
deepDive.takeaway: Put consumer, complaint and whistleblowing terms into every partner agreement, as s.627.15 requires.

provisions.title: Prohibited conduct
provisions.summary: An institution must not, in its dealings in Canada with customers and the public, impose undue pressure or coerce a person, including to take one product as a condition of another, take advantage of a person, or engage in prescribed conduct. The bank must also disclose that it does not do these things (s.627.64).
provisions.counselNote: Review bundled offers, sales scripts and in-app prompts against this section. Coercion includes more than an explicit tie-in condition.

provisions.title: Policies and procedures: appropriate products or services
provisions.summary: The bank must establish and apply policies and procedures to ensure that products it sells to natural persons, other than for business purposes, are appropriate for their circumstances, including financial needs. Section 627.07 stops pay and benefits from undermining this.
provisions.counselNote: Build suitability checks into product journeys, and test partner commissions against them.

provisions.title: No provision without express consent and agreement
provisions.summary: No product or service may be provided in Canada until the bank has the person's express consent, has entered into an agreement and, for an ongoing product, has given a copy of it. Use of the product is not consent. Oral consent needs written confirmation without delay.
provisions.counselNote: Design the app so that consent is a deliberate act, stored with the terms version and a timestamp, with a copy of the agreement sent.

provisions.title: Cancellation periods: products or services
provisions.summary: For an ongoing agreement, the customer may cancel within 14 business days if it was made by mail or telephone, and within 3 business days in other cases, unless a prescribed period applies. The bank must waive cancellation charges and refund amounts received, and may recover only use-related amounts, expenses it reasonably incurred in providing the product, and any prescribed amount.
provisions.counselNote: Confirm the period for each product. Retail deposit accounts fall under s.627.11 and SOR-2021-181 s.5. Build a cancellation route in the app. Deposit accounts other than retail deposit accounts have a prescribed 14-business-day period after opening (SOR-2021-181 s.3).

provisions.title: Advertisements
provisions.summary: Any advertisement in Canada made by an institution must be accurate, clear and not misleading.
provisions.counselNote: Apply the test to app store listings, social posts and partner landing pages the bank publishes. Deposit insurance claims are a separate regime (see stage 9).

provisions.title: Other products or services
provisions.summary: Before entering into an ongoing agreement with a natural person, the bank must disclose the features of the product, every charge and penalty, the person's rights and obligations, and the information in s.627.65(a) to (c), unless another disclosure rule applies.
provisions.counselNote: Build the disclosure pack into onboarding for each ongoing product without its own disclosure rule, and record that it was delivered.

provisions.title: Promotional and other offers
provisions.summary: Where a natural person takes a promotional, introductory or special offer for non-business purposes, the bank must disclose the post-offer rate, charges, rights and obligations, and the cancellation period. Disclosure is due 21 and 5 days before the end of an offer longer than 30 days, and 5 days before a shorter offer.
provisions.counselNote: Set the disclosure dates in the offer record so that notices send automatically and are logged.

provisions.title: Procedures for dealing with complaints
provisions.summary: The bank must set complaint procedures satisfactory to the Commissioner, designate a Canadian officer to run them and staff to receive complaints, and file the procedures. It must not use misleading terms such as 'ombudsman', and must acknowledge each complaint in writing.
provisions.counselNote: File the procedures with FCAC and refile after each change. Every channel that takes complaints needs a named route into this process.

provisions.title: Record of complaint
provisions.summary: The bank must keep a record of each complaint for at least seven years. The record includes the original written complaint or a recording, the complainant's name and contact details, the date received, a description of the complaint, and the actions taken.
provisions.counselNote: Set the retention period in the records schedule (see stage 7). The duty is the bank's, so a vendor or call centre that keeps the record must meet it.

provisions.title: Designation of body corporate
provisions.summary: The Minister, on the Commissioner's recommendation, designates a body as the external complaints body for complaints the bank has not resolved to the customer's satisfaction or within the prescribed period. Every bank must be a member, and the designation is published in the Canada Gazette. The sole body is OBSI (reported; check the designation notice).
provisions.counselNote: Escalation to the external body is a statutory route, not an option the bank can withhold. Confirm the designation date and the current contact details before publishing them.

provisions.title: Voluntary codes of conduct and public commitments
provisions.summary: Codes and public commitments that protect customers must be disclosed, available at each branch and point of service and on each website, and provided in writing on request.
provisions.counselNote: Keep the codes and public commitments in one list, and check that each one is available where s.627.66(a) requires before launch.

provisions.title: Period for dealing with complaints
provisions.summary: For the purposes of s.627.43(1)(a), the prescribed period for dealing with a complaint is 56 days after the day on which the complaint is received.
provisions.counselNote: The 56-day clock runs from receipt, not from triage. Start the service-level timers on the date the complaint first arrives, through any channel.

provisions.title: Definition of wrongdoing
provisions.summary: In Part XVI.1, wrongdoing includes a contravention of the Act or its regulations, a breach of a voluntary code of conduct or public commitment the bank has adopted, and a breach of a bank policy or procedure.
provisions.counselNote: Adopting a public code makes its breach a whistleblowing matter. Check the codes and commitments the bank publishes before it publishes them.

provisions.instrument: Financial Consumer Agency of Canada Act (F-11.1)
provisions.title: Regulations: violations and penalty maximum
provisions.summary: Regulations designate which contraventions of a consumer provision are violations that FCAC can penalise. The maximum penalty is $10 million for a violation by a financial institution, and $1 million for a natural person.
provisions.counselNote: Map which consumer provisions are designated before rating the bank's exposure. Penalties are administrative, so the process differs from a prosecution.

checklist: **Map every customer touchpoint:** Include app flows, partner sites, call centres and marketing, and tie each one to the consumer provisions.
**Build consent and cancellation into onboarding:** Record express consent, the agreement and the cancellation window, each with a timestamp.
**Set a complaints clock:** Date-stamp every complaint on receipt, run a 56-day timer, and refer unresolved matters with the complete file.
**Keep complaint records for seven years:** Capture the s.627.44 fields in the case tool, including at partner hand-offs.
**File and publish the procedures:** Lodge the procedures with FCAC, publish complaint routes and annual figures, and avoid 'ombudsman' terms.
**Put consumer terms in partner contracts:** Cover s.627.15(a) to (d): consumer rules, complaint routing, whistleblowing and the s.979.4 conduct duty.
**Review ads and offers:** Sign off advertising (s.627.14) and promotional disclosures (s.627.61) before release.
**Prepare for the annual FCAC examination:** Keep an evidence file of consent logs, disclosures, complaint records and training (s.627.02, s.659).
itAngle: **Consent evidence:** Store each consent event with the terms version shown, the channel and a timestamp. Oral consent needs written confirmation (s.627.08(2)).
**One complaint record:** Build the s.627.44 fields into the case system, so that the record, the quarterly report (s.627.46) and the annual figures (s.627.47) come from one source.
**Electronic documents:** A notice the Act requires is not satisfied by an electronic document unless the addressee consents and designates an information system for receipt (Bank Act s.995(1)(a)).
**Notification engine:** Promotional-offer disclosures (s.627.61) and cancellation reminders need scheduled, logged notices rather than manual sends.
virtualBankNotes: **Opening accounts:** s.627.17(1) assumes a request made in person at a branch or point of service. For app-only opening, check the prescribed manners under s.627.17(3) and the current regulations.

**Basic banking:** A member bank may not require a minimum deposit or balance (s.627.17(4)). A refusal to open a retail deposit account must be given in writing, with the information in s.627.65(a) to (c) (s.627.19).

**No branch, no posters:** Complaint routes and the FCAC contact details must be disclosed to customers and the public (s.627.65). The codes and public commitments must be available at each point of service and on each website (s.627.66(a)).
**Digital complaints:** A complaint raised in chat, an app form or email is still a complaint, whatever the channel (s.627.01). Acknowledge it in writing with the date received (s.627.43(4)).
**Partners carry the front end:** Much of a digital bank's sales may run through a partner's app. s.627.15 applies to it, so test the partner's consent and complaint flow, not only the bank's own.
pitfalls: **Clock from triage:** Starting the 56-day count only when the right team logs the complaint, rather than when it first arrived.
**'Ombudsman' in the help menu:** Calling internal complaint staff an 'ombudsman', or using a term that suggests independence, breaches s.627.43(2).
**Partner gaps:** A call centre that does not route complaints, or keeps no record of them, leaves the bank exposed under s.627.15(b) and s.627.44.
**Unreviewed content:** Partner or influencer material the bank makes or issues must still be accurate, clear and not misleading (s.627.14).

glossary.definition: The rules in Part XII.2 of the Bank Act and its regulations that govern how a bank deals with customers and the public, including sales conduct, consent, disclosure, cancellation and complaints.
A clear agreement from the customer to a product or service. Using the product does not count as consent (s.627.08(3)).
A time limit set by regulation rather than by the Act itself. For complaints it is 56 days after receipt (SOR-2021-181 s.14).
The window within which a customer may cancel an ongoing agreement, set by s.627.1 or the regulations. Typically 14 or 3 business days.
The body designated under s.627.48 to deal with complaints the bank has not resolved to the customer's satisfaction. Every bank must be a member.
The Commissioner of the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada. The Commissioner judges whether the bank's complaint procedures are satisfactory and examines compliance with the consumer provisions.
A penalty FCAC imposes under the FCAC Act for a designated violation of a consumer provision. It is an administrative process, not a prosecution.
In Part XVI.1, a breach of the Act or its regulations, of a voluntary code or public commitment the bank has adopted, or of a bank policy or procedure (s.979.1).

A personal deposit account (held by natural persons, not for business purposes) opened with a deposit of less than $150,000, or any greater prescribed amount (s.627.01). It has its own cancellation and account-opening rules (s.627.11; s.627.17; SOR-2021-181 s.5).

title: Supervision & enforcement
oneLiner: OSFI supervises continuously, rates each bank, and can reach records a vendor holds for the bank, so vendor contracts must support supervision.
keyPoints: **Continuous supervision:** OSFI examines every bank at least once a year and rates it on risk. The rating sets how closely the bank is watched and where it sits on the intervention stages.

**Ratings:** The [[ORR|Overall Risk Rating (ORR)]] runs from 1 to 8 and measures risk to the bank's viability. A separate Tier Rating reflects size, complexity and impact on the financial system. Both are confidential.

**Powers:** The Bank Act gives OSFI access to records, directions of compliance, prudential agreements, capital and liquidity orders, removal of directors and senior officers, and in the end control of the bank.

**Integrity and security:** Supervision now covers whether the bank protects itself against threats to its integrity and security, including foreign interference. Those expectations reach vendors and their staff.

**Confidentiality:** Ratings, intervention stages, s.485(3) orders, prudential agreements, every direction under s.645, and examination reports and related correspondence are prescribed supervisory information. The bank may share them only with listed recipients. Unaffiliated vendors are not among them. A group affiliate is, but only if it keeps the information confidential.
**Counsel's role:** Keep OSFI informed early, keep vendor contracts aligned with supervisory access, and document every rating-related decision.

conceptMap.caption: The Superintendent's toolkit runs from information and directions to removal of directors and control of the bank. Several tools need notice and a chance to make representations first, including directions, removal and control of the bank.

items.label: The bank's board and auditor
items.note: Prompt notice of substantive issues

items.label: FCAC and FINTRAC
items.note: Separate regimes, same bank

items.label: Records and information
items.note: Includes records held by vendors

deepDive.heading: Continuous, risk-based supervision
deepDive.lede: OSFI rates every bank and adjusts its intensity as the risk picture changes.
points: **Annual examination:** Section 643(1) requires an examination at least once a year. It covers compliance, financial condition and whether the bank has adequate policies against threats to its integrity or security.
**Overall Risk Rating:** The ORR scale runs from 1 to 8. It reflects the level of risk to the bank's viability, and the weakest category is the starting point, subject to supervisory judgment.
**Four categories:** The framework rates business risk, financial resilience, operational resilience and risk governance. Only larger institutions in Tiers 1 to 4 receive category ratings.
**Tier Rating:** A 1 to 5 scale based on size, complexity and impact on the financial system. Tier 1 is high and Tier 5 is low.
**Notice of change:** OSFI communicates ratings privately and writes to the bank whenever a rating changes.

**Hong Kong comparison:** The HKMA rates banks under its CAMEL approach and can act under Banking Ordinance powers such as s.52; OSFI's counterparts are the Overall Risk Rating, the intervention stages and directions under Bank Act s.645.
deepDive.takeaway: A weak operational resilience score can drive the overall rating, so vendor outages are a supervisory matter, not only a commercial one.

deepDive.heading: Intervention stages
deepDive.lede: The Guide to Intervention links the overall rating to a stage and a supervisory response.
points: **Stage 0 (ORR 1–4):** Normal supervision. The bank is resilient and adheres to its integrity and security policies.

**Stage 1 (ORR 5):** OSFI places a bank here when there are warning signs about viability, integrity or security, with no expected impact within two years. Weak integrity policies that are not fixed in time are a typical trigger.

**Stage 2 (ORR 6):** Material concerns, with viability at risk within two years. OSFI may require a third-party monitor for compliance and integrity and security policies, or a third-party expert after major operational disruption.
**Stage 3 (ORR 7):** Severe concerns, with viability threatened within one year. Urgent correction is required, and OSFI may place staff on site.
**Stage 4 (ORR 8):** The statutory conditions for taking control are met or will be met shortly. OSFI can take control, seek a winding-up and report to CDIC.
**Surcharge and letters:** A bank at stage 1 or higher pays an assessment surcharge. Any stage change comes with a formal letter to the chief executive and the board.
deepDive.takeaway: Plan for stage 2 early. A third-party monitor or expert is the realistic escalation for a vendor-driven failure.

items.label: Stage 1: warning signs
items.note: Viability concerns, not expected within two years

items.label: Stage 2: material concerns
items.note: Third-party monitor or expert possible

items.label: Stage 3: severe concerns
items.note: Viability threatened within one year

items.label: Stage 4: take control
items.note: Statutory conditions for taking control

deepDive.heading: Statutory powers
deepDive.lede: The Bank Act powers run from information requests to control of the bank.
points: **Records:** Section 643(2)(a) gives the Superintendent a right of access to records, cash, assets and security held by or on behalf of a bank. That reaches records a vendor holds for the bank.

**Directions:** Section 645(1) lets OSFI direct a bank to stop an unsafe or unsound practice and remedy it. Section 645(1.1) covers inadequate integrity and security policies. A bank must first get a reasonable chance to make representations, unless OSFI makes a temporary direction, effective for up to 15 days, which continues after that period if no representations are made or OSFI does not revoke it.

**Agreements and orders:** A prudential agreement under section 644.1 sets measures to improve safety and soundness. Section 485(3) lets OSFI order more capital or additional liquidity, even where the bank complies with the rules.

**People:** Section 647.1(1) lets OSFI remove a director or senior officer it considers unsuitable. Under section 647, a bank under a direction or capital order must give OSFI nominee names at least 30 days before an appointment.

**Take control:** Section 648 lets OSFI take control of a bank's assets, or of the bank, where the statutory circumstances exist. Control beyond 16 days is possible unless the Minister advises that it is not in the public interest. For a proposed action beyond 16 days, OSFI must notify the bank and allow written representations within at most 10 days.
