deepDive.heading: Confidentiality and vendors
deepDive.lede: Supervisory material is confidential, and an unaffiliated vendor is not an authorized recipient.
points: **OSFI's duty:** Section 636(1) makes information obtained in supervision confidential. Section 636(2) lets OSFI disclose to other regulators and federal bodies for purposes related to financial supervision, including threats to integrity or security, if OSFI is satisfied the information will stay confidential.

**Bank's duty:** Under SOR-2001-59 s.2, a bank must not disclose prescribed supervisory information, which includes its ratings, intervention stage, section 485(3) orders, prudential agreements and directions.

**Permitted recipients:** Section 3 allows disclosure to affiliates, directors, officers, employees, auditors, securities underwriters and legal advisers, if the bank keeps the information confidential.

**Vendors:** Unaffiliated vendors, such as a cloud, core banking or outsourcing provider, are not among the section 3 recipients. A group affiliate is, but only if it keeps the information confidential. Give vendors only the facts they need to do their work, never the rating or the letters.
deepDive.takeaway: Treat every supervisory letter as restricted. Check any investor, partner or vendor update against SOR-2001-59 before it goes out.

deepDive.heading: Other examiners of the same bank
deepDive.lede: OSFI is not the only examiner, and conduct and money laundering have their own regimes.
points: **FCAC:** Section 659(1) requires an examination at least once a year of compliance with the consumer provisions, and section 659(1.1) allows a special audit. The FCAC can also use compliance agreements and directions against banks (s.661 and s.661.1). Section 19(2) of the FCAC Act sets a $10 million maximum penalty for a financial institution per violation.
**Penalty factors:** Under FCAC Act s.20, penalties take account of intention or negligence, harm done, duration, ability to pay and prior violations within five years.
**FINTRAC:** Under PCMLTFA s.62, an authorized person may enter premises, use computer systems and copy records to check compliance. The bank must give reasonable assistance.

**FINTRAC penalties:** PCMLTFA s.73.1 lets regulations classify violations as minor, serious or very serious, with a maximum of $20 million per violation for an entity (and $4 million for a person), and a cumulative cap for a notice of violation of the greater of $20 million and 3% of gross global revenue.

**Coordination:** The Financial Institutions Supervisory Committee brings OSFI, Finance, the Bank of Canada, CDIC, FINTRAC and FCAC together. OSFI copies CDIC on letters and tells CDIC when a bank changes stage.

deepDive.heading: Working with OSFI
deepDive.lede: OSFI expects early notice and an accountable board, so 'no surprises' is the working rule.
points: **Substantive issues:** OSFI expects to be promptly notified of substantive issues affecting the bank. The 2018 Corporate Governance Guideline says so (confirm on OSFI's site that it is still current), and the board must oversee senior management's response.

**Incidents:** OSFI's 2021 advisory expects a technology or cyber incident to be reported in writing within 24 hours, or sooner if possible, to OSFI's Technology Risk Division and the Lead Supervisor, with regular (e.g. daily) updates. Criteria include an impact on a third party that affects the bank, and a disaster declared by a vendor. The advisory is not law. When in doubt, report.
**Foreign interference:** Suspected interference should be promptly detected and reported. OSFI should be informed immediately of any report to CSIS or the RCMP.
**Board duty:** The board is responsible for strategy, risk appetite and oversight of senior management, and should consider regulatory findings when it evaluates them.
deepDive.takeaway: Report early, in writing, with known facts and a plan, and confirm every oral briefing in writing.

provisions.title: Examination of banks
provisions.summary: OSFI must examine each bank at least once a year to check compliance, financial condition and whether the bank has adequate policies against threats to its integrity or security. OSFI has a right of access to records, cash, assets and security held by or on behalf of the bank.
provisions.counselNote: Access extends to records a vendor holds for the bank, so the vendor contract must let OSFI reach them. The integrity and security examination point is the supervisory hook for the vendor programme.

provisions.title: Prudential agreement
provisions.summary: OSFI may enter into a prudential agreement with a bank to implement measures that maintain or improve its safety and soundness, and to set or improve policies against threats to integrity or security.
provisions.counselNote: A prudential agreement often arrives after an examination. Negotiate its deadlines and reporting obligations, and assume vendor remediation will count toward them.

provisions.title: Superintendent’s directions to bank
provisions.summary: OSFI may direct a bank to stop an unsafe or unsound practice and to remedy it, or to take measures to fix inadequate integrity and security policies. A bank must have a reasonable opportunity to make representations, except that OSFI may make a temporary direction, effective for up to 15 days, which continues after that period if no representations are made or OSFI does not revoke it.
provisions.counselNote: A direction binds the bank, and the bank must answer it. Prepare representations quickly and with evidence, because a temporary direction can take effect before the bank has answered.

provisions.title: Removal of directors or senior officers
provisions.summary: OSFI may order the removal of a director or senior officer it considers unsuitable, including for contraventions of the Act or a direction. Section 647 requires a bank subject to a direction under s.645, a s.485(3) order or certain prudential agreements or undertakings to give OSFI the names of nominees and senior officers at least 30 days before the election or appointment (or a shorter period OSFI allows), and within 15 days after electing a director not proposed by management.
provisions.counselNote: Build the nominee notice into board and senior appointment timetables. A removal order can follow from a failure to fix a supervisory finding.

provisions.title: Adequacy of capital and liquidity
provisions.summary: Despite compliance with the regulations, OSFI may order a bank to increase its capital or provide additional liquidity in the forms and amounts it requires. The order sets the form and amount of capital or liquidity that OSFI requires.
provisions.counselNote: A capital or liquidity order can follow a business or operational problem, so tie vendor-driven losses and outages into capital planning and stress testing.

provisions.title: Superintendent may take control
provisions.summary: Where the statutory circumstances exist, including an inability to pay liabilities as they fall due, OSFI may take control of a bank's assets for a limited period or take control of the bank. For a proposed action beyond 16 days, OSFI must notify the bank and allow written representations within at most 10 days.
provisions.counselNote: Take control is the end of the escalation ladder. Keep the vendor and resolution plans current, because control and resolution planning depend on access to records and services.

provisions.title: Confidential information
provisions.summary: Information about a bank's business that OSFI obtains in administering the federal financial statutes is confidential. OSFI may disclose it to listed regulators and government bodies, including for purposes related to threats to integrity or security.
provisions.counselNote: This is OSFI's own duty. It does not bind the bank or its vendors, so the bank must impose its own confidentiality terms on anyone who receives supervisory material.

provisions.title: Prescribed Supervisory Information
provisions.summary: Section 1 lists the ratings, intervention stages, section 485(3) orders, prudential agreements, directions, examination reports, recommendations and related correspondence, and the CDIC differential premium category that are prescribed supervisory information. Section 2 bars the bank from disclosing them, and section 3 lists the recipients who may receive them if they keep them confidential.
provisions.counselNote: Map every disclosure of rating-related material to section 3. Unaffiliated vendors, investors and partners are not on that list, so they should not receive ratings or letters.

provisions.title: Examination of banks
provisions.summary: The FCAC Commissioner must examine each bank at least once a year to confirm compliance with the consumer provisions, and may direct a special audit for the purposes of the FCAC Act and those provisions.
provisions.counselNote: The examination is of compliance with the consumer provisions, and sales and complaint handling by the bank and its partners are the likely focus under the consumer provisions. Keep records of each sales channel a vendor or partner runs.

provisions.instrument: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act
provisions.title: To ensure compliance
provisions.summary: An authorized person may examine a reporting entity's records and business to check compliance with Part 1 or 1.1. The person may enter premises, use computer systems, reproduce records and copy them, and the entity must give reasonable assistance.
provisions.counselNote: FINTRAC examiners can ask for records held by a vendor or agent. Make sure the contract gives the bank a way to produce those records during a FINTRAC visit.

provisions.ref: ORR, Tier Rating and risk categories
provisions.title: OSFI Supervisory Framework
provisions.summary: Describes how OSFI supervises institutions. It sets an Overall Risk Rating from 1 to 8, a Tier Rating from 1 to 5, and category ratings for larger institutions. Intensity of supervision follows from those ratings. The page was modified in May 2026.
provisions.counselNote: OSFI expects this framework to drive the bank's supervisory dealings. Check the current text before quoting ratings, because the framework’s effective date and category rules may have changed.

provisions.instrument: OSFI Guide to Intervention for Federally Regulated Deposit-Taking Institutions
provisions.title: Guide to Intervention (stages 0 to 4)
provisions.summary: Maps the Overall Risk Rating to intervention stages 0 to 4, describes the supervisory response at each stage and lists OSFI's legal powers. The guide is flexible, and OSFI may intervene earlier or later and with different tools.
provisions.counselNote: The stage is the single most important signal for a vendor-driven problem. Know the stage 2 tools, such as a third-party monitor, before a finding arrives.

provisions.instrument: OSFI Guideline B-10, Third-Party Risk Management
provisions.title: Third-Party Risk Management Guideline (B-10)
provisions.summary: B-10 expects the bank and OSFI to be able to evaluate a third party's risk management practices, or to appoint independent auditors to do so, and to access audit reports on the service (s.2.3.3.3). OSFI's supervisory powers should not be constrained however an activity is sourced (Overview).
provisions.counselNote: Write the B-10 evaluation and audit rights into the vendor contract, and do not let its terms limit OSFI's access.

checklist: **Build supervisory access into every vendor contract:** Include OSFI's right of access to records and systems held for the bank, under section 643(2), and the bank's own right to produce them quickly.
**Give evaluation rights over vendors:** Give the bank and OSFI evaluation rights over the vendor, including through independent auditors (B-10 s.2.3.3.3), and do not limit OSFI's supervisory powers.
**Keep a supervisory correspondence log:** Route every OSFI letter, direction and request through one named owner, with deadlines diarised from the date of receipt.
**Prepare integrity and security evidence:** Keep current policies, threat assessments and vendor due-diligence records ready for the annual examination under section 643(1).

**Restrict prescribed supervisory information:** Limit ratings, stages and directions to the section 3 recipients of SOR-2001-59, and check every investor or partner update against it. SOR-2001-59 section 4 allows disclosure of orders, prudential agreements and directions only where securities law requires disclosure of a material fact or change. Take securities counsel's advice before relying on it.

**Plan the notice path for directions:** Know who answers a section 645 direction, how representations are prepared, and how a temporary direction is handled, including whether it continues after 15 days if it is not revoked.

**Set nominee and board timetables:** Track the section 647 nominee notice for a bank subject to a direction, a section 485(3) order or certain prudential agreements: names are due 30 days before an election or appointment (or a shorter period OSFI allows), and within 15 days after electing a director not proposed by management.

**Map consumer and AML examinations:** Identify which vendors and agents touch sales, complaints and identity verification, and what records FCAC and FINTRAC could request under section 659 and PCMLTFA section 62.
**Test the escalation playbook:** Run a tabletop exercise for a stage 1 or stage 2 scenario caused by a vendor failure, and record the decisions and the notices sent.
itAngle: **Records access:** Section 643(2) reaches data held for the bank in the cloud or by a processor. Design retrieval, logs and exports so that OSFI's access is practical, not theoretical.
**Examination evidence:** Examinations look at policy, configuration and access evidence. Keep system records of access, changes and testing in a form that can be produced quickly.
**Threat monitoring:** Integrity and security expectations cover vendor access to bank data and systems. Monitor privileged vendor access, and record suspected interference for OSFI reporting.

**Stage-readiness metrics:** Track the operational indicators that feed the Overall Risk Rating, such as outages, incident counts and recovery times, so that the bank sees a stage 1 trigger before OSFI does.
virtualBankNotes: **Vendor records are bank records:** A digital bank's core and cloud data sits with vendors. Section 643(2) gives OSFI access to it, so the bank's architecture must allow OSFI to reach that data.

**Stage risk is concentrated:** With few branches and heavy reliance on a small number of providers, a single vendor failure can drive an operational resilience concern. Expect OSFI to ask about concentration.

**Stage changes reach the board:** Each stage change comes with a formal letter to the chief executive and the board, and OSFI meets the board and often the auditor. Keep the board papers aligned with what the vendors actually deliver.

**Fintech partners see less:** Partners that promote the bank's products need the consumer-facing rules and must not receive ratings or letters. The bank's supervisory picture stays inside the bank and its listed recipients.
pitfalls: **Sharing ratings:** Giving a vendor, partner or investor the rating, stage or a supervisory letter, which SOR-2001-59 section 2 prohibits.
**Contracts that limit OSFI:** Terms that restrict OSFI's access to records or its audit rights, which OSFI expects to be unconstrained.
**Late incident notice:** Waiting for a vendor's root-cause report before telling OSFI, when the expectation is a written report within 24 hours.
**Ignoring a direction clock:** Treating a section 645 direction as correspondence, and missing the representation window or the time limits in the direction.

glossary.definition: OSFI's 1 to 8 assessment of the risk to a bank's viability, starting from the weakest category and subject to supervisory judgment. It maps to intervention stages 0 to 4.
OSFI's 1 to 5 rating of a bank based on its size, complexity and impact on the financial system. It helps set how much supervision the bank receives.
The OSFI and CDIC guide that maps the Overall Risk Rating to stages 0 to 4 and describes the supervisory response at each stage. It is a guide, not binding.
An additional fee OSFI levies on a bank rated at stage 1 or higher, on top of its normal assessment.

A direction under Bank Act section 645 to stop an unsafe or unsound practice, or to fix inadequate integrity and security policies, after a chance to make representations, or as a temporary direction effective for up to 15 days that continues after that period if no representations are made or OSFI does not revoke it.

Ratings, intervention stages, section 485(3) orders, prudential agreements, directions, examination reports, recommendations and related correspondence, and the CDIC differential premium category that a bank must not disclose except to the recipients listed in SOR-2001-59 section 3.
OSFI's power under Bank Act section 648 to take control of a bank's assets, or of the bank, where the statutory circumstances exist. It sits at stage 4.
An independent party that OSFI may require a bank to appoint at stage 2 to check compliance, including its integrity and security policies.

title: Recovery & resolution
oneLiner: Resolution decides whether deposits, data and vendor services keep running when a bank fails, so vendor contracts must work under a CDIC order.
keyPoints: **Escalation:** OSFI's Guide to Intervention moves a bank through stages 0 to 4 as its risk rating worsens. Stage 4 is where the statutory conditions for taking control are met, or are about to be met.

**Taking control:** Bank Act s.648 lets the Superintendent take control of a bank's assets, or of the bank itself, on listed circumstances. For control beyond sixteen days, or control of the bank itself, the bank must first get notice and up to ten days to respond (s.648(1.2)).

**CDIC orders:** after a report from the Superintendent, the Governor in Council may vest shares in CDIC, appoint it receiver, direct the creation of a bridge institution or order a conversion (CDIC Act s.39.13).
**Stay:** once a CDIC order is made, no person may end or amend an agreement with the bank, or accelerate it, by reason only of the listed triggers. Contrary terms have no force or effect (s.39.15).
**Payout:** the bank must produce depositor data and stop withdrawals within tight deadlines, so data held by vendors sits on the critical path (Data and System Requirements By-law s.2).
**Vendors:** agreements should stay enforceable in resolution, return data in a usable form and not inhibit OSFI, a resolution authority or a compensation scheme (B-10 Annex 2, item 12).

conceptMap.caption: A CDIC order starts a set of steps that end in a sale, a bridge or a payout. The stay limits what counterparties can do while they run.

centre.note: Made by the Governor in Council

deepDive.heading: OSFI's escalation to stage 4
deepDive.lede: Resolution starts well before a CDIC order, with OSFI's supervisory ratings.

visual.caption: Stage numbers match across OSFI's documents. The labels for ORR 5 and ORR 8 differ, so cite the stage number.

items.label: Stage 1
items.note: Warning signs of safety and soundness concerns

items.label: Stage 2
items.note: Viability at risk within two years if unaddressed

items.label: Stage 3
items.note: Viability threatened within one year

items.label: Stage 4
items.note: Statutory conditions for taking control met or near

points: **Guide to Intervention:** the guide maps the Overall Risk Rating (ORR, 1 to 8) to intervention stages 0 to 4. It is a guide, not law, and OSFI may intervene earlier or later than the stages suggest.
**Stage changes:** OSFI sends a formal letter to the chief executive and the board on any stage change. Banks at stage 1 or higher pay an assessment surcharge.
**Stage 4 powers:** the guide lists taking control, requesting a winding-up order, reporting to CDIC and triggering conversion of non-viability contingent capital.
**Integrity and security:** both OSFI's framework and the guide treat integrity and security as ratable risks. A vendor breach or a foreign-interference concern can move a bank up the ratings.

**Confidentiality:** the bank must keep its ratings and stage confidential. Do not share them with vendors, who are not on the list of permitted recipients (see stage 12, supervision). (Supervisory Information (Banks) Regulations, SOR-2001-59, ss.1 to 3.)
deepDive.takeaway: By stage 3 or 4 the options are narrow, so vendor exit and continuity terms must be settled while the bank is still at stage 0.

deepDive.heading: Taking control under the Bank Act
deepDive.lede: The Superintendent can take control of a bank before CDIC is involved.
points: **Power:** Bank Act s.648(1) lets the Superintendent take control of a bank's assets for up to sixteen days. Longer control, or control of the bank itself, needs the Minister not to advise against it on public-interest grounds.

**Triggers:** s.648(1.1) lists the circumstances. They include failure to pay liabilities as they fall due, assets too thin to protect depositors and creditors, eroding regulatory capital and CDIC terminating deposit insurance.
**Integrity and security:** s.648(1.1)(i) also covers continued operation by the directors or officers being materially prejudicial to the bank's integrity or security.

**Notice:** before acting under paragraph (1)(b), the Superintendent must notify the bank of the proposed action. The bank may make written representations within a period of up to ten days (s.648(1.2)).
**Scope:** control reaches the bank's assets and the assets under its administration. Systems and records held by vendors for the bank are part of that analysis, so map them.
deepDive.takeaway: Section 648 deals with the bank's assets and control. It does not, by itself, stop a vendor from ending its contract.

deepDive.heading: CDIC's path to an order and its tools
deepDive.lede: CDIC acts on the Superintendent's report, and the Governor in Council makes the orders.

visual.caption: The orders in s.39.13(1), from share vesting to conversion. Each carries different limits.

items.label: Vest shares
items.note: Specified shares and subordinated debt go to CDIC

items.label: Receivership
items.note: CDIC becomes receiver and may sell or assume liabilities

items.label: Bridge institution
items.note: Needs a receivership order first (s.39.13(1.1))

items.label: Conversion
items.note: D-SIBs only, after a vesting or receivership order

points: **Sequence:** the Superintendent reports to CDIC after giving the bank a reasonable chance to make representations (s.39.1). CDIC may then ask the Minister to recommend orders (s.39.11).

**Bridge:** a bridge institution is designated for two years. The Governor in Council may extend that by up to three extensions of one year each (s.39.3711). It must assume insured deposits posted in the bank's records as of the date and time in the order (s.39.202(1)); items not yet posted are deemed moved to it (s.39.202(1.2)).

**Restructuring:** CDIC as receiver may sell or dispose of assets, have another person assume liabilities or restructure the business (s.39.2(2)). A CDIC receiver transaction with a bridge institution needs no Minister or Superintendent approval that would otherwise apply (s.39.2(2.1)).
**Other tools:** CDIC can also arrange an assisted transaction, use its FIRP powers to complete a sale or restructuring, or give financial assistance (CDIC Act s.10; reported; check).
**Assumption of liabilities:** a person who assumes a bank's liability under such a transaction becomes liable in place of the bank, on ministerial approval where one is needed (s.39.2(6)).
**Vendors:** a bridge or buyer may take over vendor contracts. Assignment and change-of-control clauses must allow that without a fresh negotiation.
deepDive.takeaway: Each tool moves the bank's business somewhere else. Vendor contracts must follow the business, not the legal entity that signed them.

deepDive.heading: The stay on vendor contracts
deepDive.lede: The CDIC stay limits what counterparties may do once an order is made.
points: **Scope:** after an order under s.39.13(1), no person may end or amend an agreement with the bank, or accelerate it, by reason only of the listed triggers (s.39.15(1)(e)).

**Listed triggers:** insolvency or weaker finances, pre-order non-monetary defaults, and pre-order monetary defaults remedied within 60 days after the order, the order itself or a related change of control, and assignment or transfer to a bridge or third party.
**Void terms:** a term that would let a counterparty cut the bank's rights to use its assets on those triggers has no force or effect (s.39.15(2)(b)).

**Limits:** the stay does not stop termination for a default after the order. A provider may demand cash for post-order services (s.39.15(5)(a)), and need not advance money or credit after the order (s.39.15(5)(b)).

**Assignment:** s.39.152 applies similar protection when an agreement is assigned to a bridge institution or a third party. Subsection (2) excludes eligible financial contracts from the non-monetary default and 60-day monetary default limbs (s.39.152(2)).
**Compared with Hong Kong:** like FIRO, the CDIC Act overrides termination rights in a resolution, but only once an order under s.39.13(1) is made (s.39.15(1)).
deepDive.takeaway: A vendor cannot end the contract only because the bank failed or was placed under a CDIC order. It can still end the contract for an unremedied post-order default, so draft for that.

deepDive.heading: Continuity and the payout clock
deepDive.lede: Deposit insurance depends on the bank's data and systems, which vendors often run.

visual.caption: Deadlines run from CDIC's instruction or from the determination time. The times come from the by-law and CDIC's guidance.

items.label: Withdrawal hold
items.note: After CDIC's instruction (DSR By-law s.2(1)(b))

items.label: Standardized data
items.note: Or 4:00 p.m. the next day, if earlier (s.2(2)(a)(i))

items.label: Interest data
items.note: Or 4:00 p.m. on day 2, if earlier (s.2(2)(b))

items.label: Depositor access
items.note: CDIC's aim under its guidance, not a by-law limit

points: **Data:** a member must be able to produce depositor data as of the determination time, grouped by depositor, insurance eligibility, insurance category and account type (By-law s.2(1)(a)).
**Withdrawals:** the bank must be able to stop withdrawals by account type within six hours of CDIC's instruction (s.2(1)(b)).
**Format:** CDIC's technical requirements describe pipe-delimited Unicode text files sent over a secure channel (reported from the requirements document; check the current version).
**Vendors:** CDIC's guidance asks members to list third-party vendors in the data process, the server and backup locations, and recovery objectives. Certification is annual (reported; check).
deepDive.takeaway: If a vendor cannot produce deposit data or stop withdrawals within these hours, the bank cannot meet its CDIC obligations, whatever its capital position.

deepDive.heading: Recovery and resolution planning
deepDive.lede: Recovery planning is the bank's own task. Resolution planning under CDIC's framework applies to the largest banks.
points: **Recovery plans:** the Guide to Intervention says OSFI reviews recovery plans for systemically important institutions (stage 0). Whether a digital bank will be treated that way is for OSFI to decide; check.

**D-SIB resolution plans:** CDIC's page says each domestic systemically important bank (D-SIB) must prepare a resolution plan. CDIC assesses it against four objectives: protecting eligible deposits, maintaining critical services, protecting the economy and minimizing risk to taxpayers (reported; check).

**Bail-in:** CDIC's page says conversion reaches certain senior unsecured debt and some preferred and subordinated instruments, while ordinary deposits and GICs are not affected (reported; check). A conversion order is available for a D-SIB only (s.39.13(1.2)).
**Designation:** a new digital bank is not among the six D-SIBs named on CDIC's page. Check OSFI's current designation list before assuming it stays outside that group.
deepDive.takeaway: Ask early whether OSFI or CDIC would expect a recovery or resolution plan from the bank, and collect vendor data for it now.

provisions.title: Superintendent may take control
provisions.summary: Lets the Superintendent take control of a bank's assets for up to sixteen days, and longer or control of the bank itself in listed cases, unless the Minister advises that this is not in the public interest. The circumstances include failure to pay liabilities and eroding capital. The bank must get notice of the proposed action.
provisions.counselNote: Control reaches the bank's assets and the assets under its administration. Keep a current list of which vendors hold records or systems the bank needs, so the bank can respond to a notice.

provisions.title: Order
provisions.summary: The Superintendent reports a non-viable federal member institution to CDIC after giving it a chance to make representations. CDIC may then ask the Minister to recommend orders. The Governor in Council may vest shares in CDIC, appoint it receiver, direct a bridge institution or order a conversion, the last only for a D-SIB.
provisions.counselNote: The sequence runs from OSFI to CDIC to the Minister. Map which vendor systems each step needs, because the data requests come quickly once an order is made.

provisions.title: Stay of proceedings
provisions.summary: After a CDIC order, creditors cannot enforce against the bank. No one may end or amend an agreement with the bank, or accelerate it, by reason only of listed triggers, including insolvency, pre-order non-monetary defaults, and pre-order monetary defaults remedied within 60 days after the order, the order and assignment to a bridge. Contrary terms have no force or effect.
provisions.counselNote: Draft as if the stay is narrow. It does not stop termination for a post-order default. The cash-payment point in subsection (5)(a) is reported; check the current text.

provisions.title: Restructuring transactions
provisions.summary: Lets CDIC as receiver sell or dispose of assets, have another person assume liabilities or restructure the business. Some transactions with a bridge institution are excepted from approvals that would otherwise apply. A person who assumes a liability becomes liable in place of the bank, on approval where one is needed.
provisions.counselNote: A vendor contract can pass to a buyer or bridge with the business. Check the assignment and change-of-control clauses to confirm they allow it without a new negotiation.

provisions.title: Assignments to a bridge institution or third party
provisions.summary: Once an agreement is assigned or assumed by a bridge institution or a third party, it cannot be terminated or accelerated on the same grounds as the stay, subject to the exceptions in subsection (2).
provisions.counselNote: Subsection (2) excludes eligible financial contracts from the non-monetary default and 60-day monetary default limbs in subsection (1)(a)(iii) and (iv), so check whether a vendor contract is caught.

provisions.title: Deposit liabilities assumed
provisions.summary: A bridge institution must assume the bank's insured deposit liabilities as of the time in the order. Deposits and withdrawals made on or before that time but not yet posted are treated as made with the bridge institution.
provisions.counselNote: The cut-off position depends on the bank's ledger and transaction logs. Confirm with core banking vendors how they record posting times, so the cut-off can be reproduced.

provisions.title: Duration
provisions.summary: A bridge institution is designated for two years. The Governor in Council may extend the designation by up to three extensions of one year each, on the Minister's recommendation.
provisions.counselNote: The bridge is temporary. Vendor contracts assigned to it should run past the designation period, or include a path to re-contract with the buyer.

provisions.instrument: Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Data and System Requirements By-law
provisions.title: Capabilities
provisions.summary: Members must be able to produce depositor data as of the determination time, to stop withdrawals by account type within six hours of CDIC's instruction, and to deliver the data by the earlier of six hours after the determination time and 4:00 p.m. the day after the determination date.
provisions.counselNote: Vendors that hold deposit ledgers and contact data are on the critical path. Test the extract with them. The timing limits are in s.2(2)(a) and (b) of the by-law.

provisions.instrument: OSFI Guideline B-10, Third-Party Risk Management Guideline
provisions.title: Provisions for third-party agreements: default and termination
provisions.summary: For high-risk and critical arrangements, the agreement should cover default, termination, cure, return of data and records in a usable format, and survival. It should not inhibit OSFI, a resolution authority or a compensation scheme in stress or resolution, and should stay enforceable in resolution where payments are not in default.
provisions.counselNote: This is the drafting anchor for the vendor clauses in stage 5. OSFI expects it, but it is a guideline, not law.

provisions.instrument: OSFI Guideline B-10, Third-Party Risk Management Guideline
provisions.title: Exit strategies and plans
provisions.summary: For critical and high-risk arrangements, OSFI expects defined exit triggers, stressed and non-stressed exit playbooks, supporting contract provisions and regular review. Scenarios should be severe but plausible.
provisions.counselNote: An exit plan that has never been tested is weak evidence. For core banking and cloud arrangements, record the exit steps and the data needed to carry them out.

provisions.instrument: Guide to Intervention for Federally Regulated Deposit-Taking Institutions, issued jointly by OSFI and CDIC
provisions.title: Guide to Intervention
provisions.summary: Maps the Overall Risk Rating to intervention stages 0 to 4. Stage 4 is where the statutory conditions for taking control are met or about to be met. Its powers include taking control and triggering conversion of non-viability contingent capital. The guide is not binding.
provisions.counselNote: OSFI's page gives the issue and effective dates; confirm them there before citing the guide. Documents OSFI will ask for at stages 3 and 4, such as vendor exit plans and data return terms, should already exist.

provisions.instrument: CDIC web page, resolution of large banks
provisions.title: Resolution of large banks
provisions.summary: Says each D-SIB must prepare a resolution plan, assessed against four objectives. It also describes the bail-in scope and states that ordinary deposits and GICs are not affected. The page does not give a statutory source for the plans (reported).
provisions.counselNote: A digital bank that grows toward D-SIB status would need vendor data for its resolution plan. Confirm the current designation criteria with OSFI before planning on that basis.

checklist: **Map the critical operations:** list each vendor that supports deposits, payments, records, the app and the CDIC data file, with its role and location.
**Put survival language in every critical contract:** the agreement should stay enforceable in resolution where payments are current (B-10 Annex 2, item 12).
**Add a no-inhibition clause:** the agreement must not stop OSFI, a resolution authority or a compensation scheme from acting in stress or resolution.
**Require data return:** on termination, deposit and transaction data must come back in a usable format, without unreasonable expense.
**Test a point-in-time extract:** run a depositor data extract, including vendor-held data, against the six-hour and 4:00 p.m. limits.
**Confirm the withdrawal hold:** confirm that the bank and each relevant vendor can stop withdrawals by account type within six hours of CDIC's instruction.
**Check the stay against each contract:** after an order, list which termination grounds the stay blocks and which remain open, such as a post-order default.
**Plan the bridge path:** confirm each critical contract can be assigned to a bridge institution or buyer, and that consents do not block the transfer.
itAngle: **Continuity path:** the ledger, core banking and deposit data store must run on a buyer's or bridge's systems, or be extractable. Test that path, not only the primary cloud region.
**Point-in-time data:** a depositor extract as of the determination time is a system capability. Build it, test it and record who can run it, including interest accrued.
**Withdrawal controls:** a hold by account type is a control the platform must support. Test it end to end, including the app and any payment partners.
**Recovery objectives:** record backup locations, recovery time and recovery point objectives for deposit data, and align them with B-13's disaster recovery expectations.
virtualBankNotes: **No branches to fall back on:** deposits, records and customer contact all run through the app and vendors, so resolution-day continuity depends on them.

**Depositor messages:** prepare app messages for a withdrawal hold in advance. CDIC treats saying deposits are 'insured' or 'covered' as misleading and suggests 'eligible for deposit insurance' instead (reported from CDIC's bulletin; check).

**Sale or bridge:** pre-existing deposits stay insured on the same basis after a sale to another member. Review the app and CDIC symbol messaging for the new entity (reported from CDIC's pages; check).
**Exit planning:** a digital bank with one core or cloud provider should test the move to a second provider, as B-10's exit expectations assume.
pitfalls: **Assuming the stay covers everything:** it protects only the listed triggers. It does not stop a post-order default or a provider's refusal to extend credit.
**Relying on one cloud:** an outage or insolvency at one provider can stop deposit data and withdrawals at the same time.
**Vague survival clauses:** a clause saying the contract survives termination, with no data, continuity or access terms, gives little real protection.
**Sharing supervisory status:** telling a vendor the bank's OSFI stage or CDIC correspondence may breach the rules on prescribed supervisory information.

glossary.definition: A federal institution that CDIC causes to be created under a s.39.13(1)(c) order, to take over a failed bank's insured deposits and business. It is designated for two years, extendable under s.39.3711.
The conversion of certain bank debt and shares into common shares under a CDIC order. CDIC's page says it applies to D-SIBs and does not affect ordinary deposits (reported; check).
A domestic systemically important bank. OSFI designates these. CDIC's page names six. The status brings resolution planning and conversion powers.
The point at which CDIC measures a bank's deposit liabilities for a payout, under the Data and System Requirements By-law. Data about those liabilities is due within a set time after it.
The bank's own plan for restoring viability in a stress. OSFI reviews these for systemically important institutions, according to the Guide to Intervention.
A person appointed to take control of a failing bank's assets and business. Under s.39.13(1)(b), CDIC may be appointed receiver, with power to sell assets and arrange assumption of liabilities.
The statutory freeze under CDIC Act s.39.15 on creditor action, and on termination of agreements for listed reasons, once a CDIC order is made.
The Superintendent's power under Bank Act s.648 to take control of a bank's assets or of the bank. The guide links it to stage 4.
An order under CDIC Act s.39.13(1)(a) that transfers a bank's specified shares and subordinated debt to CDIC, free of most adverse claims (s.39.13(2)).
